And Muhammad Mustafa, may God bless him and his family and grant peace, and his noble and generous descendants — blessed is he who follows after me; whoever holds fast to them after me shall be guided.

The Mahdi is the best of all creation, the true Messenger, and the Seal of the Prophets and Messengers. The purpose is the guidance and calling of both mankind and jinn, and the completion of all religions and faiths, bringing blessings to every soul. There shall be resurrection, the reckoning, the fruits of Paradise and Hell, the Bridge, and the Scale, just as the Messenger gave glad tidings of what God willed, and nothing else. Faith in its outward form is beneficial, and true faith in reality is sincere. It must be devoid of doubt and negligence, purely devoted and genuine. Complete faith and wholehearted belief require that one follow all outward and inward commands, obeying what is commanded and avoiding what is prohibited, just as the Messenger made clear in the religious law, and the scholars and leaders of the faith have confirmed this. It is recorded in the books of jurisprudence in the chapters of religious law and legal schools that whoever holds fast to the testimony "There is no god but God" — faith is established in the heart, filling it completely. Those who walk this path, with God's grace, will find benefit and guidance. "Those who are faithful to their trust and their covenants" — and the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "There is no faith for one who has no trustworthiness, and no religion for one who keeps not his covenant." And he said: "Whoever loves for the sake of God, withholds for the sake of God, gives for the sake of God, and refuses for the sake of God has perfected faith." And for sixty-some years during the period of prophethood, revelations descended, events unfolded, and religious reports multiplied — the traditions of this community of Muhammad in the religion of Islam became many. A detailed account is recorded in the books of jurisprudence. Those who follow their own desires and passions are on the path of misguidance, bound by the devil, who is your manifest enemy. They are of little worth. The people of guidance, argument, and proof are established. "Worship God; this is the straight path." And the noble Messenger has commanded: do not deviate from it.

[Margin: Guidance]

One of you — until his heart is upright, his heart cannot be upright until his tongue is upright, and his tongue cannot be upright until his deeds are upright. The uprightness of deeds depends on the correspondence with scholars, and every effort should be spent in that regard.

In the existence of a person, through the inner blood and the roots of the pillars of Islam and the roots of prayer — the slain ones of God have been made foremost in one path, those of the people of idols who sought from Ash'ab, and the four schools: the Sunni, and the Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki, and Hanbali have come — if one recites in a loud voice it is supported. The Shi'a consider the people of the four Sunni schools as hypocrites and Kharijites and Nasibis; similarly the Sunni scholars consider the Shi'a unreliable, but both groups have gone to extremes, the greatest of which is prejudice. The Prophet (peace be upon him) forbade fanaticism, and it is wondrous that in Islam people rush into the world fighting one another through jihad, and have laid waste to all, pulling people into marriage contracts unlawfully.

Regarding them it has been said: "We ask of you no reward except love for our near ones" — and those who profess "There is no god but God," the scholars and the noble ones — the school of the Sunnis is the Shafi'i-Muttalib school, as the lover of the people of the foundation composed verse, and al-Shafi'i said in his poem: "If loving the family of the Prophet is Rafdh, then let the two weighty ones bear witness that I am indeed a Rafidhi." For this reason, from the bond formed in Egypt, he was won over, and commanders came and went, and love for the household and their descendants is not remote from the Sunnis, and by proof: "I ask of you no wage except love for the near of kin" — and the Master of the faithful of the religion — those who draw near.

"Come, whoever considers me an opponent: those who seek the way have no such business to do with me. The seal of the Prophet's hand in the inscription of pride is no honor: for flattery in abundance means the lines of consideration mean nothing." He who is among the devoted ones in the treasury of this school of the faithful — the poor one, the son of Qutur, it is witnessed for the Master of Hind: in his heart is the love of the descendants of Mustafa. "I sought that the happy and Adam's children be befriended, and that the lover of Ahmad be given priority." "I am a Rafidhi among all the people of the world, and above him the Sunnis and the companions of the Kharijites stand."

I am not restrained by what is external, nor do I hold back from the origin of things: some people are generous to the living.
Knowledge and practice together do not suffice: those who seek the people of hellfire are the true companions.
Since the Shia sect is established in submission: do not count among us the name of one who bears the title of Khadiji.
To illuminate the soul by spreading knowledge: blame falls on what is denied and deficiency is seen in what remains.
Do not act on mere supposition, do not make it obligatory: this is the sect's foundation — O Lord, bestow Your grace upon all creation.
Based on the belief of the noble: the morals of al-Nasiri were such that no description can encompass them.
The people of Rum are predominantly sincere: purified are those who, through hardship, remain in inviolability.
And purity and integrity in the house of Islam, devoted sincerely to the love of God, remembering Him and holding fast to it.
And hypocrisy, laziness, and their like, and accumulating them — all effort is thrown to the winds in such a state.
Whoever truly seeks the next world by sowing goodness, and meeting the honorable with cutting off passion and turning away from lust.
God's word came: "They were not commanded except to worship God, making religion sincerely His."
And God Most High said: "He will grant them their good deeds and will give them from His presence a great reward."
The elders said: sincerity, purity of conduct, and guarding oneself from vain pursuits.
That secret arrives at one who obeys, seeking closeness to God, who knows and acts accordingly.
One who is righteous gains benefit through pure obedience, and the reward of God Most High does not fail those who strive.
When one reaches this station, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever purifies himself and sincerely follows the Messenger..."
The worshippers' community: only those who act. And the doers are only those who act with sincerity.
And the workers' community: only those who are sincere. But the sincere face a great peril — namely, proper Conduct (Adab).
To regard oneself and others with mercy and reverence, to strive with people sincerely, and to speak well:
If you hear from them benefits regarding sins, raise your sight and improve your vision.
It would be good to say with God Most High: "My Lord brought me near with good calling — and the best of grace lies in proper Conduct."

And lineage (nasab) — one who does not seek it in the proper manner will not attain nobility through it. It has come in the words of the wise: "Adab (culture/refinement) is what is feared for it and for excellence, or for the intellect, not for origins and lineage, for one who loses adab loses his lineage." The framework of adab is a means to every virtue, an elevation to every noble rank, accepted from all who practice the crafts of refinement. And among the sayings of the wise: "Adab is in the form of the intellect, and the sense of everything." Learn from every source.
One reads: when fate is agreeable, the image of a person emerges from a drop of water — clear and bright, lasting as long as stone endures; but one without intellect and adab — his true nature is not fit to be called human, and those who travel among the Arabs say: "Knowledge comes from purity and clarity."
"Adab benefits the young in time of leisure, but after old age it profits little — it is wasted."
Concealment of faults and practice of the art is something that serves, whether one is young or old; if it does benefit, it covers as a canopy covers, and the free remain young. It keeps away those who are strangers and shields the children of families and turns away women.
The Prophet, peace be upon him, and the Commander of the Faithful said: "The believer is the mirror of the believer, showing what he sees in his brother." And in the book of the Wise it is said: "The hearts of the rational are fortresses against the wicked." The poet says:
"He does not speak — every year when two come together he remains silent." And regarding secrets:
A friend who is dear keeps the secret of the heart; a good friend does too.
The noble man and the seeker say: with a friend, the silence of one who has heard is permission — the trust is established, and one fulfills it day by day, giving two or three lessons.
It is said that 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said: "The finest of people is one who humbles himself below his station and is just above it." From the words attributed to al-Masih (Jesus), peace be upon him:
A man said to him: "I saw the Prophet Yahya (John), the master." He said: "And I saw the master." He said: "And I saw the master healed the blind and the leper," and so he said.

He said: "I shaped forms from clay in the likeness of birds, then breathed into them, and they became birds." He said: "Yes." He said: "I have a need—" The most honored among men is one who is not [proud]. As for the Messiah, peace be upon him, he overcame [his opponents] with knowledge and proof. Kindnesses were multiplied. Dirham by dirham were the categories of gifts counted, the desires [were measured], and one maintained balance, bringing together on every side what was due. Each person found it easy by nature to understand and follow [the path of] kindness, doubling [goodness]. The Arabs said: "Be just, even if it costs you thousands." Doing good is the remembrance of those with pure hearts and tongues, removing [ill] from the mines [of character] and abstaining from exposing secrets. Speaking truth, they narrated [reports] and called to goodness and strength. They said: "Help one another in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression." The interpreters have explained: remembering righteousness and piety is knowing God's contentment and seeking the pleasure of His creation—to be blessed companions of the Prophet. "There is nothing like righteousness for lengthening life," and 'Umar said: "Righteousness increases one's lifespan." And Jesus son of Mary said: "Righteousness has three parts: speech, sight, and silence. Whoever speaks of other than reflection [of truth] has harmed himself; whoever looks not with contemplation has gone astray; and whoever is silent for other than humility has harmed himself." Among the sayings of the wise: harm to the community and to life is one who acts [badly], and righteousness is a fine path. The Arab poets said: "Goodness returns to the one who does good—let your goodness be your companion." Righteousness increases life. Among the sayings of the Commander of the Faithful: "Righteousness frees the slave." Shaykh Sa'di said: "Love—choose good companions, and kindness will come to you." Choose good companions, for proven virtue illuminates the heart of the world. Mix with people of sound religion, associate with the pious, obey religion.

By God, and in accordance with the way of Mustafa, they arrived, and the son was present at the arrival.
Then near the lips and in the heart, the goal of annihilation was found, and truly the presence of the Exalted is wondrous.
The Prophet said: "The best thing in a man's Islam is that he abandons what does not concern him." And Ali said: "Truly the friends of God Most High have no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve." Those who looked at the inner reality of the world, when people looked only at its outward form — how magnificent and yet how fearful it is!
So fear that your hearts may die, for "Work, for you are warned" — those who are like mirrors, increasing and diminishing.
Withdrawal from people is the best path. And the Prophet said: "Whoever lives long in Islam will find safety, though the sorrows of old age will befall him." So the crow — let it seek the beloved, calling out to it, bringing it pain and suffering.
The heart's desire and the joy of sorrow and the gift of life — whoever's heart does not know the remembrance of God is lost. The Muslim who truly knows God Most High — the ancients turned away from worldly ambitions and kept their hearts open to the unseen, and if they found conformity with the nature of things in outward forms and meanings, God Most High was not absent from their hearts.
And the one who submits his heart to the All-Knowing — from the perspective of his own benefit — and in speech, it is said that the believer does not complain, because the complaints of calamities and the turning of people away from contentment are a gift of God. And peace is like the one who is cast aside, and after mentioning all that, we return to Ahmad Hijazi, who said: "Al-Munfa'i — do not do any useless thing."
Know that what comes to you by destiny — even if it passes away and disappears — will return. And if it departed and came back, that is what matters. So do not waste yourself on useless endeavors. Al-Munfa'i: do not pay attention to every worthless thing. If the pleasure of the Exalted is not attained in this world, do not weary yourself seeking permanence. May the pious turn away from harmful things, and may the bad be expelled.

One is strong and great, and one is weak and small, and one is grand and humble — all together are known.
Lice kill the wicked and insects kill the lowly; all seeds are taken by force.
Detachment (al-tawakkul) means cutting off hope from comfort and seeking certainty — relying truly on God Most High, accepting increase and decrease,
and whether or not news comes, one who is exalted and sublime will find God sufficient, and travel to the Most High is necessary.
"Whoever puts his trust in God, God is sufficient for him; God accomplishes His purpose and has appointed a measure for all things."
It is narrated that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "O son of Adam, do not be alarmed —
provision will come as long as your soul is filled with hope for it." And he said: "Be like the birds that go out hungry and return full."
As for the provision of the Tarabid after their settlement and companionship — in the discourse on the matter of tawakkul,
know truly, as one who understands, that benefit and harm come from God alone,
and what has been destined will come; one who trusts need not fear, and it is obligatory
to acknowledge that there is no turning away from what has been decreed. The Arabs have a proverb: sufficiency comes from God.
Whoever truly relies on God — even if given little — will not complain. What has been apportioned
will come; steadfastness and keeping one's covenant (al-thabat wa husn al-'ahd) strengthen
and fortify the self. One who persists will reach all goals and will not be
broken, and will be aided against every sudden adversity and defeat.
A wise man said: Cut off regret and do not weep over loss; find tranquility
and do not seek more. The Arabs say: "Every father has a master."
But the noble among men is known by steadfastness, and the people of Persia say: Learn
all virtues from steadfastness; all excellence is known by steadfastness. One who goes out into the world —
O brother, seek steadfastness; inconstancy harms you — if you desire one thing, pursue it.

And so it has been said that whoever shows the qualities of the chameleon and the peacock — meaning one who shifts and changes — will never find prosperity and good fortune in the affairs of state. As for the third day, it has been said in the scriptures: reflect on this fully and completely, for this is the foundation of all matters. The keeping of good faith and covenant, holding firm to what one has pledged and promised, not going back on one's word, maintaining goodness and steadfastness in the same way — all of this is called the keeping of the covenant. It has been said: faithfulness to the covenant is part of faith, and breaking a promise is its opposite. The Prophet, peace be upon him, commanded: the keeping of covenant and good faith, for the covenant binds — if a man departs from his covenant, he falls from honor. A man who is not faithful to his covenant is not worthy to be considered a man. Whoever does not keep his word and fulfills not his covenant, he is as nothing. Al-Hadd wa'l-Jihad — meaning striving and exerting effort — refers to urgency and exertion of effort in achieving one's goal: not being slothful, not going astray, and not falling short. This is what separates one who attains his goal from one who does not. Every state declines when its holder grows negligent and double-faced. Providence grants success only to those who strive in the path of God with full dedication, traveling the path of truth without hesitation. "Those who strive, We guide them to Our ways." Therefore, let no one be deterred from seeking what is sought. It has been said: whoever knocks at a door shall find it opened. The wise minister Nizam al-Mulk in his counsels to kings wrote: upon you is the utmost exertion and striving. Do not be separated from diligence. Among the sayings transmitted is: whoever abandons effort and devotes himself to ease, transfers his affairs to others, speaks only of comfort, will find the state slipping from his hands. He made laziness prevail in his affairs, and it has been stated by the eloquent: "From slothfulness comes the ruin of kingdoms." Negligence and sloth yield nothing. Strive with diligence and effort.

To reach one's goal, war prepares the soul and establishes it — for the pleasures of Gog and Magog are spent in praiseworthy ways, while on the contrary, the schemes and expenditures of the vile and harmful come only from strife and lust; they do not remain in the benefit of the accursed Satan, and the ancient notion holds: the free man lives modestly, and the discourse says "the slave becomes free when he rests." Begin, then, from the start of matters; be mindful of origins, and know the ways of entry and exit. Think well, resolve firmly, and form a good image in your mind. Do not leave things scattered, and give no one a pretext or cause for hesitation. One of the two things is this: that no one recognizes the work done, and the other is that things remain unknown. Place auspicious seeds in joyful moments, and move forward — for it is said: "The first thought is the last action." This quality belongs to the wise, who are the foundation of all understanding. The wise man recognizes the outcome of a matter at its beginning, while the ignorant man sees it only at the end when the expense is already spent. Among the wise sayings it is told: a king was asked, "Who is the most resolute of kings?" He answered: "One who controls his forbidden impulses, defeats his desires, understands his own nature, is content with what he receives, and is not angered by pride." The second point: when the soul finds no escape from a difficult place, it is overtaken by terror and sorrow — follow the right path, proceed correctly, and stand firm like a pillar. Those who hold firm in their resolve are guided, and as recorded in the Collection of Stories, it is said...

On the dispute between the Commander of the Faithful, Ali (peace be upon him), and Muawiya, son of Abu Sufyan —
Muthaym, one of the wise men, came to him, and Muawiya, in giving [judgment], said who is the wrongdoer. Ibn Hashim said:
"The one who seeks counsel with sincerity and who restrains himself from stubbornness — by God, he has attained the reward." And Muawiya said:
"Counsel is one of the finest virtues of the righteous. Take the right course, and keep to good counsel."
In verse it is said: "When reason calls you to take counsel, seek the noble and the sound of mind, and do not make the corrupt your support, for the strength of the predator lies in its wings. Restrain the tongue."
He worshipped and sat in the company of the virtuous, and preserved the finest of qualities and manners.
From this, the undesirable increases. And thus it was that on the night of the Ascension (Miraj), the Noble One (peace be upon him) brought the blessed, pure, and goodly greetings, and said: "Peace be upon you, O Lady, and the mercy of God and His blessings." The angels replied: "Peace be upon us and upon God's righteous servants." And like Moses, who came forth and was guided — and it was said: "Lord, show me!" The answer came: "Look to the night." And it was said: "Good, good!" And in the Noble Book [it is written]: "The Most Merciful taught the Quran, created man, and taught him speech." And in the traditions, from the Prophet: "Verily, eloquence is a kind of sorcery," and "May God have mercy on one who corrects his tongue."
And the Messenger said: "A Muslim is one from whose tongue other Muslims are safe." And it is said: "Whoever guards his tongue is saved."
It is known that Mamun said: "The finest speech is that which suits the occasion."
And in my view, the tongue is like a branch — its fruit determined by the direction of the face. And in the saying of the wise: "Were it not for the tongue, man would be nothing more than a mere image, resembling an animal."

The poet says: "Go beyond what is apparent in speech, for what concerns me is the singular expression of logic." In speaking, one who is not [merely] of Sindbar's tradition but of true discernment — as it has been transmitted — if you ask him for meaning, he will say: "We do not reduce a precious jewel to mere rubble." Up to the point where it has been said: "The tongue of the wise man follows the heart, and the heart leads the tongue." Sheikh Saadi of Shiraz spoke on this subject, saying: "Think before you speak, so that your words may be proper — do not speak what is unbefitting." The speech of a human being is better than the braying of an animal. And the crowing of a rooster is [also] a kind of speech. It is recorded in the Jami' al-Hikayat that someone asked a wise man: "What is the best thing that reveals a person's inner state?" He answered: "A person in need is like a natural bird — it makes its tongue known." And it is better for a person in need to be like a natural bird, for affection keeps one safe, while chattering [reveals weakness]. Some of the wise men and the ignorant have said that the greatest elements and the common understanding are expressed in speech. It has come down that God Almighty says: "One hundred steps of patience are better than one hundred steps of rashness." In the Akhlaq-i Nasiri it is said: "One who possesses this quality is considered rare and esteemed among the Arabs." A worn-out instrument used as a beast of burden, and one who swallows anger when provoked — this is deemed worthy. And one who is able to repay a harm but chooses not to — such action and conduct is praiseworthy. After this, in the section on perseverance, and in the words of Ubayd, Ibrahim said: "From the Prophet, blessings of God be upon him, it is transmitted: 'There is no forbearance except through deliberate practice.'" And it is said: "There is no forbearance except through patience, and no clemency except through trial." And it is said: "Knowledge comes from the learned, and learning comes through the effort of study." Whenever knowledge is paired with forbearance, the foundation of virtue and patience is thereby established.

The Prophet said: "Nothing I have gathered is more excellent than knowledge." Regarding the wonders of creation, it is related — as narrated from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abd al-Wud, traced back through a chain of transmission — that the Blessed One said: "On the Day of Resurrection, when all creatures are gathered, a caller will cry out: 'O people of distinction, come forward!' They will rise and go toward Paradise in great procession. The angels will say: 'We are your guides toward Paradise — what distinguished you?' They will reply: 'When we were wronged, we were patient; when we were harmed, we forgave; when harm was directed at us, we showed generosity.' Then it will be said to them: 'Enter Paradise, for you are among the righteous.'"

Among the sayings of the Commander of the Faithful, the most honored among men for forbearance and wisdom, Sheikh Sa'di has recorded the following: Salman was asked: "What keeps one from falling into ignorance?" He answered: "Think of others as you wish them to think of you; show mercy and understanding; protect your honor and guard your dignity."

It was a duty upon them to deliver the message and render service to the faith. Sa'd and Qaas came forward. The Messenger of Islam said: "Ride, and let your religion prevail." He said to Sa'd: "By God, you have informed me — and I am the Commander of the Faithful." This is related from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abd al-Wud, through a connected chain. The Blessed One assessed his wealth, departed, bowed his head in greeting, and told him what had transpired. When he was asked, he descended and came close; he struck him not — for it is a virtue to show restraint — and treated him with care, for natural temperament guides one toward affection.

Baghdad, and it is dominant, and they said that the spirit of al-maddah is the secret of modesty. The first is to feel shame before God Almighty, for it was among the greatest of people. The meaning is that the eyes are kept down, and truthfulness is maintained, and the reality is that God Almighty — and it was said, the Prophet said: Consider how modesty relates to good character, and he said: whoever guards himself among the people and avoids showing off, and leaves behind the adornment of worldly pleasures, and remembers death and returns — has indeed been saved by God. Modesty means feeling shame before creation, lest people find fault with you and be embarrassed, and it is recorded in the sources that modesty is part of faith, and modesty and restraint are branches of faith. And in the books of the learned it is recorded that one who has two qualities granted to him by God — forbearance and modesty — is fortunate. And it is quoted in the Book of Religious and Worldly Conduct from al-Mu'tazib that modesty is the foundation of faith. And it was said: for the modest person, worship is humility. And it is said that modesty is among the most alive of virtues. Feeling shame and turning toward good deeds leads to righteousness. And in the Book of the Essence of Wisdom: whoever has little modesty, let his conduct be as his modesty. And the words of the wise have come: save yourself and make your soul more noble than the generous. And Salih ibn Abd al-Quddus says: when a man is given something, let him be reserved, for there is no good in one who, when he receives, has no modesty remaining. Guard this, for it leads to nobility and generosity. And in the sayings it is reported that modesty is the greatest virtue — how beautiful it is in people. And the words of the wise say: when people live with modesty, it is as if God has adorned them. For those who are brought back to life through modesty, their honor is protected, and the violation of that is impossible. And it is possible to be a person of virtue and wealth when the soul is at rest.

One should not let the time of choice slip from one's hands, as it is not fitting for someone of noble nature to behave so. After the hardship passed, there came among the words of al-Mutawakkil the Abbasid this saying: "The world is in ease and difficulty." He was well aware of the nature of affairs and the reality of what the rational soul desires and seeks — with complete enthusiasm remaining for what brings little benefit in the morals of Nasiri. He says subtly: "From this branch comes the portion, and haste to rush into the matter of the rein" — for what happens must be dealt with according to the requirements of reason and religious law, proceeding with forbearance over the devilish impulse. The second is from the Most Merciful, and it has been said: "Deliberation is better than excessive haste," and it is said: "Haste is the lamp of regret, and deliberation is the key of well-being." It is said that the four elements of happiness are: soundness of character, the face of reason, attainment of goals, and love among people — and generosity and compassion. Compassion brings forgiveness, and it warns the mindful one — that is, the one who is captive to meaning — to know how to manage affairs and not to withhold his gift, and to exert himself beyond what is overwhelming, and to persist toward his goal with what he is capable of, seeking to kill the enemy and to liberate those in his care. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "One who shows little compassion is better than one who performs many outward acts of worship." And he said, peace be upon him: "The merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful — show mercy to those on earth and the One in heaven will show mercy to you." And he said, peace be upon him: "Whoever does not show mercy to people will not be shown mercy by God." And it is recorded in the Wonders of Creation that the Messenger, peace be upon him, once met a Jew on the road among the polytheists — water was flowing — and he said something about a great matter, saying: "This is for you." And he entrusted his own self to the Muslim's care; the man took it upon his shoulder, and together with the Jew he carried him up the slope. When he entered within, the Prophet said: "The one who carried is a Muslim" — and so the account ends.

A man brought me to the home of a Jew who had a book. He reported that this [person] came to seek faith, and said: "This compassion is from the habit of the fathers and mercy upon those who are owned — it is most fitting." Al-Ridha is the state of contentment. Being [in that state], come — one who is forbidden from gracious acts, having done favors, relying on them, and riding together. The divine decree has been carried out; proclamation was made to those erring, and the hearts of the seekers [were addressed]. As for explaining [it]: you found yourself bewildered, like this man of noble rank. The Exalted [God] does not demand; He addresses with a gentle word — you are the addressed and we are the addressees, and the intermediary between us. He cast away the news and sent it forth. To the son of Adam He directed all care: "I have tested your heart and your body, and if you are not satisfied with My decree, I will give power over you to the world until you flee in distress." The loneliness of the open land, the glory and seclusion, and the pleasure therein — "So long as your heart is content and you are [at peace]" — and the minister as a shroud; from adornment in the abode, the bed will be spread. In all of this, from Noah, seeking remedy through the All-Merciful, the Guide — the noble one came. Al-Ridha [contentment] with what has been ordained, and patience upon it. The trust in God suffices — "whoever recognizes for himself the mark of contentment with the divine decree, and patience upon tribulation, has truly known" — so the grace of God is upon the one content with destiny. The seeker of pleasure and one who turns away from his Lord, opposing it in appearance — the Exalted has said: "Whoever comes ill from among those who are discontented, it is not decreed for him" — so seek contentment for yourself and be guided. It has come in the organized [verse] of the Commander of the Faithful, Ali: "Peace be upon you." He said: "Praise to God for what has passed — and thus your benefit." And among the Persians it is said: [the meaning being] that one should render devotion and come down [in humility].

It is hoped that to be good is the general custom — to be good is desirable. As for gentleness (al-rifq): one should be steady-handed, peaceful, caring toward companions, and attentive. It has been related that: "If gentleness were a physical form, people would be more beautiful than it; and if anger were a physical form, people would be more ugly than it." And it is said — blessings of God be upon him — that gentleness loves gentleness, and by gentleness one obtains what one does not obtain through pardon, nor through anything else. And he said: "Whoever is deprived of gentleness is deprived of all good." And he said: "Whoever is given a share of gentleness is given a share of the good of this world and the next." And it is said: "Gentleness does not enter into a thing but that it adorns it, and harshness does not enter into a thing but that it ruins it." The Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, said: "If people were to be sought after, what would bring them together would be this." It has reached us in a hadith: "Gentleness is the key to success." And it is said that whoever exchanges harshness for gentleness will find that gentleness brings benefit, and whoever combines gentleness with generosity — generosity means giving freely to those in need. The wise say: one should give to whoever comes in need. God the Most High says: "Whoever is saved from the greed of his own soul, those are the ones who succeed." It is said that God praises two kinds of people and grants them blessings. It has been narrated that the Prophet said: "God created creation for the sake of good character." And it is said: "Generosity, even if it wanders in Paradise, its origin is at the gate that opens to this world." And it is said: "The masters of this world are the wealthy, and in the next world are the pious." And the Prophet, mercy be upon him, said: "A wicked miser shall enter the Fire even if he is a sinner, and a miser shall not enter Paradise even if he is a scholar." And among the creatures is one who has faith.

God the Almighty would accept repentance, and "do not kill yourselves" — so that you may be safe and at peace. The good and the repentant — if they had not taken to the path of Islam, the cause of harm would have come from the fire and smoke of what is desired. And there is a story about it: one who fulfills the needs of those who ask will obtain reward, and thus the matter will be set in motion.

The true meaning of generosity is to give of oneself to the utmost, beyond what is customary, and this is confirmed and established. From this, you will understand that if a person does what is appropriate, giving a hundred dinars as charity while forbidding wrong and recognizing virtue, though this may seem trivial — truly faith is established when one gives charity and fulfills obligations, for this is right conduct.

God registers the names of those in the heavens, and their deeds are recorded and shall not be lost. Greetings to those who dwell in Paradise: "And for those who fear the Day of Judgment" — and the generous one is their companion. Even if generosity were uncommon, truly the most praiseworthy of people is the one who does good to others.

Among the Arabs it is said: love for giving spreads across kingdoms, and it illuminates the free person. And in the words of the wise: "The sultan should be a servant to his subjects." And it is said: "Give to the worthy before they ask" — freeing people from the need to beg. When a wise man acts with goodness, the truly free and noble person will not demean himself.

Abu Talib said: "The noblest of Adam's descendants are those who are truly valiant." The generous ones spend their days giving. The noble servant conveys the message, and it is said: "Do not seek it from the heart, for what the generous man possesses is not to be withheld." It is said: al-Masiyasah — meaning, give orders and follow through, maintaining justice in the land always.

Do not prevent people from visiting, and do not break your own word. As the hadith says: "Each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock" — meaning, bringing people together is obligatory, and dividing them is forbidden.

Good governance was practiced, and the Prophet said: "Were it not for the sultan's rule, people would devour one another." The poet struck, saying that the politics of the sultan
Is always in effect; without it, no one would drink clean water. And in the sayings of the wise it is said:
There is no authority except through men, no men except through wealth, no wealth except through prosperity, and no prosperity
Except through justice. And governance revolves around this — if it does not stay in its center
And the affairs of the world are not kept in order, it will not be accepted. And governance
Will not flow toward others until one governs oneself first. The Commander of the Faithful Ali, peace be upon him, said:
"He who does not govern himself well cannot govern others." Aristotle said: "Do not dwell with one who
Separates himself from virtue; be the ninth after him." And in the comfort of the West it is said: whoever governs himself well,
His governance endures. The most important step is to engage in a matter for which one is truly needed.
The cultivation of the heart is the goal; and if commanders act with fear and danger, they sacrifice body and soul,
Bringing contentment to the spirit and removing hardship from their backs. The Prophet said: "Indeed God
Loves generosity." And it is said: "He slays Jarir and 'Atrib." And in the era of
Islam, no one could match the Commander of the Faithful Ali, peace be upon him, in valor.
It has been related in accounts that he went forth, and traditions report
That people added to the narrations, and afterward it was recorded in the world's judgments that no one could write it down fully.
And that venerable one departed, and his famous stations are well-known — and from the lineage descends:
Umar ibn Abd — the Messenger told me of it — the contest with Ali in knowledge of the brave men.
"The humiliation of Khandaq is greater than the worship of the two worlds." And in the tradition it is said:
And the son of Abd, the humility of Khanaf, is greater than the worship of the two realms. And in the praise of
That great one it was said: "There is no brave youth except Ali, there is no sword except Dhu'l-Faqar" — in bravery.

Traditions of gratitude, its calming effect, and the gathering of poets on that subject — what the sages of Semnan have said:

The soldier who was lowly in body was great in courage. The soldier who was not great in stature and not famous — yet through his bravery and valor he exceeded the demons in deed. Firdawsi composed verses in the tongue of a guardian: "The soldier who drinks the wine of courage — his heart is pure of selfish desire, beloved; he asked nothing and found ease of heart without reproach in all matters of fear." Courage is like a mirror of a great man; humility comes with good manners and acceptance of noble character.

Gratitude — to give thanks is to act for one's own benefit, for God Most High must be given thanks for every blessing He sends. Whoever does not acknowledge the blessing will find himself deprived of it and will fall into ingratitude. They will be struck by calamity and punishment, for God Most High has said: "We will assuredly try you," and as evidence for this, the word of God Most High: "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you," and the saying: "Remember Me and be grateful, and do not be ungrateful." And Luqman said to his son: "Be thankful to God," for if the custom of ingratitude departs, it is said: When the first and last are gathered together, a caller will call out with a voice that all creation hears from the first of the noble ones: "Let those who did good works for God's sake come forward, for none shall be gathered except those who remember God, even if they be few." Be patient with people. And it is said: "He who does not thank people does not thank God." Among the sayings of the eloquent: "Gratitude is fulfilled on the day of blessings." And in the sayings of the wise: "Whoever does not give thanks for small things does not deserve great ones." It is also said: the one who gives thanks for obedience is better than the one who merely fasts. In the words of the virtuous: "God is with those who give thanks and not with those who are ungrateful," and it is said: "Ingratitude for blessings is the inheritance of Hell." The poet says: "Ingratitude is the beginning of unbelief — and how many have become unbelievers through ingratitude."

Heading: On the Encouragement of the Soul Toward Great Undertakings in Anticipation of Sublime Remembrance

Just as justice, piety, proper conduct, swiftness, and the safeguarding of religion are the pillars of one's affairs, likewise the Arab scholars have said: "Whoever holds himself accountable is saved, and whoever guards his religion is preserved."

It has also been said: "The most praiseworthy of virtues is patience" — which is the stillness of the soul in the face of desires, and resistance to the passions that the soul is drawn toward. It means bearing hardship with composure, keeping the heart steadfast, and fulfilling the rights of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — as alluded to in His noble words: "O you who believe, be patient and endure and remain steadfast" (Quran 3:200). And whoever endures hardships with patience will find reward.

It is said: "You will only be given patience." And it has been said: "Patience is the key to relief." And: "Patience is worship." And: "Know that the forerunner of relief is patience." And the Commander of the Faithful said: "Faith has two halves — half is patience and half is gratitude." He also said: "Patience is a shield against misfortunes and an aid in difficulties."

And it has been transmitted in verse: "Bear a little patience, for hardships become easier, and every matter has its proper time and its rightful arrangement. Be patient in long waiting, for God grants us power when we are steadfast." And the Exalted has said: "Indeed We will reward the patient their recompense without reckoning" (Quran 39:10).

Bearing hardship patiently over calamities is the mark of the wise. The wise man who is pure of heart: when a calamity befalls him he does not multiply his grief by lamenting it. Patience reduces suffering. And in the sayings of Abdullah ibn Abbas it is recorded: "The best of qualities is justice according to the Law, and the Imam who is pure inwardly and outwardly, devoted to the Muslims."

He said: "Perfection consists in three things: chastity in religion, patience in afflictions, and excellence of conduct."

In the name of the City, and in the words of the Abbasid Caliph al-Mustansir it has come: "One who is patient in hardship" — the Abbasid Caliph said: Let him who claims brotherhood prepare for adversity and be patient for a little while. And Sheikh Sa'di said: Do not sit alone fleeing from the turning of fortune; patience is bitter, but like a lion it finally prevails — so endure patience. He who bestows and gives, and does not tire of giving, attains companionship; and the true comrade is he who opens the door to his friend and walks the path with him. One must keep one's attention and mind occupied with the means of peace and tranquility of a true friend, and strive to bring about what is good, and turn away from what is repugnant to the heart. Know that backbiting, slander, spreading rumors, and self-praise are qualities rarely found in a true friend — and a sincere friend is rare, and such a companion is hard to find. He who is truly a friend gives his skin for you; he who seeks justice finds it nowhere else; the reward for such a one is friendship itself. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Hold fast to sincere brothers, for they are a comfort in ease and a protection in hardship." The foundation of action is the servant's faith in God Almighty — and the way of the wise friend is known to all, and the scholar of the Arabs has said: "He who does not choose patience has no wisdom." And it is said: the cure for longing is the survival of the beloved — and among Arab proverbs it is said: the quenching of thirst is in the persistence of love and closeness of affection — the path of the righteous friend. And Ibn al-Rumm said: The greatest virtue is to have a great true friend — one who is sincere and straight, whose heart is as warm as the sun, and whose words are true. A true friend is one who, if you are afflicted with a calamity, strives to deliver you from that calamity by every possible means.

He also said:

It becomes easy, and in that path, one who runs toward it, the fat of pine resin sleeps well in resin.
From the Messenger of God — may God's peace be upon him — it is narrated: "Hold fast to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. A man continues to tell the truth and to seek truth until he is written with God as a true believer (Siddiq). Hold fast to truthfulness, for it is the gate of the gates of Paradise." And the poet Saadi says: "Speak the truth and be steadfast in it, lest falsehood bring you to ruin." And in the speech of the eloquent, among the pages of: "Truthfulness does not dull the sword of truth." And Ibn al-Mughira said: "The perfection of truthfulness is the perfection of intellect."

The clarification of the mind: this is the technical term for the extraction of what is sought. When this quality is attained and maintained, it produces and preserves this noble trait, and no meaning remains hidden, and the shallow-minded are quickly exposed. It silences the ignorant and gives answer to the questioner, and this quality in men is predominant. Through it, great thoughts and ideas are illuminated, and pardoning is completed from the heart. Nothing else remains — in the hearts of people, that thought rules. "I seek refuge in God from their evils, and may God have mercy on their great and small, and be pleased with their affairs, and guard their comings and goings, and the best of those who keep away from them."

Truthfulness in caring for orphans: fulfilling the state of young people and their proper guardianship. These people are partners in attaining the pleasures of this world. It has been said: one cannot sever one's own bond, nor can one find attachment to one's self through any other means. God the Most High said: "And fear God, in whose name you ask of one another, and (reverence) the wombs." And from the Companion via the Messenger — peace be upon him — it is narrated that love expands provision in...

And we ask Him regarding the noble Prophet — may He have mercy — and it is said: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day..." The Prophet — may God praise him — said: God the Exalted said: "I am God, I am the Merciful (al-Rahman), I created kinship (al-rahim) and derived its name from My own name. Whoever maintains it, I will maintain connection with him, and whoever severs it, I will sever him." And he said: "Maintaining kinship brings wealth to the poor, increases wealth for the rich, is beloved in hope, and a support in difficulties."

It was said in answer to a man who asked about drawing near to Paradise and distancing from the Fire: "Worship God and associate nothing with Him, establish prayer, give alms (zakat), and maintain ties of kinship."

And the scholars say that maintaining ties of kinship has twelve benefits:
First: the pleasure of God Almighty.
Second: joy and happiness.
Third: the rejoicing of the angels.
Fourth: the praise of people.
Fifth: increase of one's offspring.
Sixth: increase of one's lifespan.
Seventh: blessing in one's livelihood.
Eighth: nearness to the righteous.
Ninth: distance from sin.
Tenth: increase in the goodness of one's deeds.
Eleventh: the forgiveness of one's sins.
Twelfth: the fulfillment of one's wishes.

As for silence — it is restraint. Do not speak carelessly, especially before those who mock. It is reported from the Prophet — peace be upon him — from the companions: "Whoever is silent is saved." And it was said: "God has mercy on whoever speaks good or else keeps silent." And it is said: "Whoever speaks carelessly, his speech falls into hellfire, for from careless speech comes punishment." Jesus son of Mary said: "Along with worship, nothing is better than silence, and keeping away from people."

Restraining speech is a virtue, and the wise man said: "When the mind is complete, speech is brief." Al-Bayda'wi said: "When a man lacks full reason, his speech is like that of someone who calls out to Layla in the night" — meaning, like a thief who wanders in the dark seeking an intimate companion but finds none. So guard your tongue from harm: as is said, "the woman who cuts off her own head repents her haste." If you cannot keep an enemy from becoming your enemy, at least try not to lose a friend — for if an enemy cannot be turned to a friend, at least let him not become a destroyer of friendship.

Make your own conduct your mirror, and do not speak of anyone else's affairs, so that remembrance of your own deeds occupies you. The wise and alert man of good character is the one who guards himself from greed.

The one who knows, the one who is young and perceptive by nature, acts correctly and truly in what is right. Serving a good master is fine; to speak of old things and be unpleasant is ill-advised. A great woman is worthy, and a great wise man is a helper and supporter.

Do not listen beyond what is proper; to speak cuts the tongue and wounds. Giving tongue to meaning, while sitting in silence on the path, is better. As Sa'di has said: Silence before the hearts of men is best — do not speak at random.

Like a stream of water flowing to its source, seek out the one worthy of companionship. Do not drive your heart to quarrel; speak pleasantly so that good words flow back to you. Do not let the tongue run loose; say one thing, not two. Long speech is a great fault — this is the sum of it.

The glorification and honoring of the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, and of those close to His presence, namely the angels, and the infallibles upon whom be the blessings of God, and the saints of the faith — all require obedience. The commandments and prohibitions of the lawgiver must be followed. The greatness of God's command appears outwardly in its proper form.

Guard yourself so that by these meanings you do not make yourself a target, and at no time neglect anything or cast aside obligation, lest you fall into disgrace. The one who destroys the foundations of religion will find that the lazy-natured person, however long he persists, will ultimately bring ruin.

In obedience and worship, and those who turn away from it, Ibn Saffara gave an answer and a response that it is easy: What we consider the strongest of deeds is perseverance in obedience to God and patience upon this. God and worship with a firm foundation, and one whose hearing is wasted and whose knowledge is squandered. And it is blessed among the messengers, as reported: "My nation is ruined by two men: a sinful scholar and an ignorant worshipper" — because when a scholar is sinful, the pillars of worship become intoxicated with wrongdoing, and the devotee becomes inclined to abandon it; and when the ignorant one acts without knowledge, whatever he does he remains unaware. Therefore nothing from these two shall be accepted in the station of recognition. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: "There is no worship in which there is no expenditure," and for this reason it is commanded: "Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim man and Muslim woman," and it was said: "Seek knowledge even unto China." Seeking knowledge is obligatory, for whoever does not pursue the path of knowledge cannot properly fulfill his duties. Until one becomes aware of this, it has been commanded: "Knowledge is of two kinds: knowledge of religions and knowledge of bodies." For a true seeker of knowledge, both are necessary, and not seeking is a calamity. Knowledge can be acquired from these two branches, and on the path of divine religion, however much one seeks is never sufficient. The scholar, being absorbed in worship, rightfully occupies himself with all other things so that this action falls within the grace of justice. God Most High commands: "Indeed, God commands justice and goodness," and the Messenger of God said: "Just worship surpasses sixty years of ordinary worship," and the Almighty said: "By justice the heavens and the earth stand upright" — meaning thereby that if the celestial spheres and elements each became dominant, the world would cease to exist, and the order of the universe could not be maintained. In removing injustice and establishing justice, God Most High commanded David His prophet in matters contrary to His command.

"Judge among the people with truth" — that is, with justice — and it has been said: "In justice lies the safety of the sultan and the prosperity of cities." In the words of the Abbasid caliph's guide it is recorded: "Justice compensates for the absence of all armies and prevents what fortresses cannot prevent." And in the Arab proverb it is said: "The child of kings is justice." And the great Nushirwan said: "The commander who is fair and just — whoever follows the path of justice and uprightness will become a leader, and his name will be raised in the world, even as Fereydun and Tanav." Among rulers, sultans, ghazis, and their like, the meaning and truth of this is expressed in verse:

Fereydun the blessed was an angel, formed of musk and ambergris —
He attained this through giving; be generous like Fereydun, and so too shall you be received.
The blessed Nushirwan is remembered — Nushirwan was famed throughout the world.

A poet said: more than the fame that rises up, greater still is the name — the supreme aspiration.
Felicity and wretchedness in this world depend on whether one regards the terror of death as nothing, and does not fall short of the station of health and soundness in the next world. And one who remains here seeking elevation has found salvation. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "God loves those who seek great matters, noble ends, and lofty goals." And it is said: "A man flies by his ambition as a bird flies toward its direction." And in the tales of the worthies it is recorded that Ibrahim — whom some call the uncle of Ibrahim — sought intercession for the people before the Divine Presence, and was told: "Low ambition is unworthy." Regarding Shaykh Khalid it was said, and Shaykh Sa'd composed a quatrain: Seek high companionship and noble aspiration — a man of purpose attains his aim. Wisdom and reason are the fruit of the mind: that is its true mark and benefit.

Erasing from the heart and inscribing upon the human heart the station of metaphor — through you it has arrived, and through you it stands upright at the station of retribution and reward, though retribution has been abandoned and vengeance sought until the seal of forgiveness was reached and the matter was complete. And forgiveness of it is the best remedy, for it will not reach the level of complete goodness — as the birds of the unseen and the faithful have said: "Turn away from the people, for God loves the doers of good." And God said: "Take the way of forgiveness, and command what is right" — meaning that the Prophet, peace be upon him, desired forgiveness above all; so forgive, for God will forgive you likewise.

It is said: When the servants stand before God, a caller will call out: "Let those who are owed a reward from God stand" — and it will be said: "What is their reward?" He will say: "Those who used to forgive people — enter Paradise without reckoning."

And it is said: Forgiving the criminal is among the qualities of the generous. And it is said: The best of qualities are three — whoever possesses them has attained the fullness of faith: he who, when content, is not led into falsehood; and when angered, his anger does not overcome him; and when he has power, he forgives. In the Jami' al-Hikayat it is recorded from a source that among the best qualities of people of this world and the next are: forgiving one who cut you off, giving to one who deprived you, and pardoning one who wronged you.

It is narrated from 'Abbasi that it has been said: "If people only knew the value of forgiveness, they would eagerly seek it." And in the words of the wise it is said: Forgiveness is measured by the reform of the noble; and it is said that the character of the generous is quick to pardon. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said: "I came to know the conditions of people through kindness — from the goodness of God and through forgiveness from God's power." And the beginning of forgiveness is this: ask for it earnestly, and be swift, for it is not proper to delay. And from being slow in food, drink, clothing and so forth — as the Quran has indicated to those who follow and oppose: "God guards those on high." And among those whom his right hand possesses, those are not blameworthy — whoever seeks beyond that, David is witness.

And these are the transgressors. And in the book Thamar al-Akhbar, from the Prophet (peace be upon him), it is narrated: whoever fulfills his obligations in evil conditions, and does not fall into the fire — From a man named Salim, asking about it: why does a man who falls in love lose his mind? He answered: because in their faces is beauty and in their nature is chastity. It is transmitted that David, peace be upon him, said: O my son, do not follow the black horse, and do not be distracted by a woman. And it is said in the speech of the wise: how many a person of beautiful outward qualities, through chastity of soul and grief, attains freedom from desire. Through desires and goals of the self, one arrives at true annihilation, and through adherence to proper conduct and dealings with the Truth — meaning: having one's will in accordance with God's will, and in pursuing the Truth, striving and putting aside one's own wishes and desires, and being devoted to the will of the Presence. The one who has abandoned egotism is refined; the caravan leader said: if you desire union, leave behind your own desires; and if you desire God, abandon thoughts of self-interest.

Hanifa Ibn Ma'na said — (verse): I will not act improperly, for in seeking the whole of falsehood, one cannot remain upright. The thought came to him: do not make your heart light and unstable; and another said: whatever you do, the result will return to you. Keep a friend close, for that friend will stand by you; do not let your desires distance you from your goal. Yes — whoever becomes annihilated in God's will truly remains, as the masters of the path have said. Beyond this, from the marks of one who has no desire for other than God, is such a person. And another said: religion gained through the world's ways brings no true benefit; for if you rise beyond your own self, your spiritual state will be inquired after by religion itself. This is a wonder.

Ever-living is the prophet — the one who has not died does not forget the sign of the Friend — the companion of Abraham was not consumed in the fire — like Khidr, the water of the living spring is not for just anyone — the Sheikh Bayazid Bistami said regarding the reality of annihilation (fana): "Seek the essence in both worlds, and what is given is priceless." 

From the direction of the valley of union, from the gaze of the beloved, fragrance came — and the reckoning of fortune: love has found its foundation in nothingness, and in nothingness it has struck what is not. Junayd of Baghdad said: "There is nothing in existence except God." Contentment (qana'a) is the ease of managing one's affairs in food, drink, clothing, and other things, and refraining from excess in those, and by will reducing even what is enough, and acting in accordance with religion.

As the Prophet said — peace be upon him — "Contentment is a treasure that does not perish," and he said: "Whoever is content is satisfied," and the great Ali — upon him be peace — said: "Know your measure and do not seek beyond your station," and before that: "Contentment is the head of wealth and the foundation of the soul, and the comfort of the heart, and the rest of the body." In the words of the wise: "Contentment is the head of wealth and the foundation of the soul, and the connection of souls, and the goodness of breath," and the cause of satisfaction, and the origin of spiritual annihilation (fana).

Love — how many wanderers: one who found no solitude found nothing — how can one who has no contentment find dignity? Love — alchemy, let me teach you a little — it is not found in the mine or in the craft — it is rare in the world — the alchemy of the secret of contentment is not found — and others have said: every day a man sought his daily bread, and from the broken jug water came — he was ordered so that it appeared, with wisdom like that of Daniel in Babylon — he sought the object of desire. 

The treasury: "Whoever has contentment has wealth" — and if the wealthy fall from bad fortune — in the right and the good, reduce excess, and many came — patience helped them along. 

Passage: O contentment, you made me free of need — and riding on you, I was never brought low.

For patience is a virtue, and wisdom is the command of stability — this is the lore of speech.
Do not waste idle words and foolish questions.
Take care in all affairs, keep your nature cool, and be mindful of the people.
The generous one is he who acts with magnanimity and seeks for others what is good.
He sought and persisted among the people, distributed wealth abundantly in accordance with occasions.
He placed generosity upon the hearts of people and spread grace among the common folk.
Fourteen times he exercised piety and gratitude, placing thanks within discourse as required.
Generosity is to forgive the ungrateful, to pardon the unbeliever, and to receive people with good character.
Generosity is the very essence of blessing — and in the words of the Commander of the Faithful, Husayn ibn Ali, peace be upon him, it is stated:
True generosity is giving before being asked. The mastery of the self is the breaking of the ego — this is the root of it.
If the soul desires anything, it must be tamed; one must train oneself not to follow the soul's every whim and the sources of its passions.
The qualities of great kings are predominant, and generosity answers requests for wealth.
They are patient and do not resent bearing hardships, and are capable of enduring unpleasant matters with forbearance.
They are not destabilized by pleasant or unpleasant events — until those self-breakings arrive,
and the forbidder from passion, for the grieved one, their abode is assured. And from that nearness to the presence of Divine Glory —
"I am with those whose hearts are broken" — may this grow.
It means that the will of the Divine Presence — Majestic is His name — is especially this:
"For those who do good, there is the finest reward and increase" — and Khwaja Nasiruddin Muhammad Tusi says:
The fourth is wisdom: make the proof your argument against every affliction, and make the proof your remedy against every sorrow.
Restrain yourself so that you do not lose or be stripped of your honor, which is manliness.

A sincere and genuine desire leads to the benefit of generosity and spending wealth, and to gaining recompense. Some scholars have said: "Among the obligations of chivalry (muruwwa) is to restrain oneself from what is forbidden, to withhold from harm, to judge with equity, to refrain from oppression, not to obey in what is not deserved, not to be overbearing toward the weak, and not to prefer worldly things over nobility." Among the rights of chivalry are those which the prophets—peace be upon them—enjoined, and which are only maintained through commitment and care. It has been said: "Chivalry belongs to one who fortifies his religion, maintains ties of kinship, and honors his brothers." The outward aspect of chivalry is manifest in its pillars, meaning to purify the self. Beware of what causes one to miss the mark—persistent bad character and low moral conduct, for these bring only loss and disgrace. Among the obligations is to seek what is beneficial and to fulfill deeds graciously and without burdening others. It has been said: "The strong man is one who masters himself." It was also said: "Chivalry cannot be attained unless one is grounded and free of base qualities. The man of chivalry is one who is patient in difficult circumstances." The outward and inward aspects of chivalry are as follows: Reciprocity (mukāfāt) — meaning that when one sees a person doing good to him, he should return it accordingly. It is incumbent upon one to repay kindness and to keep account of deeds and actions. In this world and the next, recompense is due, and the natural order demands that reciprocity be fulfilled.

Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna said: "Were it not for giving, grant me" — to which the king replied: "Every fault is that the noble king should act for his subjects." In the elevated words reaching the Lord's command, there are lofty matters beyond reckoning.

Concerning the deeds of Ispandiyar and the citadels and the ways of abundance — he did not show the path of commerce and the conditions pertaining to that lineage — the qualities of purity were made manifest and honored.

The mystic sayings were conveyed and the divine meanings declared to be of heavenly origin. They rose and departed, and rose again, and from the novice, if he strives, the intimate companion emerges from the new tent.

As for the great saints and noble masters: they were characterized by the special quality that — as the Commander of the Faithful, Ali (peace be upon him), declared — "Whenever I turned to the door of knowledge, strengthened by inner power, attaining stations from my inmost self, I drew near to the Divine, Glory be to Him, how great is He!"

Husayn said: "I am the Living One" — this is the meaning conveyed in noble speech by the divine light. He showed the people of Hallaj's path and said "I am the Living" — and gave the example thus.

The Lord showed mercy: "I am the Living One" — the Shaykh Abd Allah al-Siddaqi reported that Hallaj said: "I speak openly of the Generous One; I speak of Him in secret" — "Be faithful" — this was made known, and with tongue given and with the form of remembrance beyond reckoning.

So he accepted it, and put it into practice, and performed faithful observance of the covenant. As the Prophet said to Moses regarding the ten purifications, and the poet said in verse:

"Loyalty upon generosity is an obligation, and good conduct is the established custom, and the building of noble character is our foundation."

For one who keeps company with the fair-minded, yet sees the base man turn away from equity, come to the last of those faithful. And a companion of faithfulness — the poet said: and I searched for it but found no stone — know this: From whomever there comes more than enough, that man is in faithfulness, take heed. When a man comes to his covenant, the covenant of the noble man runs clear. And the most excellent of the faithful —

Among the people, from those who have heard it, thus they said: "Chivalry has perished, loyalty has been abolished." The great ones said: Among women, swords, and horses, seek faithfulness from none — know this: Expect no loyalty from a woman at all; and faithfulness in a horse and in a sword —

From this, the poet makes an absolute judgment about women's fidelity — though this is an opinion and its correctness is doubtful — while also displaying oppression toward chaste women, counting it as evidence against them.

Good people say: Among the reports concerning the prophets of Asia, this is true — among them there are of excellent character. And among the steadfast, one sees many who are witnessed for: chastity, purity, intelligence, shrewdness, affection, compassion, faithfulness, and patience.

Most men are surpassed by them. Hear what is said of each woman's virtue: she presents herself well even in the absence of others, and in general this holds. Among the many kinds of men, the greatest keep company with and rely upon the strong and the steadfast.

The interpretation of "Our Lord, grant us good in this world and good in the hereafter" — a harmonious wife: a good companion delivered to you — such a man grows in his friendship. Uproot the tree of regret: if your companion is agreeable, be grateful for that; every day be —

Do not keep a heavenly beauty merely for appearance; if your companion relieves your grief, keep her close by your side. And praise be to God —

فض [fayḍ — "abundance/outpouring," likely a page-end catchword or chapter marker]

On the merits of the Prophet and the grace of divine favor upon his family, and from beginning to end
The favors that were commanded, as the fathers of verses said, "Had all of creation been alike—"
The wishes were fulfilled for the men, so do not be ashamed of the name of the seeker.
And the remembrance is the best of what elevates; the son of the poet grew, and the moon and sun became his adornments.
Words were spoken: the sun never dims, and it was commanded: "The rulings come from the Compelled."
From the beginning it was as a mirror, reflected in the morals of Nasiri, described thus:
Dignity and gravity are known among his people, and composure is the foundation of his aim,
And in pursuit of goals, the intelligent one does not cease until the desired is obtained.
And remembering the learned ones and seeking the pure of knowledge, and it was said: "My son, from the
Masters of knowledge, do not depart, and it was said: whoever seeks knowledge is as though he has lived for two thousand years."
And it was said: "Whoever does not honor the elder, and does not show mercy to the young, and does not command what is right
And forbid what is wrong"—and from Ibrahim al-Khalil, peace be upon him, it was learned:
The white hair of one's beard and hair growing white is like a sanctuary of dignity and nobility.
Al-Khidr, may his glory be exalted, asked: "What is this, O Lord?" And God, blessed and exalted, said:
"God prolongs the life of the eloquent one, and his head and cheek are a blessed adornment."
And in the words it has come: honor the great with generosity, and honor the young with kindness.
Al-Dhabil: the remedy for weeping and the virtues of a man of good character described thus:
The heart goes to al-dhabil and through al-dhabil the merits become clear and approved.
It is established by the tradition of the Prophet that good people should keep to this, and in the noble words it has come:
The good ones among the jinn and humans are commanded rightly, and likewise the self, from the best of goodness—
A person becomes one who is rejected and driven away; and God the Exalted wills that one reaches and attains the goal.

It is beyond human conception to imagine men turning their heads among people, and in the companionship of the Prophet, peace be upon him, who kept away from anger and was the furthest from it, displaying good character and pleasant disposition, purifying the heart and soul. As the Sheikh Sa'di, may God preserve him, said: if half the good character remains, the bad character will depart, and one's own self will be saved. And the wise have said: virtues and merits are by nature moderate, standing between two extremes, and faults extend toward excess and deficiency on the outer limits. This is why there are many pleasures and joys, and the news of these pleasures has spread among many people in various directions, nurturing the heart broken by stories and tales heard from others. The third is the pain of retaliation, the path of sincerity, the ruby of the mines, and the nightingale of the gardens — and in some cases the sunnah appears in the best of names, with detail and elaboration, without needing to mention that it is well known among the people of this path, meaning the states and movements and stillness of human beings, as the days and nights bear witness to this, against which gladness and joy are limited. But in the meaning that they have said: for a time we raised noble men, but today in their place we find those of low station and are no longer safe from that. So that up to the summit of those beautiful ones, the tedium of repetition goes on and on, so that the pleasures, reckoned in number against the sorrows, seem as nothing. By the remedy of the one who seeks a cure through it, meaning the cure that comes — as if examples were given and analogies drawn — that has no equivalent among those who came before. And the only refuge is in God and the remainder of life is in the hands of time.

One should mention the vices and qualities of the people of religion — those destructive traits one must guard against — such as mockery, idle talk, gossip, slander, adopting the ways of foreigners, fornication, falsehood, and similar things. And extreme oppression and cruelty cause people to be cursed and condemned. He urged people to sincerity until the people were honest with one another, and before that the people had been given to mockery. Mockery and the pursuit of lowly things call one only to humiliation. The nobles' wealth is consumed in this way.

Consider: when one reflects and departs on a journey without heed, spending freely — "Do not overspend, for God does not love the spendthrifts. Indeed the wasteful are the brothers of devils." And it is said: there is no good in extravagance; rather, the deed lies in caution, economy, and keeping away from ruin and poverty. The sustenance of life is rightly measured. It is said: do not be heedless; do not stretch out the hand to the full extent of stretching, so that you end up blameworthy and destitute. Whoever is given to extravagance follows the path of illusion and fantasy, pursuing the promptings of devils, striving after vain desires.

Thus it is said: extravagance exhausts wealth quickly, and in many traditions it has come down that generosity is praiseworthy while extravagance is not, and that contentment with sufficiency is better than striving toward excess. The great one who is given to extravagance loses his standing.

It is said: the miser who withholds from the needy and does not give willingly is blamed; yet the one who gives out of need to others, what he gives — if he gives one part to himself, he gives two parts to others, and if he gives good to another before himself, then whatever he gives, even little, brings him honor and dignity.

Worms of the earth devour all things, and whatever it is, it is done — they devour and destroy, and nothing remains.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever is stung by a hornet, it is as if fire has touched them, and its venom is like fire in this world."

From the sweetness of honey, some things flow toward fire, and in response to the question about allowable things, it is commanded that:

The Messenger performed the circumambulation of Mecca, and he saw three men standing in a circle, and he approached them.

One of them said: "O Messenger of God, forgive my sins," and pleaded that the Prophet intercede for him saying, "My Lord, forgive my sins."

The greatest of them asked about the smallest sin, saying: "O Messenger of God, what is my sin?"

One of the neighbors said: "O Messenger of God, my sin is greater than the heavens and the earth."

The Prophet said: "O Messenger of God, your sin is greater than the Throne."

He replied: "God is greater and higher," and the Messenger of God said: "Your sin is the first and the last of matters."

He said: "O Messenger of God, I am a man of wealth and means among the people."

"So what path will save me from the Fire?" The Messenger said: "Do not let the world deceive you — God, Blessed and Exalted, says:

'I swear by the One who brought me forth — if you stood between the Corner and the Maqam and prayed a thousand prayers, and wrote until rivers of tears flowed from your eyes, and you wept endlessly, all your deeds would be in vain —

O God, You have housed them in the eight heavens; they have filled them; and the disbelievers are in the Fire.'"

The Commander of the Faithful, Ali, may God be pleased with him, said regarding the management of wealth: "One who inherits and passes on must be present, lest he be overcome before receiving it — for haste in spending leads to dissipation."

He said: "I found that when they circulate wealth, gratitude for it diminishes, and the character of generosity is corrupted."

"Truly, in this world, the poor man is examined, and in the Hereafter, the wealthy are called to account."

"Do not be hasty with your shrouds and do not give your wealth to the destitute, for they will not repay you — rather, treat them as equals among you, and seek what is in your hands, for that is better, and do not pursue what is beyond your reach."

Blame me in the matter of camels, for lowliness and humility — may God relieve my burden, O Abu Shabr. The she-camel was a treasure among the noble ones, and in good character toward Nasiri it was free of baseness and blame. He sought wisdom and conversations and stories of the ignorant, and brought them forth abundantly. By this restraint, keeping himself composed, he granted it to Khurasan. As mentioned, and among the Arabs, just as Hafiz wrote in his Shifa, it was preeminent, and in that great name it was held in highest esteem — the proud one kept it so. The Arabs considered it the highest and most noble of qualities to surpass others, and they would consider themselves above others in pride and superiority.

God Most High has declared war on pride among people, making it an enemy — as in the verse: "Do not walk upon the earth with arrogance; you will never split the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height — all of that is hateful in the sight of your Lord." And He said: "God does not love any arrogant boaster." And in a sacred hadith: "Pride is My cloak and greatness is My garment — whoever contests Me in these, I shall cast him into the Fire." And the Messenger of God described those who are arrogant, and God said: "No one who has even a mustard seed's worth of pride in their heart shall enter Paradise." Be humble with the humble and firm with the arrogant, for that is the sign of true knowledge. To display arrogance toward the arrogant is acceptable. The three qualities of character, nurturing, and the self — all three together: meeting people peacefully, traveling and moving among them humbly, appearing to love them outwardly while harboring enmity inwardly, and acting against them. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Guard yourself most carefully against usury, both the manifest and the hidden." And the Commander of the Faithful said: "Let no one elevate himself above another by news or possessions, nor bless anyone as a sovereign." He who isolates himself wearing a woolen garment, withdrawing into a hermitage to appear devout —

The heart yearns from sorrow; from seeking its own ease and sincerity, from sorrow.
And others have said: "Sebb" — the pain of the bit comes to the face of a chestnut horse.
The poison that came upon Karbala rises as its own outward appearance, rightly guided.
The dihla of the nightingale's union with its nature creates hypocrisy between the tongue and the ignorant hand.
Outwardly a friend, inwardly an enemy — and in the assembly this means that the sheikh's reproach is fitting.
(B) In the pasture, a safe sheep in annihilation does nothing — the people-despiser denies the right.
