The air of Ta'if is mild and fine, with fruits aplenty. When Adam was driven out of Paradise to the mountain, it is written in the Book of Caves that he descended to a place called Karoub. It is said that when Adam left Paradise, for a hundred years less he wept and lamented, until divine acceptance came to him. Paradise was a place of great longing; he did not depart from it willingly. He descended to the earth, and the House of God — the Ka'bah — was before him, and Adam was commanded to visit it. Adam found the House in ruins, for at the time of the Flood it had been laid waste, and at the time of Adam's death it was taken up to Paradise. After Adam, by the command of Seth, all people and the whole house were preserved. During the time of Noah's Flood it was ruined, and for two thousand years it lay desolate. When Abraham, the Friend of God, peace be upon him, and Ishmael came from there — from that wilderness — and Sarah, his daughter, grew jealous, the Friend of God was commanded by divine decree to leave Hagar and Ishmael in that barren and empty land. He sought water, running between those two hills, and saw nothing. Now those two hills are seen by the pilgrims on the hajj. And Ishmael, peace be upon him, wept, and struck the earth with his heels, and water sprang from beneath his feet. Hagar came running, and poured sand around it so that it would not spread. For this reason it is said she exclaimed "Zam Zam!" (Stop, stop!). Hagar settled there, and Ishmael too grew up in that land in good manner. After some time, by divine command, Abraham and Ishmael were hastened to build the Ka'bah.

[This passage from the Book of Wonders discusses Mecca and the Zamzam well:]

The region of Marwa, with its surroundings, and the black stones are among the wonders of that place. It was said regarding the black stone that the milk-white stone was a protection for the children of Adam, and it was said: "Whoever looks upon it with both eyes and speaks with the tongue will testify for every heart." It lands gently upon the water and the swords strike it firmly, and the fingers cannot grasp it. A guide led people to that place and brought them good news from it. Among its greatest wonders is that it guides travelers and shows the way. The son was there and the story of it is known — no one was aware of it. It is known that Abd al-Muttalib, the grandfather of the Prophet, saw it in a dream and was shown its location. At that place, horses were gathered and weapons were readied for sacrifice, and disputes arose. Some fled, and at that place and along the Arab roads, it is desolate and without sense or reason. On its top are twelve marks, and upon its surface a square structure was built and adorned. Water was drawn from it by pots and it became water, which was first white, but due to those unbelievers who rubbed their teeth upon it, it became black. The well of Zamzam has been blessed since the time of the Banu Abbas, when a noble lady came to Mecca and brought people there. They settled and the circumambulators came; the caliphs made it flourish until the pilgrims came. Again, others have taken charge of it, and now in Mecca the people are occupied with trade and commerce of Mecca and its surroundings. Ibrahim demanded and commanded that all should come to the Sacred Precinct. The first route was from Medina, and the carved inscriptions and milestones remain.

From there to Makkah, along the route of the Milky Way, two miles, with nine stations and a mile, was the Haram. And its Miqat, from there to Makkah, along the road of Egypt and Syria, is Nalu in the rocky terrain. And its Miqat is Juhfa, and from there to Makkah is three farsakhs, and to the sea a mile, and along the road of Yemen and Tihama, seven miles less a few farsakhs and a mile, was the Haram stations. And from there to Makkah via the Kaf road, and along the road of Najd to Makkah, ninety in stations, the Haram and its Miqat. And from there to Makkah along the road of Ta'if is twelve miles, three farsakhs and two miles of Haram, and its Miqat is Dhat al-'Irq. And from there to Makkah is twelve stations and one part. There were signs there and the miles were marked, and in each one trees were planted. Outside the Haram there were gardens of pleasant trees of Yemen, and abundant pastures, and running water, and around the Miqat places seven hundred and thirty-three miles, forty farsakhs and a mile was established at Masad al-Haram, the celebrated city of San'a, and the circumambulation place of the Hajj pilgrims was the House of Dhikr-Kaba, between the fortress of Asna. In the great mosque of the lands of Persia, the fortress of 'Umara, facing the direction of Sana, with the Masjid al-Haram and the Ka'ba attached, and the Masjid al-Haram surrounding it. The Banu Sanbiya is on the Iraqi side, and there is the northern part and the gate of Safa to the east. From the time of the Prophet's mission, in the era of the Messenger, the Ka'ba was covered with a cloth, as the Negus, king of Abyssinia, on behalf of the Church of Antioch, heading toward Syria, was shipwrecked in the sea by the Fughalians, and having come by the route of Andalusia, with his permission they brought the Ka'ba's cover among them and covered it. Timbers were installed under its roof, and the blessed Prophet with his noble hands placed the Black Stone back in its place before the Quraysh.

He placed it at the Iraqi corner, set upon the threshold, standing firm at that station, and so it remained in that city.
And that Deccan stands opposite, at the position of Zamzam, near it, and the corner likewise stands in correspondence.
The Shami corner is set, and with it the path of the noble corner of the Yamani side; it is set and the noble Junbi side is aligned.
The Balli corner is set, and with it they approached Mecca and turned around in it.
It is said that this opening, through which Zamzam is sprinkled, dates from the time of Abdullah.
When the Banu Umayya were building the wall, they made the Kaaba oblique, having dilapidated it, and they made a new boundary around it; they placed it against the wall from inside, and the Black Stone on the side of the house within the wall.
It is said that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, commanded that the Black Stone be placed in the house, it became necessary that it be set from inside, by the authority of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf — that is to say, this arrangement was falsely made. The Black Stone was carried and placed at the corner, and the house was constructed to a height and a length proportionate — four cubits high, and the height of the house upon it was eighty-eight cubits — with a leaning inclination.
They put the waterspout on the first side, so that the house stands in its proper position. Then Sa'd Abu Jawnt al-Sabiri lived there and was a contemporary of it, and left.
The city of Mustafa — may God's blessings be upon him — was thus in his time, and it is said: "God has forbidden the people of the house."
They forbade and covered the special features of the house.
The bird flew above it, and Uthman made the columns, and Umar raised it — praise be and glory to God — and Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan built a great structure in that mosque with heavy stones.
He constructed the roof of the mosque with fine timber and adorned it; Abu al-Mansur, the Abbasid, restored the mosque and the circumambulation area, establishing it anew, and upon it al-Mahdi continued.

The year is seven hundred and something, and it has increased beyond that, and the length of the place is established at three hundred and seventy according to the region of the khawaniq (hospices) and madrasas and the rest. It is very fine — from among them, a pious ascetic from Qazvin, for the sake of pilgrims and travelers, built a hospice, and donated a thousand dinars to Mecca so that permission would be given so that from this quarter a door would be opened into the Sacred Precinct. The house of Majd Yusuf, where the birth of the Prophet took place, is in this area, facing toward the sanctuary, and the news of it is well known. The mother of Harun al-Rashid, on the west side, is an old structure, and nearby is the Well of Zamzam and the Dar al-Hanwa, also to the west. And the Dar al-Imara (governor's palace) and Mount Safa are on the eastern side of the sanctuary, and the road runs between them. Between them is the Hill of Abu Qubays, and Mount Marwa is on the western side of the sanctuary. The two names Safa and Marwa were the names of a man and a woman who had been there in the Age of Ignorance (Jahiliyya). The people of Mecca used to go from Mount Safa down to Mount Marwa in memory of them, and to take heed. Their original names are those of the two hills. Their mention appears in the noble Quran: "God the Exalted said: Indeed Safa and Marwa are among the signs of God," and the Prophet commanded it. It is said that when the Day of Judgment is about to come, a fire will emerge from these hills, and the boundary of the Haram and the Hatim and the authorities are situated between Mount Safa and Marwa. The Miqat known as Qaf'an and its outskirts is the position of the Miqat of Ihram. The Masjid Nimra is at the end of Mina, and the Masjid of Hanif faces westward toward the sanctuary and guards it, and Mount Arafat faces eastward toward the sanctuary and guards it, and the boundaries of the Haram are...

Abu Bakr [mosque] is three miles away, and the mosque of Aisha is outside the sanctuary boundary (haram), and the first chamber extends to the area of Adhi, which lies between two mountains whose far end is toward Arafa. The cave of Talib ibn Amir is there, and the pilgrims pass the markers of the afternoon and noon prayers here, and the standard of Abd Allah ibn Amir ibn Kawb is also attributed to this place, and the place called Lafad is in Mina. Muzdalifa and Hajj markers of the evening prayer are passed here, and the mountain of Hira is in that direction. Batn al-Makhis is a valley between Mina and Lafad, and Mount Hira is in the direction of Mecca. The Prophet circled the circuits and came there at each station, and the Prophet commanded: "Dwell, O Bahri, in Sind," and he manifested a miracle, taking the middle of Dhu Ba'. Sind is close to Batha — about one parasang — and Mecca is adjacent to Qabia. The cave of Nur al-Hilal is on the road to Medina. It is near Jabal al-Rawda, which belongs to the people of Mecca, on the road at that stage. Al-Safa and Hafith are on Mount Abu Qubays, and Salih is buried there. In the city of Mecca, the Dar al-Nadwa is near the Sacred House, in the direction of the mosque. Ishmael and Hagar slept beneath the Kaaba, and the messengers of Khadijah came and went before the Hijra, and they were received at the pulpit area. The cemetery is on the outskirts of the city, and the young ones were named and registered — first and last among them Abu Umama al-Bahili and his descendants, and Uthman ibn Anama and others. Among the great saints is Abd al-Rahman, revealer of secrets, the master of hadith. Muhib ibn Ali al-Kinani and Abu Sad al-Habbani and al-Rumali, in the time of the Caliph Isa, in the year thirteen-hundred-and-thirty, performed the hajj in Mecca, and a great massacre took place, and the well of Zamzam was filled with the slain, and this is recorded.

And in the circumambulation area, three thousand people were killed, and the Black Stone was taken away, and they returned with it. They threw it into a well at Mirbiz, and it remained in the hands of the Qarmatians for twenty years. In the year three hundred and thirty-nine, in the region of Kufah, the chamberlain Abu Kalam Muti' the Caliph retrieved it, and the Caliph sent it back to the Kaaba, and it was set in the Iraqi corner where it remains to this day — may God the Exalted preserve it until the Day of Resurrection.

Now, setting aside that account, following the arrangement that the author — may God preserve him — will mention in the discussion of the regions: the distance from Mecca to the great cities and the lands of Ibrahim, according to the route described:

To Sultaniyya, which is the seat of royal power, by road: three hundred and eighty-odd farsakhs. By way of Damascus, it is better than any seat of power; by way of Sa'id: one hundred and eighty farsakhs. By way of Damascus and the region of Makhna: two hundred and some farsakhs. By way of Damascus and the province of Fars and Shabankara — Shiraz, which is the seat of the province of Fars — by sea route to Baghdad; and by the sea road to Baghdad, the seat of power is Saba; it is also reachable by sea.

The seat of the province of Khazar by sea route: to the province of Kurdistan, Sinjar, and Zad; the province of Diyar Bakr, Mosul, by way of Kufa, and by way of Damascus, Nakhchivan, by way of Kufa and Damascus. The province of Arminiyya and Tiflis — its seat of power — is by way of Baghdad. Khilat is by way of Baghdad; and Maragha, Nakhchivan, and Jurjan — whose seat of power is by way of Baghdad — and Barda' and Baran and Mughan by way of Baghdad, and Shirvan, and Qabusname by way of Baghdad and Quhistan and Nifrawz, by way of Baghdad, and the province of Khuzistan and Sarkar — whose seat of power is by way of Baghdad — and the province of the Persian Iraq, whose seat of power is Isfahan, by way of Baghdad; and Burujird by way of Baghdad, and Qazvin by way of Baghdad, and by way of Damascus.

Province

The kingdom of Khurasan, Nishapur, and other populous lands — those outside the cities of Hindustan — by the reckoning of Sa'd, in longitude and latitude, seek it as has been mentioned in most places. Since it is based on atmospheric calculations, according to Ptolemy it is weak and [unclear], and the direction of the northern latitudes brings forth [results], and toward the eastern region of the province of Hind, Delhi, Fatuh, and Somnath: distance in degrees is seven hundred and fifty, and the farsakhs of Tarbū are thirty-four degrees. Khitai, the seat of the kingdom of Machin: distance fifty, and in degrees two hundred and fifty farsakhs. Chin (China), the seat of the kingdom: distance fifty and some degrees. Kirghiz and others: three hundred farsakhs, the Khan formerly the seat of the kingdom of Khata, forty-some degrees. Nīrūz, Sukkar, and others: distance twenty degrees, one hundred farsakhs. The valley: distance twenty degrees. Fandhār and Kashmir: distance eighty-some degrees, nine hundred farsakhs. Dār al-Amn: distance in degrees seven hundred and fifty farsakhs, the city of idols. In degrees eight hundred and fifty farsakhs, Khwārazm farsakhs and some degrees. Six hundred farsakhs, Samin and Bulghar: distance eighty degrees, seven hundred. Fifty farsakhs, Safābān: distance twenty-some, in degrees seven hundred and seventy. Fifty farsakhs, Kahtāl: distance twenty-some, one hundred and twenty farsakhs. After Silka: distance seventy-some degrees, eight hundred and fifty farsakhs. The barrier of Gog and Magog: distance seventy-two degrees, one thousand five hundred and fifty farsakhs. On the western side, Hajjāj ibn Muṭarrif set out and reached [there], and it was not far from Medina, so that the total from Medina amounts to eight hundred and eighty-eight farsakhs, and from Egypt [continues on next page].

The city is one hundred and fifty farsakhs; Alexandria is in the middle and ten farsakhs [from it].
The seat of power of Syria is one hundred and sixty farsakhs; the lands of Abyssinia, Baghdad, and twelve [farsakhs].
In Hijr, three hundred farsakhs; the lands of the Maghreb and Abd al-Mumin, Sa'd, in the sea.
The refuge farsakhs of Africa, three; the seat of power, from Dalas, forty-eight [farsakhs].
One thousand two hundred farsakhs for the province of Berber; Sa'd, twelve, in Hijr three hundred.
The farsakhs of Tehran, after it, four; in Hijr, eight hundred and fifty farsakhs.
[Heading:] The route to Baghdad — the Qipchaq steppe, farsakhs; the Alans, Circassians, Ibn Fara.
The district farsakhs; Saqlab farsakhs.
Syria and the highlands; the messenger to Yunan (Greece) — the southern side; the people of Ibn Diyara.
First: Mecca — one should go from Ayda l-Madina to Mecca; it amounts to about eight [farsakhs].
Farsakhs of Safalin: one hundred and forty farsakhs; Imam: one hundred and forty farsakhs.
Aden: one hundred and twenty farsakhs; Anan: one hundred and forty farsakhs; Saranda.
Three hundred farsakhs; and other provinces whose exact longitude was not recorded.
For the provinces neighboring it, by which the amount can be estimated, the total is known.
By estimation, God the Exalted willing, the other lands of Asia are recorded hereunder.
[Heading:] Showing the breadth of the world: Herat — farsakhs; Balkh — farsakhs; Ard [farsakhs].
Farsakhs, Wabr, Albak, Armenia, farsakhs; farsakhs; Yazd.
Route to Baghdad — farsakhs; route to Damascus — farsakhs; Qazvin — route to Baghdad.
Farsakhs; Kurdistan — three days; farsakhs; Diyarbakir.
Mosul; and the route via Najaf, and the route via Damascus, and the route via Karbala, Tiflis road.
The king's seat: route to Baghdad — farsakhs; and Bajilat; and route to [Baghdad] and whatever [follows].

And so on.

Jurjan is a seat of government; the road to Baghdad is [a certain number of] farsakhs, and to Bab al-Abwab likewise. The road from Mughan to Baghdad is [a number of] farsakhs; via Tharwan and Kushtasf to Baghdad [a number of] farsakhs. From Mosul via Najaf [a number of] farsakhs, and via Damascus [a number of] farsakhs. Fartaq, Tripoli [a number of] farsakhs, the lands of Nubar [a number of] farsakhs. Islibnah and [a number of] farsakhs; Khan Baligh is the seat of government of Khitai. In the region of Jabr [a number of] farsakhs; Diyar al-Awn with the tribe of Sa'd, and two degrees. Towards Armenia Minor [a number of] farsakhs, and [a number of] farsakhs to Tantalbah, and [a number of] farsakhs.

The Sanctuary — may God the Exalted have mercy upon it — and the resting place of the Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him. The city of Medina lies in the second clime. Some have said it has been known from ancient times as Yathrib, and in the book of the Climes it is said that Yathrib belongs to the kingdom of Muzasib. That city has its people and community. It lies in a direction such that the valley of Aqiq is to its west and north, and Mount Uhud is to the south [at a distance of] two farsakhs, and salt flats are nearby. The Prophet, peace be upon him, came to terms with the rulers of Persia at the time of the Battle of the Trench; he dug a trench in the sanctuary, and God — glory be to Him — repelled them. A small wall of twenty [cubits?] was constructed; the city is modest in size but blessed. It is fertile, with date palms, streams, farmland, and fine produce. Its people are mostly merchants engaged in trade. Medina is greatly visited. It was said in al-Muslih, quoting the Prophet Abraham: "I have made Mecca sacred; Medina too is sacred by the grace of water."

Among them are the scattered leaves, and it is not lawful within it to shed blood by fighting, nor to cut its trees except [illegible]. It is said: whoever is able to die in Medina, let him die there, for I shall intercede for whoever dies within it. And another said: visiting from afar for the sake of Islam is forbidden except to Medina, whose reputation and renown has spread. The headquarters of the Prophet's mission became renowned, its armies arrived, and the noble domain entered into it. It lies between east and north, and the qibla of Medina is between the two directions. It was the wish that before the arrival of the Prophet, peace be upon him, the rulers of Ghazni and others, and the people of Banu Qurayzah and Banu Nadir would come and settle there. Someone among the Ansar said he would remain, and the tribute after tribute was collected from it, and its special taxes became famous, so they were brought in. The fragrance of fine wood spread from it, and Abu Bakr and Umar and others were present. The Prophet's mission reached Medina after the migration. At that time it was a simple place, built from palm trunks and stone, and a mosque and house were constructed. Khalid and Umar and Uthman added to it considerably, and its walls were decorated and engraved with inscriptions of Hajjaj and Walid ibn Abd al-Malik. Then Abd Allah al-Abbasi further adorned it with fine work. And al-Ma'mun the Caliph made further additions and built caravanserais and schools in its surroundings in abundance. In the time of the great rulers, fine buildings were constructed, and baths were built, and before that there were no baths in Medina. There are also dwellings and residences for the people. Regarding the virtue of the mosque, as mentioned by the companions of the Prophet and as Ibn Mani and al-Muzabri described the gardens of paradise in connection with the Prophet, peace be upon him.

The servants [of God], and in the days of Sarhanfa, a sermon was delivered there, and it is in the noble district of Medina. It is within the city, and the burial ground of Medina is near Baqi', and it is in the noble quarter of the city. There too is the burial place of Ibrahim, son of the Messenger of God, and named among the companions and associates are Imam Hasan ibn Ali, Abd al-Muttalib, and Abbas — may God be pleased with them — and Imam Zayn al-Abidin, Imam Muhammad al-Baqir, and Imam Jafar al-Sadiq, and Uthman ibn Affan. And the bones of the greatest companions are buried there, including Sad ibn Zurara, who passed away in the year the Messenger arrived in Medina. The last of them was Sahl ibn Sad, who died in the seventy-first year. Among the noble and honored ones buried there are Malik ibn Anas, Nafi, the first of the reciters, and Sumayy — they are all buried there. The prayer niche and pulpit of the Prophet fell into Uthman's hands there. It is situated at an appropriate place two miles from Medina, facing the qibla. In that gathering there were steady foundations, and as time passed, in the surrounding quarters of the city there were notable and reliable [structures], the most notable of which were the best. And it was said that beneath it lies the great valley of Ta'if, and among the many valleys — Wadi al-Fara — it is a fine and elevated place, and it is exalted. God commanded that those who bring the pure ones to the valley, as God had caused to be built in the mountains, like a fine platform, and cut from the mountains — that place had the shelter of the righteous. It was commanded that one should proceed there; al-Shurayb — "and for you is the morning." It is well known, and the eloquent saying of the Commander of the Faithful Ali, may God have mercy on him, was a ruling, and none of his descendants knew it, until the Messenger himself came and corrected it.

It was his own special property, and he commanded that Mu'bad and the Lady Fatima and Ali wished to receive a blessing from it. 'Umar prevented them and did not consider it lawful, and said that it was an auspicious sign. As the Prophet (peace be upon him) said — meaning that the prophets leave no inheritance, and what we leave behind is charity — he sent word to Medina, to the fortresses, similar to the domains of Ali and the Prophet. 'A'isha had given it to the Commander of the Faithful, but the Muslims did not accept it and said it was cursed. The shares of the leaders and protectors and governors and commanders — and Shana and Raha and the desert Arabs and the general populace — and Abu Bakr and Hamza and Ghiran — were dispatched straight to Medina, straight to the stages of the road. On the way, Ali's sons went ahead, and having sent word to the Prophet Ahmad, he wrote about ignorance and holy struggle. They sent word that in Medina, at the Friday stage, it is said to be from the ten districts, to the side of Bakr and the crossing of Musa, on the road to Egypt and Syria, named the city of Bajand. All were gathered there, from the region of Surda, in the settlement of the forty, and it was difficult and narrow. All of this was transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn Mas'ud was in the city of Jerusalem, and it is called by the Arabs Bayt al-Maqdis, and in Hebrew they call it thus, and it is in the province of Syria. Palestine was counted among the regions; its longitude was given and its breadth was established on the equatorial line, elevated, and its extremity was set, and it was recorded. Wahb ibn Munabbih the Sana'ani, and Shu'ayb, and Ya'qub — and he commanded the Khazars — took in marriage, and his household was joined to his own household in marriage. And on the road they saw the captives and the travelers, and religious knowledge grew, and angels came down continuously. And the intended purpose of the people of Moses — praised be the Almighty — went forth, and thus it was done, and the final destination was reached.

And this became one of the proofs that when the light of the lantern was extinguished from the column of the Masjid al-Aqsa, it was brought out and given testimony to the claim of others. And among the Bani Isra'il it received full acceptance, and horses were brought to adorn that mosque, and the Bani Abbas caliphs and sultans undertook great elaborations in its construction until it became without equal, reaching perfection. In the quarter of the inhabited world, from the highest point to those buildings — and in the era of Islam too, that mosque was made to face the Kaaba, properly oriented toward the qibla. The Bani Umayya and the Bani Abbas caliphs and sultans undertook great elaborations in its maintenance until it became without equal, and the Franks spent the money of the Muslims on it. They destroyed the Islamic prayer niches and gathered much wealth there, and in the time of Saladin — may God protect him — Islam recovered it, and the hunting ground of Muslim faith was restored. It is written: "And verily We wrote in the Psalms, after the reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants." And the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was informed of this, and from here he arose and sought zeal. He came and settled as a devoted visitor in the sacred mosque, which is one of the most esteemed places of visitation; and most of the great prophets, peace be upon them, came there. And the mihrab of David is also among the most honored, both in construction and in nobility; and among the books it is mentioned that the Station of Abraham, the Friend of God, is about fifteen miles away — some four farsakhs and a few miles — and the enclosures around it are among the well-known places.

The Book of the Forms of the Climates has come, sent to the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis), the village called Kazan, known as Nasir al-Jabal. The birth of Jesus, peace be upon him, took place there, and the Christians call it by this reason. Here is a summary in the description of the conditions of Iran and an overview of its qualities and purposes — an introduction to the mention of the pleasures of the land of Iran from among the kingdoms of the world.

The description of its length, breadth, limits, direction, and the facing of Iran's lands: as for the history, in describing the inhabited quarter, Iran is among its greatest parts, as the sages and philosophers — called "the First Teacher" — have said, and likewise they call it: within it are both a king and a wise man, and that birth of the prophet, peace be upon him, upon this land — he divided it into seven directions, one in the center and six around it. Look: to the south is the land of India; the second is the land of Zanj, Yemen, and Abyssinia; the third is the land of Egypt, Syria, and the Maghreb; the fourth, which is the middle, is the land of Iran; the fifth is the land of Rum; the sixth is Turan and Khazar; and the seventh is the land of China and Tibet and Transoxiana, who divided the boundary of the realm into seven parts.

He set up for himself a strong base in Yemen, gave generously to all directions, and the middle part — which was the most balanced — he gave its station and place to Iran. He gave it the name accordingly, and those who followed it were called Muslims, and this is why the nation of Iran became known. And these kings among the sons of this realm — as they call Iran — I will say: the name of Iran was given, and the Arabs call it Kanua. The fourth inhabited quarter was given its cold and southern share, and the third part was given to the white and red lands, such as this one, and so on.

Between Bisam, Daw, and Narsin, Iran is the subject, and Halab [Aleppo] is to its west. The summary is that the minimum latitude of Iran falls within the inhabited quarter [Rab' al-Maskun], and the details of its surrounding regions and environs show that the length and breadth of the land of Iran, according to astronomical calculation, falls in the middle of the inhabited quarter, based on [the calculations of] Ptolemy regarding its longitude and latitude. From its own meridian and from half the latitude, and in the latitude of the northernmost settlements, the cities of the second and fifth climates are located. According to the second longitudinal zone, from Arpinih to Tarlas, the distance between the two longitudes of Iran, calculated according to Ptolemy, would be eight hundred and sixty-six parasangs [farsakhs]. By the reckoning of the noble Abu Bayjan, it is seven hundred and sixty parasangs. From the city of Sultaniyya to Bursa, three hundred and forty-six parasangs. From Sultaniyya to Burujird, three hundred and [several] parasangs. From the observers' stations and their coordinates — to the Gate of Light — From Qurran, the width of the distance between the two latitudes of the breadth of Iran, measured by astrolabe and calculated according to Ptolemy's method, is three hundred and ninety-eight parasangs, and by the reckoning of the noble scholars, it is three hundred and [several] parasangs. And four-tenths and two-thirds, according to Abu Bayjan, two hundred and seventy-two parasangs, measured and reckoned by the stars. And from Sultaniyya to the Gate of Nur Mubarak, its area according to length and breadth as measured by the astrolabe — and this figure indicates the longitude and latitude of Iran — and all of Iran's measurements of longitude and breadth are straight and consistent.

There is no true correspondence, and there is much difference in this, as we have mentioned. The line of the equator is the highest position, and there too the best nourishment is to be found, as the scholars have agreed. On this basis, the inhabited world extends one hundred and eighty degrees in longitude and ninety degrees in latitude. The first of the seven climates is one hundred and some degrees in longitude, and its latitude is approximately thirty-eight degrees. Now that we have set out the description of Iran's longitude and latitude, know that Iran falls in the middle of the seven climates, and that is what makes it the finest. Iran's longitude from Sind is established at one hundred and some degrees and its latitude at thirty-five degrees, and this is confirmed.

God knows best and is most wise. As for the boundaries of Iran, they are as follows:
Its eastern boundary is the provinces of Sind, Kabul, Saghaniyan, Mawarannahr (Transoxiana), and Khwarazm up to the Nile region, and Bulgaria. Its western boundary includes the provinces of Byzantium, Rome, the Maqfur, and the Kunuz, the Sabs, Syria, and its northern boundary includes the lands of Armenia, Arran, Rus, Moxoene, Burtas, and the Dasht (steppe), stretching toward Farab, Khwarazm, Alan, the Franks, and the boundary between the lands of Abul-Abat and Iran, up to the region of Alexander, reaching the left bank of Mazandaran and Kubid. Its southern boundary is reached by way of Mecca, along the coast toward Yemen and the province of Syria, and through the Persian Gulf connected to the Indian Ocean, up to Sistan.

The provinces of India — if sometimes their rulers have been under the dominion of Iran, and some places have not acknowledged the rulers of Turan — since we have described the boundaries and extent of Iran, it is necessary to set forth what follows.

Showing that the qibla direction for lands lying between south and west — those facing toward the Kaaba — is such that the side on which the Black Stone stands at the corner of the Kaaba is the honored direction. The prophetic tradition testifies to this, for the Two Pillars (the Rukn and the Maqam) are like two eyes, and God has lit them so that their light illuminates all between east and west.

From the middle line of the minaret and the inhabited central strip, some fourteen degrees toward the west is the beneficial point; and since the qibla of each place varies from another in its longitude and latitude, for instance: Iraq, Azerbaijan, Iran, Mughan, Shirvan, Kashaf, Asfan, and the Kurdish regions, and all of Iran, Kurdistan, Rum, Mazandaran, Tabaristan, Jibal, and some of Khurasan — these are indicated as having their qibla facing northward, directed slightly to the left, toward the side of Istanbul.

The rising of the 'Abur and Qal'at al-Arab is to be taken into account in the direction of qibla. At the time of the two equinoxes — vernal and autumnal — the west is to the right hand and the east to the left.

Nearby Armenia, Rum, Diyarbakir, Sabawur, and Georgia should incline their qibla somewhat toward the east, as is proper.

Khuzistan, Fars, Sanbil-Kara, Kirman, the Maghara regions, and some of Khurasan should direct themselves toward the west as described, so that the face of the qibla is rightly found.

Makran, Hormuz, Qays, and adjacent lands should face due south.

For each city mentioned in the principal text, the method is established thus: the seeker of the qibla direction should determine it according to the meridian line, and by bringing out the east-west line in the desired degree, extract the result.

To determine the direction of the qibla, it is necessary to know the longitude and latitude of the desired city.
It has been said that the longitude of Mecca — may God Almighty clarify it — and the latitude of that world is established.
If the longitude of the desired city is equal to the longitude of Mecca, then place the desired city and Mecca
at the midpoint of the meridian line, and if the latitude of the desired city
is greater than the latitude of Mecca, then the direction of the qibla along the meridian line is from
the south side, that is, facing south toward the qibla, with the north behind — this is the proof.
Likewise, if the latitude of the desired city is less than the latitude of Mecca, the direction of the qibla along the meridian line
will be toward the north, that is, when facing the qibla one's face is toward the north.
And if the latitude of the desired city is greater than Mecca, one must lie toward the west of the qibla, and if it is less, one faces east, and in most of the four directions
there will be no great need, and knowledge of the arc measurement and the sine will suffice.
As for this geometry, once the lines of the meridian of east and west are known,
then if the longitude and latitude of the desired city differ from the longitude of Mecca,
in cities whose longitude and latitude are greater than the longitude and latitude of Mecca, the direction of the qibla
will be between south and west; and if the longitude and latitude of that city are less,
the direction of the qibla will be between north and east. And if the longitude of the desired city is greater
than Mecca's longitude but its latitude is less than Mecca's latitude, the direction of the qibla falls between north and east.
And if the longitude of the desired city is less than Mecca's longitude but its latitude is greater than its latitude —

It would be the direction of the qibla, between south and east, within the four constellations, and for this reason determining the direction of the qibla and its orientation caused difficulty in practice.

Sheikh Zahid and Abd al-Rahman Khariq composed for the Sultan of the Seljuks a method for determining the qibla for most places in Iran, which can be understood without recourse to the stars, and Ali ibn Jabal likewise addressed the determination of the qibla direction within the four constellations.

The last of these is that one should take the difference between the longitude of Mecca and the longitude of the desired city, and the difference between the two longitudes in the limit of the complement, and the complement between the two known points. These are arranged on two sides, facing each other, and where they meet defines the inclination of the qibla direction from the crescent's path, and the degree falls accordingly.

If the latitude of the desired place exceeds the latitude of Mecca, Abd al-Kharaf, departing from this Indian method, indicates: in that direction, find the midpoint between the two points, draw a line through the center and connect them — the resulting line gives the direction of the qibla for that place, and that line is its indicator.

Know that the sun has stations, and each station has a name, and there are thirty stations. The first station is Aries, which extends from the first point of the vernal equinox to thirty degrees. This station is called Farvardin, and the sun remains in this station from the first of the month of Farvardin to its end. The ascendant of people of this month is Aries, and the best of days is the day of Hormuz, which is the first day. People of this month are high-minded, pleasant-natured, and fair of face.

The second station is Taurus, from thirty degrees of Aries to sixty degrees. This station is called Ordibehesht, and the sun remains in this station from the first of Ordibehesht to its end. The ascendant of people of this month is Taurus, and people of this month are pleasant-natured, pure, and good in character.

The third station is Gemini, from sixty degrees to ninety degrees. This station is called Khordad, and the sun remains in this station from the first of Khordad to its end. The ascendant of people of this month is Gemini, and people of this month are clever, quick-minded, and pleasant in speech.

The fourth station is Cancer, from ninety degrees to one hundred and twenty degrees. This station is called Tir, and the sun remains in this station from the first of Tir to its end. The ascendant of people of this month is Cancer, and people of this month are chaste, trustworthy, and loyal.

The fifth station is Leo, from one hundred and twenty degrees to one hundred and fifty degrees. This station is called Mordad, and the sun remains in this station from the first of Mordad to its end. The ascendant of people of this month is Leo, and people of this month are magnanimous, generous, and brave.

The sixth station is Virgo, from one hundred and fifty degrees to one hundred and eighty degrees. This station is called Shahrivar, and the sun remains in this station from the first of Shahrivar to its end. The ascendant of people of this month is Virgo, and people of this month are wise, skilled, and pure.

The purpose of this chapter is the mention of the lands of Iran, and Mast, Bast, and every district therein. In describing the kingdoms and throughout the entirety of the Iranian lands, the revenue shares and districts — the treasury rights thereof — have been set apart from Khurasan, which is treated as a separate sultanate, and its accounts are reckoned apart. In the general accounting of Iran, it is noted that several times the accounts were compiled, and at the time of the first reign of Ghazan Khan — may God have mercy upon him — the total was one thousand seven hundred and some hundreds. After that, through the justice of Ghazan, the provinces came to prosperity and flourishing, and the sum reached two thousand one hundred and eighty, and now half again as much has been added to the districts. The provinces benefited from this policy, and the crown lands were properly organized and the revenue from the agricultural quarter was sustained. In the accounts for each year of the reign, in the last year, the amount recorded did not reach the figure, and the envoy was sent with the comprehensive register of the kingdom's accounts. The total was four hundred thousand dinars, one hundred red [gold], and ninety — and now it stands thus. The assessed revenues, by estimation from the time of seventy thousand and four tumans, were presented. And in the year of the blessed era, in the reign of Sultan Malik — may God protect him — it was one thousand, plus one thousand, together with several tumans of red gold coins and gold dinars. The accounts rendered amounted to thousands of tumans in gold and currency. The prosperity and flourishing of the world, from time immemorial to the present, has never been so great as in this era. In the time of the rise of the rightful state, revenues and noble incomes were established such that in this age they have reached such heights as never before. Even if one searched for a thousand years one would not find anything comparable. Such was not possible in the world before, and it shall endure — may this state never cease.

In particular, from ancient times, due to the frequency of events, both should be mentioned, and how pleasant it is to see each year renewed, and how good a custom it is. We hope that God Most High will cast His gaze of mercy and kindness upon the realm of Iran and all other Muslim lands, protecting them from the misfortunes of time and the calamities of the age, granting them security, complete safety, comprehensive goodness, perfect justice, lasting stability, and full well-being, by the grace and generosity of God Most High.

CHAPTER: On the mention of the lands of Arab Iraq, which is called the Heart of the Kingdom

The Arabs call Iran the heart, and since the heart is the sultan of the body, it is most appropriate to begin with its description. Since Arab Iraq falls within the territory of Iran, it is proper to give it precedence, and in truth, since the Commander of the Faithful Ali — peace be upon him — made it his seat of power, and the Prophet rested there, and for several years it served as the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate, precedence is obligatory. From Baghdad to the Persian Sea, the provinces of Khuzestan and Kurdistan and Diyarbakir stretch out. Its length from north to south is three hundred and twenty parasangs. Its width from the Pass of Hulwan to Qadisiyya, opposite the shores of Baghdad, is eighty parasangs. Its total area amounts to ten thousand parasangs. In the time of Umar, when Iraq was endowed as a trust for the Muslims, he directed Ali to survey it. The surveyors measured it out and calculated it to be thirty-six thousand jarib. According to reckoning, the realm measures one thousand parasangs in extent, and each parasang contains forty thousand jarib, each jarib being a square of two thousand in length and width, forming a rectangle. This is the correct figure, and it means the following:

Kaf and Baghdad: the letters [of the alphabet] converge in Amtajun. Kufa is the seat of the kingdom and the burial place of the Commander of the Faithful, Ali (peace be upon him). Baghdad is the mother of cities in the realm, and the shrine of Imam al-Najiba Musa al-Kazim and Imam Muhammad al-Jawad, and the seat of the Abbasid caliphate. Its construction was undertaken, and its fine buildings were first established, and then rebuilt in order. All its gates are arranged in the order of the letters of the alphabet. This city is in the third clime. It is an Islamic city. Its latitude on the equatorial line is 17 degrees, and its longitude corresponds to that figure. According to the calculation of the experts, the evidence of the astrologers confirms this. The people of the craft rely on this and the harm to its inhabitants is attested, as the example of Kufa shows: al-Kufi said that the fortune of Hushandak Sipandad was ruined, the hospital was built, and afterward the ascendant was ill-omened. In Aquarius, the fortress and the Hashimiyya were founded by the Commander of the Faithful Ali (peace be upon him). Abu Dawud, the Abbasid caliph, had the Imam brought and showed him the boundary wall which had been extended. In this wall, every thousand cubits there are cavalry stables. The area from the city to its surrounding districts, as it has been taken to the extreme, has great fertility. Kufa also has permission for irrigation from the flood waters in the reign of the noble kings. In the Holy Quran, mention is made of it, and its founding is attributed to the time of the Bull, and it was thus built. It is considered prosperous, and between Milla and Ghazni. When the Commander of the Faithful Ali (peace be upon him) came to the mosque of Kufa and that noble presence placed his hand upon the column, from his blessed hand the column became the support of the people from that time on.

The people came to that place for the blessing of [the shrine], and it was said that in Kufa the water of the wells was bitter, but that water became sweet, so the people of that place drink from it freely. Their language is Arabic, and there are many scholars among them. Many roads lead to their scholars, including Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr, and in the year [such], among the notable elders and scholars was Abu Umar, and the nobility of the seven provinces is abundant. In Kufa are many types of religious truths, and half a farsang from the qibla direction is the shrine of the Commander of the Faithful Ali, peace be upon him, and from the Arabs it is well-attested that the Blessed One [the Prophet] had commanded that it be so, and his blessed body was brought there and buried, and the rulers of that land paid homage to him. Similarly, the fragrance came, and it was the right thing that it came there. It was buried in the time of Harun al-Rashid the Abbasid, and they made a fine dome over it. Although armies came from various lands and tried to bring the sacred remains away, each time they were prevented from doing so. For many years the people of that land were in awe of it, and a sign was made indicating the grave of the Prophet, and the blessed body was kept there. Al-Muzaffar was mentioned, and the blessed body was washed and purified, and the people came there in great numbers. For eighty years the Daylami ruler Adud al-Dawla raised the shrine to great height, and Ghazan Khan — may God's mercy and pleasure be upon him — built a Dar al-Siyada and a khanqah there. Sultan Malikshah the Seljuk built a minaret in Kufa, and its great height reached to the sky. The Commander of the Faithful then had the minaret completed and made beautiful. On the western side of Kufa, in a garden and pleasant surroundings, in many places one comes to Karbala, the resting place of the Imam Husayn.

And from the names of Jabiri he read, the Great Love — he recounted the covenant of old.

The force and grandeur of its inhabitants: "Every harsh dwelling, however rough, seems pleasant to the eye — but in truth, that pleasantness is like the beauty of a lock without a key, worth nothing." Its cats and livestock are of a certain kind, numbering nineteen varieties. The people there use baths regularly; the people of that place are fair-skinned and good-looking, and of a cheerful temperament. They are known for their elegance, and their natural disposition tends toward refinement and grace. They are deeply absorbed in pleasure-seeking. It is very easy to oppress the common people there and to travel through. From the causes of its reputation, every sought-after thing is obtained there, and through economy and contentment, wealth is accumulated. If the lower classes there are numerous, they tend toward strength and bulk. The lower classes are very numerous; in their language, there is no sultan or ruler or governor whom they hold in regard; marrying costs five hundred [units], and there are various methods of dowry arrangement. Their pride and the totality of their city is that it is the seat of Islam, and the people of Islam there are numerous. In that place there are many Alids, the people of the Shafi'i school of the Sunna, and the Dawudi community is also there. The religions are numerous, and there are many schools (madrasas) there, among them the Nizamiyya, the greatest school in the world, and the best of all the buildings is the one built by the special servants of Baghdad. No caliph ever reached death without being brought there and buried — this is apparent from their shrines. And there are many shrines on the side facing Arabia, including the shrine known as that of Musa al-Kazim and his son Imam Muhammad al-Taqi, peace be upon them, and currently the city of Jallabad has two flourishing shrines. And there are shrines of saints and mystics, such as Ibrahim ibn Adham, Junayd al-Baghdadi, Sari al-Saqati, Ma'ruf al-Karkhi, Shibli, Husayn Mansur al-Hallaj, al-Harith al-Khubbi, Ahmad Sarraf, Abu Muhammad Ruways, Abu al-Husayn al-Nuri, and Abu Bakr al-Shibli.

And the scholars mention Ahmad Khalil and Barjani, and Abu Hanifa said that in our land there is a city that was the shrine of the Abbasid caliphs, and in the city is the shrine of Shaykh Shihab al-Din. The mention of its testaments has a complete explanation and great length. From Baghdad, the distances of the cities of the Arab Iraq are as follows: to Ya'qub is eight farsangs, to Tikrit is thirty farsangs, to Hilla the same number of farsangs. In the time of the Buyids, the divan revenue was approximately eighty tumans, fixed and established. In the region of Baghdad and the environs of Tehran, from its districts and revenue districts, they say Wasit is forty farsangs away. The mention of the affairs of each banner will come, and concerning Baghdad it is well-known — a verse:

and Abla was made in the direction of its alignment, so that every mosque built from that time onward

All the decorated structures, however many times Muhammad may praise them and call them ruins — among them is the Grand Mosque of Shiraz, both sides of which are never left in ruin, and it is blessed. As for Misr (Egypt) and its minarets, which they call Karj, built like a balance, and from the pillars of Ali they are set in motion — they call them "Junban Junban" (the shakers), meaning "move" and they move, and "be still" and they become still. This is something that seems far from reason, yet it is true, and it is among the miracles of the Commander of the Faithful, Ali (peace be upon him). The intellect cannot encompass this, and it is situated in al-Jaqa region, and its fame, honor, and grandeur are complete, and the shrines of the noble companions are numerous there. It is ascribed to the sons of the elders, and its chain goes back through ninety-odd narrators. Among those who have interpreted it are al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Muabbir, Sughlaban al-Nuri, Abu al-Darda, Dawud al-Bajsani, and other masters of sound hadith and others — and it is well known. The reason it is more pleasant is that the water there comes from the middle of the Arab lands, flowing freshly gathered, and from those rivers it is settled. It has a length of four parasangs, and the kingdom of Najw has many gardens, and the gardens are well-irrigated and the water of the Arab highlands descends to it, so that sometimes the highland water rises and irrigates the gardens of Misr. Its length is fifty parasangs and its width is two parasangs, and around it are delightful elevated places, hundreds of which are beyond description, and its pleasantness and the beauty of its fruits are world-renowned. It produces fine fruits, and cheese is made there, and the people there are dark-complexioned, following the Shafi'i school, speaking Arabic and some Persian. Most of the districts of that land are ancient, and the greatest of those cities and towns is the one where the cursed one fell, and after him Iskandar came and raised a monument there.

Abadan: its location, as stated, and the wonders of its surroundings in the world; its latitude from the equatorial line; and a tradition concerning the merit of Abadan is cited here.

It is reported that from its orchards, hundreds of Muslims are sustained against the unbelievers of India. The revenues of its district of Basra and its dependencies, as reckoned by the elder authorities, exceed the tithes.

Among the world's forty wonders, the frankincense and other produce from Abraham's time have been there; and the name of Lubban [frankincense] is pronounced differently in different places, yet its meaning is understood. The city has a gate and a market, and its total revenues and diwan taxes amount to several thousand dinars. Its buildings face the direction of the rains.

In another poem, several places in its tax districts are mentioned, with their produce, climate, and air similar to those of other regions of Arab Iraq, and the waters flowing from Balkh are sweet and pleasant to the taste. The diwan revenues and other assessments of that district amount to six thousand dinars, and among its dependencies is Tikrit.

The Fourth Clime: its longitude is from Khalid Allah, and its latitude from the equatorial line. It lies on the bank of the Tigris on the Arab side, a level and pleasant land. Its circuit encompasses several hundred villages and a fortified town, also on the bank of the Tigris, with a fine climate. Its fruits are good and wholesome, and they are gathered every year in full yield. The place called 'Afr Qut was built by the Romans; some count it among the notable places. It is said that when Abraham completed it, they cast it down and it fell into ruin.

From the Fourth Clime: it borders the gate of Dhu'l-Hawa. Its produce corresponds to that of Ukbara; its water comes from the Tigris of Basra. Its orchards are extensive and its revenues, secondary taxes, and diwan receipts amount to two and a half thousand, five hundred dinars.

Hilla belongs to the Third Clime; its longitude is a number of degrees from the Fortunate Isles [Canary Islands], and its latitude from the equinoctial line. It was built by Ahmad, the Amir Sayf al-Dawla Sadaqa, son of Mansur ibn Dubays al-Asadi, in the reign of the Caliph al-Qa'im, in the year four hundred and eighty-six. The Euphrates flows through its middle; the greater part of the city lies on the western bank, while on the eastern side there are fewer buildings. It is a land of date palms and an abode of two sects, owing to the nature of its air and climate. Most of the time the winds blow from the north, the elevation is one hundred and twenty [units], the climate is temperate, and its people are fair-skinned and stout of body, resembling the people of Baghdad in appearance; they are of Arab stock and active in their affairs. They are mostly partisans [of the Shia], and in this place they have built shrines. Their purpose and belief is that the Imam Muhammad ibn al-Askari, who disappeared in Samarra in the year two hundred and sixty-something, will emerge from there, and the revenues of the divan and other administrative matters are arranged accordingly.

Juwan belongs to the Fourth Clime; its longitude from the Fortunate Isles is a certain number of degrees, and its latitude from the equinoctial line. Qa'im ibn Naghrun settled it. It is now ruined and of little account; there is a small fortification there, and in its environs are some villages and hamlets. There is a tomb of a certain person from Sawa nearby. Its divan revenues are six thousand dinars. Hayyim belongs to the Third Clime; it was once a flourishing city, but is now ruined. It is mentioned in poetry and well known, and it was once a seat of power. In it, Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir ruled and showed generosity to kings. The foundation is still standing and was of fine construction; part of it is still upright. Its buildings are now in use and intact, and its divan revenues are seven hundred thousand dinars. Khaliqtiyya is also ruined, but to this day the traces have not entirely disappeared.

The waters of Halwan remain on the bank and cause the area to be among the notable types of places. Its revenue is two thousand dinars, and it belongs to the region of Mu'abbir. From Dahlar the water flows, and for this reason it is called Duhail, and the notable town of Sahmistan Labkha has a respected position, and there are about a hundred villages, and its elevated places are pleasant. The revenues and allowances of Baghdad are seven thousand dinars. This people belong to the fourth clime, and the city is in the middle, and the air there is better than other places of the Arab Iraq, and in its surroundings there are fine pasturelands. The revenue of its administration is seven hundred and sixty thousand dinars. The city is situated between Wasit and Baghdad, and the air there is somewhat humid, and there are date-palm groves. Dusiyya belongs to the third clime, and from Mada'in it lies to the west; it was Anusnabr. It is situated between Mada'in and Antioch, but now it is ruined. Dadh — it belongs to al-Dijayl al-Tahmirin, and its territory lies along the banks of Mihran, and its revenues are not considerable. Its administrative revenue is a certain amount. Laya'bit is in the direction of al-Khata. The administrative revenue is several thousand dinars. Samarra belongs to the fourth clime. It has a fine city with gardens and various fine buildings and villages around it. Its latitude corresponds to the equatorial line, and in relation to the Gate, its air is among the finest of the Arab Iraq lands. Al-Mu'tasim Billah Muhammad ibn Harun al-Rashid built its structures and established it as the seat of government, and it extends seven farsakhs in length. Its conditions were such that he brought people there from various places, and they built it and called it Surra Man Ra'a ("Whoever Sees It Is Delighted"), and there is a tall pavilion there.

He built and in Samarra made a grand mosque, and a stone bowl in which were inscribed love and seven sins, and half of it was placed as a border within that mosque; they recited from the bowl twenty-nine stones of proportion, and in the mosque he built a minaret of three hundred and seventy cubits, such that it rose in every era, and in the upper part of its minaret there was no equal in construction, and in the mosque there is the shrine of Imam Ali al-Naqi and of the son of Imam Hasan al-Askari, and Musa al-Abbasi surnamed him; in Samarra he built many buildings, especially a fine pavilion, greater than any seen in Iran even in times of raid, and of a name he called it Jafar and it was read as such; the Tomb of the Commander of the Faithful Husayn was destroyed by al-Mutawakkil, and the people were forbidden from going there, and they were driven away, and afterward he killed them and threw them into fire so that no trace remained; now the place is known for its suffering and its sacred precincts are ruined; grain used to come from there, and the water of the Euphrates was counted and the dues from three areas of the nature of Khorasan are reliable and its administration is well-organized and sound; that woman was named from the lineage of Khosrow, and they called her Quba, and in the time of Yaqub it was built on the bank of the Nahr River, and its bounty flows through the city, and all its villages practice agriculture, and it has many gardens and forests, and many histories and chronicles exist there, such that three hundred historians have recorded from Egypt, and its climate is fortunate, though many are afflicted with fever; and the smaller cities of this region, whose people are descended from the lineage of Khosrow, with established estates and revenues, and its administration is stable, and there the treasuries are renowned, and eighty fortresses exist.

The state revenues amount to sixteen and a half thousand dinars, arranged accordingly. It belongs to the Fourth Clime; its longitude is measured from the Fortunate Isles (Khalidat), and its latitude corresponds to the line of "Atawa." It is a middle-sized city with many provinces, having water, fine air, and good produce. Facing it is the district of Haml; Askar Shabur was built on the flanks of this region — it was a middle-sized city but is now ruined. Qadisiyya was a middle-sized city, located toward the direction of Mada'in, in the region of Arab Iraq, but is now ruined. Muqtara-Shirin belongs to the Third Clime; it is well known and great. A citadel was built there with a fine structure, and from ancient times it has been described as having streams and flowing water. The stronghold became renowned for its beauty. Fine pavilions were built there as well as watchtowers of excellent aspect, commanding the surroundings. The caravanserais there are well-maintained. The water of Hulwan is sweet, drawn from that place; the air is without equal though harsh. During the heat of summer the hot winds blow here so that habitation becomes difficult. The revenues and comforts of this place are noted. There are fine pastures and meadows around Quryan, which is a middle-sized city; its state revenues are one hundred times its local dues, totaling fourteen thousand dinars. The city of Hamra is situated two farsakhs from Baghdad, on the bank of a canal on the western side; it is a well-cultivated place. In Baghdad the caliphs built many fine structures. The Caliph Mu'tasim built there among residences and monasteries; many dervishes and pious persons reside there, and it is well guarded by a boundary. The state revenues thereof are assigned to the district of Banu 'Isa. Mada'in —

From the third clime, its longitude is from Najrar to the Khalidats, and its latitude is from the equinoctial line. Tahmurith bound the demons and founded it, and it was called Abad Khwanan and Jabantalk. The scholars say it is the greatest of the cities of Iraq, known as Mada'in. They say Mada'in consists of seven cities and six other cities: Qadisiyya, Rutiyya, Hirah, Babylon, Hulwan, and Mughruwan, and they were fine cities. Aksum is its fortress, and Jamshid founded it in Mada'in upon the drum of nature's foundation. Alexander the Roman built it — a magnificent place — and kings from Nawus onward made it flourish, though it was ruined. Ardashir Babakan then made it a city of the Arabs and built the Dar al-Khilafa there. He wished to level Babylon likewise, but could not achieve this, and for some trifling reason he fell short. The Sasanian kings mostly built the Dar al-Mulk there, and Shapur Dhul-Aktaf placed it in that position. Anushirvan the Just built a palace there — a marvel. He built it so that no craftsman could replicate it, and its courtyard and its interior were extraordinary. Its tailors' market was a hundred and some cubits long, and the treasury in it was vast, with brass gates. Its length was eighty-two cubits, and its height fifty-five cubits, and the width of this palace was great. Many works of beneficence were done there, and in its fine workmanship and solidity of construction it is said: "It is the reward of virtue and knowledge — until today it remains in ruin." It is said that a caliph went there, and when he reached it, Abdallah the minister sought to demolish it. They said it should be left, for it is a monument of ancient kingship. Another wished to ruin a nearby city, and the city itself stood solid. The caliph built it up, but it was not heard; and still it remains.

You will weep and be unwilling, as the affairs of the great ones do not vanish, and in the treasuries there is wonder. It appeared that from the grace of the origin it was established — there is no escape from the grace and recompense — and there was nothing, and it was concealed by the veil, so that generation after generation became established and it said: When the treasuries of goodness were exhausted, the whole land was ruined, and not a single person of the people remained. They made it a royal abode, and again called it ruined, and made it the chambers of the Iwan. At the birth of the Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, miracles appeared and it was shattered. This is among the greatest, and the witness is Abd al-Bar, whose lineage traces to Muhammad Mustafa. The arch remained in its place — what was hidden from the ancients was not hidden, nor was what should be known concealed from us. The work, from wherever it stood on its foundations, reached the western side to the summit and was not demolished. Such a person would come of that lineage who would cast down what is beside the gnostics, and the city was thus. God was present — it was not absent — and now the city of Ibn Khaza is on the western side. It remains, and on its eastern side, across from the Iwan, there are Persian-speaking settlements. In that land there is a well, like something of later times, among the miracles of Salman. When he died, his honey-sweetness did not cease; something fell into the well and another person was present: water rose to the top of the well, and one was given of it and departed from its place. Thus the sweetness remains. In the lower part, in a few places, the water does not give sweetness — the standard is there. The great master and lord Abu al-Wafa are buried in that land, and Shir Ali son of Ali son of Abdullah — of noble lineage — was the caliph, and from the streams many things flowed. They built villages and disputes, and a hundred and seventy villages remained and were not elevated. All the provinces of al-Mustansir are to the west, located opposite Baghdad, and from Dhu al-Hijja...

Every Jesus [ʿĪsā] has the revenues of the divan; each ʿĪsā with eighty-seven rules of Lumalan and its towns, with orderly arrangement of carpenters and wage-laborers — so it has been. Munawwar al-Mulk: some say that Solomon son of David dug it, and some say a hired overseer did so; some say that Alexander the Roman and his companion Shapur son of Isk Dalarab were the ones who expelled them from Faran, and drove them from those regions — more than three hundred and two. The benefit through ʿUmar was complete; the revenues of the divan are beyond need.

Nahr Wan: It is a city of no small size. It is located within the territory of ʿIraq al-ʿArab, in the third clime, on the bank of Samarra, and that river is called Alhaja Matar — some also call it that. The city is now in ruins.

Nuʿayminah: It is a qasaba [administrative town] between Baghdad and Wasit, situated on one side; it has much Takhlistan [fertile gardens]. Habīl and Lapish are a fortified village [dih], one of its dependencies, and it has a great fortress; it has much Takhlistan and many orchards.

Wasit: It is a city set firmly; it has a citadel, and it is on the bank of the Euphrates, set in the middle. It is one of its dependencies, and in the surrounding villages it is beneficial up to about fifteen farsakhs [leagues]. It has two banks of water, orchards and gardens, many cypresses and much Takhlistan; in every direction it draws from freshwater springs; the air is extremely temperate; there are walnut trees, almond, date-palm, and citrus trees intermingled, and its fruits are pleasant. It is neither fully a cold region nor fully a hot region, but in temperature it is known since ancient times.

The city is Islamic, and it is in the third clime. Khalid said: and its longitude is at the equator. Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf built it, and between its landmarks toward the side of the Tigris it lies to the west; it has much Takhlistan, and the city — on account of its air, as Yaqut [mentions] — Babel.

The revenues of the imperial diwān amount in total to forty-four nūmāns and
one thousand and some dinars. Chapter Two: On Karkī, Bilād, and Iraq.
It is one of the forty towns, and the climate around it is considered [favorable].
That is to say, it is related to Bakr and Jand, and is inclined toward the borders of the provinces of Azar[bāyjān]
and Kurdistan, Khuzestan, Fars, the caves, and the provinces of Jīla and Nāt.
Its length along the plain is one hundred and sixty farsakhs from Sefīd-rūy to Nārid.
And from the mountains of Nāt to the region of Nūzistān, one hundred farsakhs — before the month of Bilā.
Iraq has four notable cities, and they are counted thus: Jār Shumā [or: four of them].
The approximate reckoning of Iraq's length and breadth was one hundred by one hundred and one hundred farsakhs, give or take.
Isfahan is a complete city; in the seventh clime it was among the greatest.
That same place — before it, the air and water there were finer than any place along the Caspian shore.
Its situation is similar to that, but it is [also] good in other respects, and those who have seen it say it is fine.
The men were capable, and the town was pleasant — one could find all manner of things there.
The imperial revenues of these provinces, in terms of fifths and sixties and seventieths, remain outstanding.
According to the account, in the name of Amīn al-Dīn, the annual summary was recorded.
The registered total in the diwān of Iraq was five thousand two hundred and seventy
nūmāns of assessed tax that had been collected, but now, on account of the destruction and ruin,
it has fallen to [a lower number of] nūmāns. This is for the city of Isfahan.
Tīrawzān and Fārfān are reckoned from the fourth clime; their length and breadth [are such].
And some are taken from the third clime; their longitude extends to Ṭajz and Abarkha al-Dāt.
From the equator, the original [figure] was fourteen; there are Karan and Kūkangat.

And along the streams and plains of Hind there are no farms; some were built by Tahmuras and Dhul-Qarnayn, and they were constructed as Kayfabad of the first kings. The local people were driven away from there and the Berbers settled. The garrison took up positions and fortified the town with walls, and Hassan ibn Buya surrounded it with a double wall and a citadel. The city's ascendant is such that its star is obscure and problematic, with four signs. It has twelve gates, and the air is moderate in summer and winter. Heat and cold do not harm anyone who stays there; earthquakes and heavy rains that cause destruction occur there. The soil is such that men buried in it from outside do not decay; anything planted in the earth there grows well and is preserved, whether grain or other crops. For several years it does not suffer plague or chronic disease or epidemic, and rivers flow on the southern side. The outskirts of the city produce abundance and the city's flowing water runs well. The water of its wells is at a depth of six or seven cubits, meaning river water is nearby. Whatever seeds are brought from elsewhere do not grow well there, and if less than a certain amount is brought it will not grow as desired — unless one finds a local source. The air is such that it keeps things fresh; the air is not putrid or foul-smelling, and barley grain grows well. The middle markets are of moderate price. The southern winds blow there, settling down, and among the specific fruits: quince, pear, grape, Uthmani plum, sour plum, and pistachio grow well there. All the island's fruits are sweet, and those brought from the east ripen and people eat them well. Those fruits do not keep there and their sweetness does not last.

He gave one, and there were four doors, a great camp with no obstacle, and the people of Handlan and Wana kept it.
Elsewhere there is the place of Qazir Su, with abundant pastures that are great, full of birds and game, well managed and skillfully maintained.
In that city there are many schools, monasteries, charitable foundations and doors of goodness.
Among these is the prayer-place of the Seljuk Sultan, a stone hall in the shape of a weight, weighing ten thousand mann, brought there by the Indians; this Sultan, with the help of the commanders and five hundred strong men, carried it and threw it down from the heights, with the people of that place watching in amazement, showing their bravery.
And if they are of any sect, in their obedience in every state they hold most of their time; they cling to custom and habit at every turn, and are always pleased.
At the time of the manifestation of their customs and habits in that city, they faced the ambiguity of the matter in the manner of ambergris. For this reason it was said in verse: Isfahan is a great city but it has been diminished, as is well established. And it was said in Ambergris: it stands as Isfahan in Rome and is established. And Ismail said in verse: Nadir and the desert are a favor and a grace; the enemies, the oppressors, the lord of the tongue, and the brave one, the king and the mighty, the greedy one who fills the plain with blood and brings bloodshed, and the number of the corrupt increases; every one who joins adds a hundred. And from the holy Prophet, peace be upon him and his family: the tradition of Abdullah concerning the Dajjal, that he will emerge from the Jews of Isfahan and reach Kufa; so let him flee from Medina, for he is from the Mountain. And a people from Qazvin said: O Messenger of God, what of Qazvin? He said: whoever comes out of it, God will be with them, and there is none among them who is an unbeliever.

The revenues and fiscal rights of Isfahan amount to a station of glory, thirty-five and seven hundred, and several other sources of income are obtained, no fewer than seven districts and four quarters, with villages and ten settlements whose agricultural yields are collected.

In the northern districts there are seventy and some villages, ten of the Zahran lands of the Baman region and its surroundings, and the township of Kashmor in the environs of Isfahan, which Sayyid Iskandar built and restored, and Sassan renewed and rebuilt its structures, making it among the greatest of villages.

Ninety-eight villages exist in Khuzzan and Qartaban, with women of distinguished families, and truly this district, like a fine jewel, surpasses others; it is the garden of glory where the sun shines, and in the district of Qal'a there was the fortress of Tahmur, tied by two bonds. The Kafnanad area, together with its meadows, was built as a refuge, the district of Sabim being a fine locality.

About one hundred villages exist, with forests, orchards, and caravans and their great settlements. The district of Majin is connected to the gardens and settlements of Naghdi, altogether joined.

Forty villages exist, with Tha'sub, Waddaran, and Jar-Sasahan among them. The greatest of their villages and this district are watered by running streams, and Bulban flourishes; one hundred villages exist among the greatest settlements.

In this district the waterworks were built and other regions draw water from its channels, and Bahman-baz Isfand built a shelter for the district.

Seventy villages exist in Gurnan, Da'iyan, Gulistan, and their great settlements. Eighty villages exist in Askashan, Sarhiyan, Manar, Khurdan, Fanakarun, Kuhan, Kathim, Uwnan, and their greatest villages.

Monday and Hishnabad are among the villages of Farfan; its chief town has two villages: Ankahran and Kaman. The largest of these villages — that is, the most important hamlets, meaning those counted among them — are like the city of Bakr and Kab, so to speak, because in each of those villages there are nearly a thousand houses, with markets, schools, mosques, khaneqahs, and bathhouses. Among its notables is Sheikh Ali Sahl al-Isfahani, who is said to reside there. The city of Shahrud is below it, and that city is well-known and celebrated.

The Zayandeh Rud flows above Isfahan. Its length is reckoned from Jarabarkhaladaat to Farij, and its latitude from the equator to Karakun is within the bounds of Isfahan, which is a well-built place in terms of climate, grain, fruit, cotton, character, disposition, and the faith of its people. The fiscal revenue of the city of Shahfuruz and its environs is four thousand and five hundred dinars according to the register, and the revenue of the province of Isfahan — and Kabin Panah — is one tuman. From Isfahan to Diyarbakir and to the regions of Iraq the distance is reckoned as follows: to Disnān thirty-four farsakhs; to Abyaj Labi, Buzdalij forty farsakhs; to Buruj, Burulbar sixty-six farsakhs; to Jawfa, Dinān thirty; to Bakr Sij, Nuhum, Daljan thirty farsakhs; to Ray, eighty-six farsakhs; to Shahfarund and Ān sixty farsakhs; to Saveh sixty-four farsakhs; to Sultaniyya one hundred and six farsakhs; to Farzabin ninety-two farsakhs; to Fumisha-Fars fourteen farsakhs; to Kashan thirty-two farsakhs; to Karaj forty-five farsakhs; to Lurdkan-Buzurg thirty farsakhs; to Nazar twenty farsakhs; the distance between them twenty-six farsakhs; to Nahavand seventy-four farsakhs; to Hamadan sixty-two farsakhs; to Zanjan — this city was once rivaling Ray, and between these two cities there are many notable places.

And its other localities are favorable, and the town of Hufuf in Wawa — its revenue here was seven hundred tomans, and some of the domain of Rey was held by those whose governance brought about the killing of the blessed Imam Husayn (upon him be the curse of those who wronged him), and that story is well known. The city of Daylamites is from the fourth clime.

It is the mother-city of Iran by virtue of its antiquity; they call it the Mistress of Cities. Its longitude is measured from the Fortunate Islands, and some say from the equatorial line. The city is mild and its northern climate is pleasant, but its water is disagreeable, full of harm and danger. In this matter it has been noted — I saw a verse that the king of Alamut replied to someone: "Do not weep for what has slipped from your hands and feet," to which the other said, "You, who have no soft robe to wear, whose faint scent leads one to judge it" — the city is attributed to the Prophet. Hushang added to the construction of that building, and it became a great city. Then it fell into ruin, and after that one rebuilt it many times. Ibn Dulaf and al-Husayn revived its construction and the city grew great and prosperous, with a thousand aspirations. The ascendant of its construction is five degrees of Scorpio. Its people engaged in mutual enmity and conflict, and many thousands of men were killed and it was completely ruined. After the Mongol interregnum it fell into slumber, and then Ghazan Khan, whose name may God honor, gave orders and sent governors there. It was restored and all the notables arrived, and concerning the pleasantness of that city a debate was held between an Isfahani and a Razi — it was said that the soil of Isfahan makes people sluggish and forty of them are no match for one, while the Razi said that the soil of Rey makes a man of forty as capable as two. By this argument the Isfahanis prevailed, and the citadel of Tabarrak is at the foot of the mountain on the northern side.

It has come to pass that the province of Qasran lies beyond the dense forests; its air is pleasant and its provisions abundant. Most of the time there is plenty and cheapness there, though occasionally hardships occur. The province produces much grain and other foodstuffs for people; the province of Barndavan has cold winters and [difficult conditions], though its orchards and fruit trees are not without excellence. The majority of the inhabitants of most provinces are Twelver Shia, except for a few towns and places which follow the Hanafi school of law.

The province of Rai has given much, similar to the cities of Shahriyar and Sanuj, and its surroundings are mixed with other provinces. The province of Fatabuyeh is well-known by its name, being prosperous and populated, and its districts are of various types and ranks. As recorded in the geographical compilation, it was inhabited in the time of Bahram Gur, and it lies between Isfahan and Rai, connected to one another.
