In the geographical works and the Masalik al-Mamalik it is mentioned that the province of Fatabuyeh had one hundred and fifty prosperous stages and settled agricultural areas. We shall mention some of them as they appear in the Masalik al-Mamalik: in the time of the ministers, the revenue of Fatabuyeh was one hundred and sixty thousand dirhams. Most of the villages, way-stations, and dependencies were under the divan. Ali-Abad is one of the major villages and has its dependencies, including Kanja and others that belong to it, and its neighboring districts used to have disputes with one another. The people of Ali-Abad were known for trouble-making, strife, and ill conduct — they were such that at times they even showed enmity toward the reigning king. It had two rivers, one of which was famous, flowing past inhabited settlements of the region, and the other coming from the north of the fortress, known by a certain name, flowing past water-mills. It could accommodate forty horsemen [or: forty water-channels], and the people there held firm beliefs and accepted no one else's authority but their own.

They did not accept, and during the period of Mongol turmoil, with enmity, the ignorant and the unknowing together carried out massacres; Kuljar was ruined and surrounding villages were deserted. There are Afghans in that region; the village headmen were near the road, and the water of Siyah Ab of Sikim flows there. The people there are followers of the Shia faith and rejoiced at its victory. In those Afghan villages, the people of Anqar — including the holder of the divan's authority — were in command, such as Malik Ghiyath al-Din, Malik Qutb al-Din, and the one known as Batli Bansak.

The foundation of that place would be sought through the waters flowing between those hills toward the west; Malik Qutb al-Din built a bridge over the river, and seventeen springs flow there, none of which dry up, and a fine bridge was built. Malik Najm al-Din, a Circassian slave, was there, and he guarded the children of that locality. Abd al-Karim reports that caravans traveled through there and that Malik Taj al-Din built a structure on the bank of the Siyah Ab river; that place is now known as Bubal Karim, and in the rocky cave there is a khaneqah. Malik Ghifar al-Din together with his servants and the women went and constructed a bridge there, which remains famous to this day. Now their descendants hold the lordship of that region, and people continue to arrive there. Sheikh Jamal al-Din Mutahhar Ali, one of the children of the Shia, resides there. Those people were considered respectable; it is reported that Sultan Abu Said ibn Uljaytu Sultan convened a council at his court for Malik Shahr-Yad, and the Sultan dispatched him to take charge of the district of Malik Mashal, sending him onward to Halu.

When Malik Butaq descended from his horse, he came seeking a robe of honor. The king said he had brought a written note for the price of the robe — one that required a seal — and requested the seal. One of the advisors, Abu Aghal, informed the king and said: "The king wrote the amount in dinars." He said fifteen tumans. The king said: "Be silent! If the amount had been written in tumans with the seal applied, then the gardens would be fine and of good quality, and the people there, whom God has blessed, bow their heads in submission, and its gardens and houses, well-built and each landowner maintaining their own property independently, and the overseer of Sayyid in Naqla. It is prosperous and good; one finds there paddy and rice fields in abundance, and their water and firewood supply is plentiful, and the people there are busy and industrious. The great Khan, Malik Fakhr al-Din Thanf, built structures there, gathered the people and settled them. To the north lies the mountain region, and beyond it is the province of Makran, and another province. Its villages and districts extend three hundred and sixty parasangs in width. The province was founded by Firozan Sasan, and it is also known by the name of Firozon. Among its greatest villages are Sahnam and Siyumar. The army is strong; Rawshid, Tehran, Firozon, and Bahram are among its great villages. They were found there, and mostly at those times the raiders and brigands would be present, and at times they would come and conflicts would arise; they would overcome that province's territory and the lands of Taband, and it was a source of concern. Peaches and apricots and other fruits are found there. Among the saints resting there are: Ibrahim Khwan of the Qurra Sab'a (seven canonical readers), and Imam Abd al-Azim, and Sayyid Abd Amtah Abyaz, and Shaykh Jamal al-Din Abu al-Fath...

Of the congregational mosques and the book: The congregation of Banu Hasana al-Fatiya and Hisham — endowed upon the walls. Whatever is within it amounts to fifteen tomans, one thousand and one hundred and fifty dinars. The people of that place are mostly Twelver Shia, except for the mountain village of Markab.

Another place: The Hanafi school of thought is established there. Tehran is a notable town, and its climate and air are pleasant. This governorship has some revenue, and in that area there are considerable villages. The road has been well maintained in former times, and now it has become a proper town.

Its produce and fruits are agreeable, and the people there are Twelver Shia. The grains grown there and the fodder for animals are plentiful, and the water and air are pleasant.

It is recorded that in the time of al-Muhallab, the buildings of three cities were constructed: six thousand madrasas and khanqahs, six hundred and sixty public baths, forty-six thousand and four hundred mosques, nine thousand sultanic residences, one thousand seven hundred minarets, one thousand five hundred cisterns of running water, ninety-nine quarters and neighborhoods of six types.

In every district were one hundred lanes, and in every lane thirty mosques, and in every mosque one hundred lamps lit each night. The total number of inhabited dwellings was one thousand six hundred and ninety-six. The city was known as Sultaniyya.

Although in its earliest period it was attributed to Qand Nawbin, since in recent years the city of Sultaniyya has been established and made the seat of royal power, it is preeminent. Sultaniyya is considered to be in the fourth clime. Its longitude is such, and its latitude from the equinoctial line is such.

It was founded by Uljaytu Sultan, son of Arghun Khan, son of Abaqa Khan, son of Hulagu Khan the Mongol — his father being Ghazan Khan, and Uljaytu Sultan having preceded him.

Many a station was assigned in his own name; the ascendant of Ammar's district was in Leo — our land and people — just as Oljaytu Sultan had it founded: ten thousand dwellings, and Oljaytu Sultan had it built; its accommodations and all its memorials remained: thirty thousand dwellings, and citadels and fortresses carved from stone — the palace of Oljaytu Sultan — and other buildings are there. The revenues from it amounted to ten thousand dwellings. The Mongol of that region was inclined toward it, and its water springs and aqueducts are fine, its digestion good, its wells excellent there, of a cool and pleasant nature. It is generous; whoever passes through its air becomes enlivened, and all who come there are refreshed. Its game birds are exceedingly fine, and the hunting grounds are excellent. People come there from every province; their tongue is Persian mixed with local speech, and it is full of people of all religious persuasions. Now such great buildings have been constructed there that in no other city since the beginning have the like been built. The revenues assigned there from the divan are established. For twenty years, the Kurds who were there used to collect thirty tomans annually. And from another sovereign city: the distance to that city is required — from it to Firang (Frankish lands) is one hundred and six farsakhs; Asadabad is one hundred and thirty farsakhs; Farsakh to Panjah; Farsakh Najan is without number; Farsakh to Sava, to Mahall, and two farsakhs to Saja Sinj; farsakhs of Qandayn, fifty farsakhs to Qom; seventy-two farsakhs to Kashan; the direction of Qazvin. As for this pen, it is from the fourth climate; Abu Khalid al-Alam is the source, and its latitude from the equatorial line — by this reckoning it is estimated — and for that reason these people have always been devoted to God, and the Mulahida (Ismailis) and various factions have been there. There are many traditions about that event and its virtue, and its shrines are well known. In the memorial books it is recorded, on the authority of Samhal al-Faqih Jamu ibn Abdallah al-Kafadhani: The Messenger of God said: "Follow me and draw near to me, for he is at the gates of Paradise" — by Sakib, O Lord.

The troops read, and the account of that, although it is explained in the book of Kuzba, is here also briefly recalled. In the book of Tibyan it is mentioned that Shapur son of Ardeshir Babakan built it. Shapur the Elder gave it that name — it seems that that city had canals and houses between the rivers Jow and Abhar, which he constructed. The traces have been obliterated and its people are gone. Those who are reckoned as followers of Shapur Babakan inhabit it, and it is well known. And it is written that the fortress-city of Astan Qandin, which is now a seat of justice, is in the midst of the city of Shapur, possessing its districts. The Sasanians built it. The date of that king's construction was in the year seventy-three after Alexander, under the auspices of the architect of the constellation of Gemini. That [city] remained and still stands. In the time of the caliphate of Uthman, Walid ibn Utba al-Umawi sent Said ibn al-As al-Umawi there with forces, and he settled people in that fortress and it became a city through the Abbasid eras. In those environs he built another provincial city and called it Madinat al-Mawsil, and it is flourishing and blessed. Other settlements are well known and are fortunate and blessed. When the caliphate of the brave one was established, and the cities mentioned fell into disarray, the lords themselves departed. They settled three of those cities and others that had fallen into ruin. His death came, and his successor completed what had been begun and finished it according to the caliph's intention, and it became likened to a great city fully inhabited, and its water comes from before. In its countryside there is much abundance, and in each year a good harvest is brought in a certain manner. Thereafter the island and India abound and there is no shortage of water and fine villages, most of the time plentiful there. And that place is fine and pleasant, and its fruits and crops are good and flourishing.

And the city [continues on next page]

It has fine hunting grounds and good pastures, and about a farsang away there is a spring of water. The local people are Hanafi in the summer seasons, and the majority of the people there follow the Shafi'i school, with some Shi'a and Hanafi adherents. Despite being near Julad, the hot regions have settlements, and the fodder for camels in its deserts is better than in other provinces. The camels of middle quality are more valuable than those of other regions. There is the shrine of Imam-zadeh Husayn, son of Imam Ali ibn Musa al-Rida, and the tomb of one of the Companions, and shrines of saints and great men, such as Radi al-Din Talaqani, Abu Bakr Shadlaf, Ibrahim Marvi, Shams al-Taj Samari, Ibn Masa the hadith scholar, Malik Qan, Yibi, Nur al-Din, Jamal al-Din Husayn, Imam al-Din Bafi, Shaykh Ahmad Ghazali, and others. The government revenues are fixed at fifty thousand mans and a half, and its dependencies number about one hundred. There are prosperous villages in the district, notable places such as Qarchin, Hanaj, Farnin, Shal, Sukarna, Abad, Siyah Dahan, Suniqan, Shahshta, Sharafabad, Fazaid, Nazanin, Majin, and similar places, and the revenues of those provinces are administered by the government. Khalil Ismail ibn Abbad, the Prophet's companion, passed away in the year three hundred and seventy-three, and it is said that he saw in the books of hadith that at the end of times it would be said: "Whoever enters through the Gate of Paradise by his good deeds, its walls would stand between them." May God forgive his sins, great and small. The city is warm and hot, so it is recommended to study the hadith. It is reported from Abd al-Aziz al-Murdafi: "Seek relief from your troubles, O people." Among the virtuous of Daylam it is said she is called al-Haqaniyya, and among the brothers of al-Duzqam she is called al-Iskandariyya. Whoever makes a connection with either of them on the eve of Rajab will enter Paradise. Ahmad ibn al-Aziz said: "O God, make it so."

Until it was adorned — indeed, in one of the two of them there are medicines and a dwelling — for its own sake a grand building was constructed in the district of Jawsan. That land, which people call the "gold-digger's estate," was attributed to the settlement of Lahisht Qazwa. Among the Kamiyans, for years the master Aba Ibrahim spoke with the tongue of Diblaq. Majd al-Din was worthy of the people of learning and had no opportunity [for rest]. Amir Sharif Abu Ali Ja'far repaired those ruins and [the place called] Sunbul. Husam al-Din Muhammad ibn Abd Allah Miraj undertook great constructions and restored most of the decayed quarters; he built their noble structures and fine buildings. Imam Jamal al-Din, along with Abu Birza, when the Mongol army came that time, they [the people] fled in terror. Its shoulder-ridge extends toward Russia — it has been connected to Azerbaijan; its valleys and gorges are immense. The fourth: its length extends in a southern direction; its latitude is established, and today it is known. Siyawush the Kayanian built it, and his brother Iskandar completed it fully, and in it [there are] many castles. Baha al-Din Hande, governor of the Atabeg Tushtakin Shir, one of the Seljuqs, built it, and all of it was named after a certain [man]; its villages number several thousand, and its excellence is renowned. Its climate is cold, and its water is scarce; they say the city's air is unwholesome and harmful. The Sultanate of Genghis [Khan] carried off its people to Qazwin. Although its grain is plentiful and its summer cotton yields are low, the lords of Armenia came there. Al-Sufyani and al-Alawi, Abu Ali, and Kilas Manikat — the people of that region were prominent there, and the oppression of that city lasted for a thousand [days or years]. Shaykh Abu Bakr of Talahityan — its great mosque is worthy and fitting, and part of it is old, truly. Its villages number four thousand in that region, and its districts include Talash, Qirqan, Khutashan, Askubara, Dilan, and the districts between the borders — and in the mountains of Kuhistan it has fallen to ruin, and that province is under the rule of Taki — may God's curse be upon him.

I know [this].

That ruler himself, in the estimation of the people, is considered a warrior. When they come to that province, they are extremely fierce, and since most of them follow the Shia and other schools of thought, its revenue comes from those places. The products of its mountains are plentiful grain. It is said that Dilam is better than Samarqand, having fine water and abundant game and opponents of its army. It is counted among the cities of the Fourth Climate; its longitude is such-and-such degrees, and its latitude from the equatorial line is not precisely known. Its ascendant is Virgo, its rainfall is moderate, its air is temperate, and its water comes from two sources.

From there, water in wells during winter does not flow, but when summer comes and the sun grows warm, it flows out. After that, the water gives like other wells and yields produce. Its figs are excellent and its people are fair-complexioned Twelver Shia, extremely fanatical in their beliefs and in good agreement with one another. It is worthy of forty districts. It is said that it is the seat of paradise, worth a thousand dinars in surplus. The district of Talaqan is included in its province.

Talaqan: its longitude is such-and-such degrees and its latitude from the equatorial line is such-and-such. The Kashmarrud passes through its middle, and between them it flows through several passes. To the north it lies six farsakhs away. There is a hidden and strong fortress there, and near Qatin are the castles of Alamut and Maymundiz, which were the seat of the Ismaili rulers. For one hundred and seventy years their rule endured, and that fortress was originally in the Fourth Climate and is situated in its center.

And in the two-forties, the caller to Truth, Hasan ibn Zayd al-Baqiri, was expelled and came to Sind in the three-eighties. He gained dominance over Hasan Sabbah, and was occupied with calling people to the faith of the people of India. He built it up, and that fortress was originally called Alamut — meaning "the eagle's nest" — because it was a place where eagles nested. After several decades, Hasan Sabbah took hold of that fortress, and it remained under his command. In the year four-hundred and fifty-something, the king ordered that fortress to be destroyed and the two regions were ruined.

Most travelers say: although it appears similar from the outside, the two places are quite different from one another. And from among its notable things is that whatever is planted grows well, and whatever grain is sown yields a fine harvest. There is abundance of fruits beyond measure, more so than in Isfahan. The bread there is good and the people eat well. The people of India have known and recorded this from ancient times, and the people worshipped there. Now some of them have come to recognize the truth of their faith.

The city of Zanjan has six thousand residents and is in the fourth clime. Its longitude is calculated from Baja, and its latitude is reckoned from the equatorial line. Bolab and Dashir were founded by Bakan and named Shahin. The city has ten thousand people in population. In its geography it was called Mughal. Its climate is cold and its air is cool. Within it there are storehouses, and the city is prosperous. Two rulers have authority there, and none dominate over the others. There are two caravanserais, and the benefits of that place are abundant and much sought after. There are two buildings used for trade, and in the city and its region there is no fruit; they bring it from Tarum. There the people follow the Shafi'i school of law, and they have customary gatherings and consultations. Among the people, reason predominates and their spoken language is Pahlavi. There are many men of piety and many saints. The truth of their spiritual path is established there, and it is said to number in the thousands.

There are eight places there, and Sheikh Abu Marja Zanjani and Master Abd al-Ghaffar are buried there, as well as the tomb of Adami Kashani. Its district yields one hundred villages as dependencies, and eight thousand dinars of revenue. It belongs to the fourth clime, its longitude being from the Fortunate Islands, and its latitude from the equatorial line. It is an Islamic city, and it lies in the valley. The birth of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was among its distinguished events. It was founded by those who settled there, and its original founder is unknown. It was built under a certain ascendant, and among those who brought it prosperity was the illustrious Khwaja Tahiy al-Din Ali ibn Khwaja Malik Sharaf al-Din Sawi, who built and restored it. Its circuit is eight thousand two hundred paces, and it has had many successors. His son, the great lord Khwaja Shams al-Din Izz Nasruhu, extended it and brought people into the city, and its circumference in that era reached four thousand dirhams. It has a large population. The people there are inclined to simplicity, and there are gardens and orchards, and Zandaqan and the water channels of the district are bound with dams and reservoirs. Grain and livestock are plentiful there, but the fruits are not remarkable except for apples and quinces, which are excellent. The climate is very pleasant and the people there are Sunni Muslims, all of them, and all the villages tithe. The total revenues collected there amount to two and a half tumans. There are four districts, and one hundred and twenty-five villages in total. The first is the district of Arharum Aba Jahil Maneh, with Takhayym Abad, Sara Ashbun, Taribur, Yahid, Barnarz, and Abilad. The great villages of that district are Duqam, Hawfsal. The second district has the villages of Minur, Jayruqan, Kahindalan, Kaswa, and its major villages. The third is Juhra and Dabayt, a village district of Jubu.

The great regions of that fourteenth district of Yasin number forty-two villages, and it is an old settlement. Iran and Anza, and Shimham and Marfi are the great villages of that district — Chahaquث — whose divan revenues amount to half a tuman, which is the established assessment. And the hay of this province: the crop is planted in the lowlands, threshed, and the hay, which is of a better kind than barley and equal to it, is produced there. To the west of it is the shrine of Abu Ishaq ibn Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him), and on the western frontier is the shrine of Ishmael the Prophet, and from the abode of the elders and saints in that settlement, near the Sheikh of Oman as far as Saveh-Balagh, is a province which in former times the Mongols conquered and which was first given over to taxation. It is exceedingly fine, and most of its water comes from underground channels (qanats), and it has abundant fruit. Its revenues are assessed at ten thousand dinars, and most of the people there, being nomadic and encamped, follow no fixed school of law. The greatest of its villages are Khwanjahmah, Sanah, Qar-Abad, and Deh Samqar-Abad — these are generally settled districts — but now they are ruined. As for Merv: its length from the point of Abrakhā is [so many] degrees latitude, reckoned from the equator. It was once [great] and in the first era was devastated by the Mongols. Now little remains but the surrounding districts. Its dependencies also belong to it, and in Sultaniyya it amounts to one unit of weight. It lies in the fourteenth clime; it is a cold region and its produce consists of grain, raisins, and fruit. Reportedly, the Mongol-settled and tent-dwelling villages are called Khu'ankha — Sabasol — and it is said that wherever the Mongols were, they vanished. And whoever came among them with the burden of escorting a sayyid's daughter and others like her, revealed the matter openly there and built a hospice (khanqah), and settled people there. The people there follow the Hanafi school. In the province of Saghrd, the castle of that settlement was seized by the Mongols for horses and camels. A cistern (hawz) and a courtyard have been built there, twenty bricks wide, and its cistern is built like a lake, and the gardens of Mulla Khan have not yet been reached.

The water of each one is as much as [fills] a mill; it always flows out from there and does not stop. When the reservoir overflows and when the gate is opened it flows in its regular course, and at no time does it increase or decrease. This is among rare things. Aqbai Khan the Mongol brought the revenues of that region into the imperial treasury. The revenue of that province amounts to two and a half tumans. Tarabin and Kabchi are to the north of Soltaniyeh; Bikra, Dhul-Hasht, Darar, and their surroundings are among them. Most of the fruit of Soltaniyeh comes from there. Originally that place was a city called Farqabad, and between Upper and Lower Tadam, which was the seat of power. Now they are townships; Upper Tadam has become a town. The longitude, latitude, and position of that region are well-known. Also there is Shatanfiyah among them. That province is a productive administrative district. The first is Tadam, which is subordinate to the castle of Taj, with about one hundred villages; among them are Dayir, Jiylad, Shunurna, Dayir Ram, Hayat, and Falah by the Nile. The great villages of that place are the estates of Lower Tadam, subordinate to the fortress of Qal'at Mir: fifty-five villages. Among them are Manra'at al-Awn, Khuwarnaq, Sharznah, and Wallar and Kull from the upper region. The third is Lower Tadam, subordinate to the fortress of Faru, with thirty villages; Marwan is the most notable. The villages of the fourth, Funad and Bubylon, two notable villages, and eight other villages from its dependencies. The fifth, Funad Sufli, has twenty-five villages; among them are Kalhad, Kulchin, and Mulhal. The revenues of the treasury of that province are six hundred tumans and four hundred thousand dinars. There is a fortress that is adjacent to the Tadamin district, and five farsakhs from Soltaniyeh to the east, called Kalysh, with fifty villages. All of them had fallen into obscurity during the Mongol interregnum. The village of Qahud — the Mongols seized it and wished to make Umm al-Qura of that place — is now, due to the people of Soltaniyeh, a dependent settlement. Toward the east is Qarna, a cold and cool place. The yield of its lands is grain, a little barley, and fruit, and the people there...

They claim to follow the Sunni school, but Abu al-'Ala does not approve of this, and the frontier regions of Karaj are among the dependencies of that place. In the environs of the province, there are notable villages with revenue obligations. Among them is Taleghan, which is a province unto itself, known as Kaghaz-konan (the papermakers' town), and it has been a place of administration. The city of Minushehra-ye Zanjani has forty units of agricultural land, was well built, and has various quarters. It was named thus, and since good paper was made there, it became famous as Kaghaz-konan (Papermakers). It is now in ruins, and its extent is like a medium-sized river. The people there follow the Shafi'i school of law. Its climate is cold, and its waters flow down from the mountains above, where people who live there grow old. Its produce is mainly grain, and also nuts and grapes. The fourth section of the region: Abhar, located to the south, with some fifty parasangs from its dependencies. Its climate is cold, and since most of the inhabitants are long-lived, they light fires from those same mountains. Its revenues come from there, and its produce is grain and grapes, and its people follow the Shafi'i school. The diwan revenues of that region amount to four thousand dinars. Both Maragha and Andkhoy are two provinces a short distance away, and in climate they resemble those just mentioned. The revenues of each amount to one thousand dinars payable to the diwan. The diwan revenues of this province are shared between the diwan of Qazvin and the diwan of Tarum, two by two. The dependencies of that place originally comprised about thirty-five localities, but were ruined in the time of the Mongol devastation, and have since been repopulated. The people now cultivate the land and sell various goods. The diwan revenues of Kaghaz-konan amount to five thousand dinars. Mandan-qan is a medium-sized city in the fourth region. Its longitude is calculated by the astrolabe, and its latitude is established accordingly, with a distance of two thousand gams. Its climate inclines toward cold; its water comes from a river that is attributed to that city. The people there follow the Shafi'i school, and their grain and grapes are of fine quality, and their fruits are also good.
Revenue record [حقوف / حقوق].

The revenues of its diwan amount to approximately thirteen dinars, which is one toman, and it falls within the governance of Saveh. Its water comes from Najd and the surrounding areas. The district of Hezarouqan and Nazar-abad Ulya belong to its localities. It once had about seventy settlements. In that province, fruit and grain also grow. It resembles in form the district of Qazvin, and to the south lies Taleghan, which is about forty leagues away. Its climate is moderate, and its water, which comes from the highlands, produces in abundance figs and grain, and its character and religious customs are those of Taleghan. That province was an endowment of the congregational mosque of Qazvin, but in earlier times it came under forcible control. Its diwan revenues are three thousand dinars. Qom, Kashan, and Marin together constitute several towns. Qom belongs to the fourth clime. Talish is among the ancient places. It is said that Tahmuras built it. Its stewards have governed it, and thousands have been settled there. From its districts and valleys, thousands of revenues are apparent. Its climate is moderate. Fruit grows there, and its orchards are well-watered. They store water until summer, and the well-water there lasts until the season is done. It is slightly inclined toward an unhealthy tendency. Its products include almonds, figs, and many fruits. Among its notable fruits are large figs and red figs of fine quality. In that city there are excellent cypress trees. Its people are Twelver Shia and extremely zealous, and much of the city is now ruined. But Baku for the most part remains intact. Its diwan revenues are established and fixed. That province amounts to four tumans. Kashan belongs to the fourth clime. Its longitude is measured from the Fortunate Isles, and it was built at the time of Khatun Monkeh. It is in the constellation Virgo. In Tehran there is a fortress called Qayin. Its climate is harsh. Its water comes from Kadin, Fin, Ray, and the surrounding streams and springs.

And the intoxicating [winds] there are so severe as to cause suffering, and in summer there too, like the frozen water in winter, its benefit is moderate, and among its fruits are fine grapes. The people there are Shi'a, well-versed in knowledge, and most are physicians and of refined temperament. In that region there are many mountains and plains, and among the reptiles there are many scorpions, and it is known that foreigners are given little in the way of fiscal revenues. The fiscal revenues of that city amount to eleven tumans and seven thousand dinars, and the rest is fourteen parcels. It is largely a Sunni province, and nearby is Ardestan. The dependent villages number about fifty, and their produce goes to Kashan. Nearby are pomegranates of fine quality, and Bahman ibn Isfandiyar built a fortification there. It is in the fourth clime; its length is such, and its latitude is from the equatorial line. Bahman's daughters, the Gilani women, built it and named the city after themselves, and they later named it Kalba and also called it by an Arabicized form, Jadfaqan. Its climate is temperate, and its surrounding area extends to seven thousand pens [qalam]. Its water comes from a river attributed to that city and to Qom. Among its products, the best is cotton. The people there are mostly of the Shafi'i school, and its dependent villages number about fifty parcels. Its revenues are under its jurisdiction; the fiscal revenues of that region are four tumans and two thousand dinars. It is a district, and in every direction, if there is a village, it amounts to thirteen parcels. Farkhomran is among its most important places; its climate is temperate, and its water comes from underground springs and streams. Those who benefit from its fruits and produce are well-off, and most of the time the surrounding areas are prosperous. Its people are Shi'a, and its fiscal revenues are six thousand [dinars]. Farahan is a district, with notable villages, and its ancient seat of governance — the king built it there — and now its most important villages: its length is such…

[Marginal note:] Khaldat

The kingdom's revenues and extent: from the equatorial line, its air is temperate, its water is exceedingly good and beneficial, its crops are abundant, its inhabitants are plentiful and well-provisioned in that region, and its people are Shia and extremely zealous. In that province there are many marvels, and among them is one called "the wonder of the world" by those who know it. The revenue registered in its treasury amounts to seven thousand dinars. In the first city it lies in the middle of the seventh clime.

The revenues and extent, from the equatorial line down: it is a pleasant and well-situated land, and its produce is listed. Eight thousand dinars flow into its treasury. It belongs to the fourth clime. Its waters and springs are abundant, its pastures are fertile, and it has good harbor areas.

Its revenues amount to thousands of dinars, and it belongs to the fourth clime. Talish lies beyond the lowlands, its air and water are very good. Harun al-Rashid built a fortress there, near a mountain on the northern side, and at the foot of that mountain there are great springs called by name, with meadows, plains, and grazing lands. For six farsakhs in every direction it is known, and there are dependencies and numerous villages.

The people there are very zealous Shia; its revenue registered in the treasury is fifteen thousand dinars. It is a city of the middle of the fourth clime, and its revenue in the treasury amounts to two tumans and five hundred dinars. It belongs to the fourth clime. Jamshid once built there a great palace of fine construction, traces of which still remain. Its air is temperate and its products and revenues are notable.

It is subject to that region, and its revenue in the treasury amounts to six thousand dinars. There is a fortress there, and throughout that province Shafi governors came, and one of the governors of Shafi killed the man called "the good" among the people of that region, and so it was reported.

This district: what a harsh place it is, so that every dawn when the sun rises, in that region at the foot of the mountains it becomes apparent —
It is a great tuman of the region, and within it is a large city, and in it are the forests of Fars and the Kurdish settlements.
Within it, the revenues of its divan are established there, and the chief of the atabeks collects tribute from it; it yields more than expected.
The atabek sent to the Mongol divan: the lord of India receives a certain number of tumans, amounting to hundreds of thousands of dinars.
The details of each province under him regarding the actual revenues are not known; it is beyond the scope of the pen to record.
The fourth is the city of Yam: it is small and its climate is poor, because it faces north toward the Pleiades.
But its water is unpleasant; if one takes refuge in the rice paddies of its four surrounding areas, there is revenue for the divan.
It is established there, and the city of Susun — it is a small city and by the water —
It is situated and has many plantations and orchards, with figs and lemons, and there are many sour orange trees, and it is in the region of Kirman.
It has many orchards; Lurkan is a small city with a bad climate, and its water is unpleasant.
In sum, its revenues were considerable. The tuman of Lu is a small but notable province, with several cities within it.
The revenues of its divan, which the amir Mirnash collected, amounted to one hundred tumans, and as for the rest —
Sent to the Mongol divan: the lord of India receives one thousand dinars from the revenues of those regions.
The city of Yam is large and elongated, with two congregational mosques; its climate is moderate.
Its conditions are good, saffron grows there in abundance, and the district of Narm-Abad is one of its dependencies.
It has fifty foot-soldiers, is well-established, and within it is a fortress called the Black Tents of the Amirs.
A good city — now it is ruined; there was much fortification within it, and in its mountains —
The Ghilas people do not reside there. The tuman and its people: from within, the city has a fortress.
The fortress was built by the brave sea-captain Shuja al-Din Khanbar Shid; it had a great city,
But now it is ruined. Hamadan belongs to the fourth climate; its longitude is reckoned from the Canary Islands,
And its latitude from the equatorial line, as has been established; it is of auspicious ascendant.

The fortress and citadel of Kalban lies between the city and the district; they call it the water of this land. It was built, and now a khwaja holds it. In the beginning it was a very bold city, as is mentioned in the Tabaqat-i Nasiri: that it held dominion over Tulu, and the mention of its district was in the land of ten. When it fell into ruin, that road was found; Najshid renewed it, Imad restored it, and it was re-established there. That province has twelve thousand households; its climate is cold. Most of those who travel toward Hindustan pass through here. In the midst of the city there are many springs, and its fruit is extremely inexpensive. Grain is abundant; the milk there is good, and its people are mostly of moderate temperament. Among its notables are the narrator Hafiz Abu al-Ala, Baba Tahir Mu'in al-Qudat, and Anbar. Revenues are fixed there at an established rate, and the total income is one and a half dang. From it to Hasir is the first stage on the road; around the city, within seven to eight farsakhs, there are five rural districts: Shahristaneh, Lachimi, Ghaza-abad, Qasim-abad, Kushklat, and a great garden. The villages of that district and province are Mashan; mentioned therein are Khushfa, Khuld-barin, Bisht, and Kaka. Such is the case. By reckoning it is near; some portions are like a single unit, so that it is clearly known that in the land of Harwa there is speech, and gardens are present. The trees there face the sun; the length of Mashan is two to three farsakhs, and within two and a half farsakhs the city is in view. Within it, near Mashan, are two minarets resembling those of Abu Ansari. The sacred shrine is the second district of Arma'in, with forty-one villages. It is distant; and Daw-dad, Awqa-bad, Ta'aba-bad, Kurd-abad, Mad, Mahan, and Masin are its principal villages. The road goes forty stages; Daddan, Waqar-baran, Kumiyan, and Mileh-diwa are intermediaries, and Wanash-diwa is its chief village. The fourth category: six villages are present — Almashwud, Dadman, Ustubr, Wand, Niyad, Farghad — the chief.

The villages of that place number five, along with two residences and one pillar. There is the monastery of Karim, and for each teacher the villages — the annual state revenue of that province is thirteen tumans and six thousand dinars.
Asama is a town in the fourth clime; it is a small city. Its climate is temperate and its traces are good. Its products include grain, cotton in abundance, fruit, and grapes in abundance. The people there are fair-complexioned. Its state revenue is one tuman and five thousand dinars, plus additional dinars. Its district has five parts. The produce of the world is plentiful there.
Kahha has grains, timber, and district resources. It has forty pillars and belongs to the fourth clime. Its climate is somewhat cold, and otherwise similarly good — grain, crops, fruit abound, and infantry are fewer. Among its localities are Abdaran, Aldashan, Kulaybin, Majlad Shukri, and Bazl. The revenue of its villages amounts to nine thousand five hundred dinars.
Concerning what came before: it is now known as the district of A'lam. It has several towns; there are other places called by it, which are elevated, with abundant streams, gardens, grain, cotton, grapes, and fruit. Its people follow the Shafi'i school of law and follow the Shaykh al-Islam Sharaf al-Din. The state revenue of Hunin is two tumans and three thousand dinars, plus additional dinars.
There are two fortresses, two principal towns, and townships including Mushkan, Taqti, Wasr, and Sarkan with Afnad. There is a place called Bich, a place like Hind, with the river of Sarkan, and the villages of Nakran and Laghanra. The climate of these localities is temperate; otherwise similarly well-situated. Sarnafaj is found in abundance there. The place of Wasr — the people of this settlement are called by that name because of this. The state revenue of that place is two tumans and three thousand dinars.
Salman is reported to be in Khwalikhan. Its climate is somewhat cold; otherwise similarly, it connects by road. Built along a river, its produce includes grain, grapes, and fruit. Its state revenue is one thousand [dinars].

Six hundred dinars is its tribute, and Mehrau, Farlad, and Lamati are there, and several places were established there. Nahavand — its latitude is forty degrees, its longitude is such-and-such, and its climate is temperate. The Alvand river comes through it, and it passes by orchards and gardens. It is a prosperous land, and its cotton is beneficial. The territory around it is about one hundred parasangs. Its district includes Malabeen, Daspidam, Jahavut, and other rights and dues. Its ancient revenues are seven thousand dinars, and it includes the encampments of the Kurdish tribes settled there. About two thousand of its villages are estimated, and at the head of the city is a new garrison. As we mentioned before, the climate of the region of Fars is such that its latitude is such-and-such, and its longitude cuts the equatorial line, and its climate is temperate, and its characteristics are such. It has channels and streams running through it, and the people there are tall in stature, broad-shouldered, and with large frames. Buildings there are mostly made of raw brick, because timber is scarce. The gardens are well-tended and the city is pleasant and agreeable; its produce includes rice and other grains, and fruit and citrus are abundant, and the people of that region are mostly of such-and-such religious inclination, and they are craftsmen and workers, and the people are peaceful and hardworking. Most of them, however, are conceited, arrogant, and greedy, and lacking in good character. The legal administration there is under the authority of such-and-such, and that city is small, with little water and air resembling such-and-such. This small city in that same region, in the survey of its citadels, has about three thousand battlements. Know more from the chapter on cities — mention of the towns and their surroundings, and their revenues, and eight houses thereof.

It is a city, and most of its six districts face the wind of the south; it is about six miles in extent, temperate in climate, and its borders touch the province of Iraq (without diacritical mark), Sawqan, Gurjistan (Georgia), Luristan, and Kurdistan. Its produce is fine. Among the Caliphs, five of the Frankish lineage came here, and that Taki and Sina Pichah is Farkhaj; it is the seat of government of Adharbayjan. It was formerly the seat of Maragha, but now Tabriz is its capital, and it has nine districts. The greatest of its cities is Tabriz, and it is among the finest cities of those lands.

Two thousand tumans of revenue it yields in this time. Among the cities of the region, Tabriz is renowned. Nabide Khatun, the lady, the granddaughter of Mangu Khan, and the companion of Harun al-Rashid, witnessed this — it is recorded — in the year seventy-something and a hundred. After that, for sixty-odd years it was governed in Sind Aigh, and in the year after four hundred and something, after the end of the Abbasid Caliphate, it was destroyed by an earthquake. The Caliph came, and his appointed time came, and the first of the Ottoman rule came, and after that it was for several years in the twenty-fourth of the month of Safar, in the year thirty-something, and a great earthquake destroyed that region, and those surrounding it, and all of it was devastated.

The gathering of the Gate of Kings — Qadi Kamal al-Din Jubi — came and settled there. At that time Abu Tahir the Shirazian astrologer was present and decreed that Tabriz would be destroyed and its people ruined. The city's people followed his instructions and did not remain inside the city so that they would not perish under the rubble, and that decree proved true. The city was so thoroughly ruined that some forty thousand houses and their inhabitants were destroyed and perished. Amir Sawa ibn Bajal and Adi al-Anawi rose up. The Caliph al-Hakim was among them in the year thirty-something and four hundred, when the ascendant was Scorpio, and began rebuilding Tabriz. Under his rule it was established that Tabriz would never again be left in ruins and unrepaired. Praise be to the One who has now brought forth canals and channels in it, and has enriched its lands. Whatever is required is provided, and since the earthquake that occurred in spring, the city has somewhat recovered. It yields grain, and its citadel of Sanjiyaman has rooms, doors, and passages.

d-hi [notation]

The city's governor and those between them, the guardian of the treasury, and since in the time of Mongol expansion this place came under the control of the realm, a great multitude gathered and construction was carried out. Thus it came to be settled and the original city was established from its foundations, and Ghazan Khan came to Iran and undertook such grand constructions, estates, villages and dependencies within it as to be without compare, and two of the great edifices within it numbered five thousand chambers, and along its roads and avenues there are streams and gardens such as those of Syria in appearance. The garden of Ghazan Shah is there, built so that its pavilion has no equal among all the grand halls. On the heights of the city, the blessed martyr Khwaja Rashid al-Din Tabib established a quarter called Rab'-i Rashidi, within the outer walls of the city of Ghazan, and in it built grand structures; and on that the martyr Ala al-Din further added great constructions, and through these conquests the grand iwan was erected in the manner of a great vaulted palace, and the ceiling of the edifice served as the residence of Ghazani, built to such dimensions. Khwaja Taj al-Din Ali Shah then built a congregational mosque of magnificent scale, said to be twenty-five cubits in measure, some twenty cubits wide — and in the month of Safar the grand iwan, compared to the iwan of Khosrow by Ibn Aqlaḥun, came crashing down. In that mosque all manner of elaborate work was carried out, and marble stones of fine measure were brought, and the details thereof are many. Now several of the great buildings of Tabriz remain, and altogether the city's halls are unmatched; the city of Tabriz has abundant water flowing through it from the Mehr river, and some canals carry the water, and there are several of them.

This section opens with a chapter on the varieties of pleasure, saying that the eloquence of such a companion is sufficient, a blessing indeed. The waters of the meadows and the smoke of all the kingdoms of the region give color, and the saffron-hued lands are beautiful. The regions unnamed, with their streams and waters flowing down to the plains of Kilan and its routes, are much the same. Their climate inclines toward mildness, and their water and produce are better than those of the other lands. A treasury chapter of boundaries: its revenues are sealed and in spring it flowers forth beautifully, and its charitable endowments are remarkably fine. Its fruits in their qualities are abundant and its markets are not lacking. Affairs of administration and the distribution of surplus and the arrangements of the religious scholars are well recorded. The people of Ahmad and of Malik and of the companions of Muhammad al-Din are noted. The inhabitants in sum are of fair and handsome face, dignified in manner, eloquent of speech, and most of them are intelligent, learned, and discerning. Moreover, their craftsmen are most refined and sharp-tongued and of sturdy frame. It is said there: "The great man is the noblest of men," and neither the wealthy nor the poor there subsist from mere labor alone. They have many seafarers, and their travelers are persistent in their journeys and steadfast in their purposes. They said in a verse:

One who by nature never becomes a friend to Tabriz — such talk is worthless to the people of the world.

Tabriz draws one close. One who happens upon it and tests it is conquered by its love. And the great Imam al-Din Tabrizi said in reply: Speak not against Tabriz, and whatever its outward flaws may seem — its very core is as pure as a polished mirror, free of the rust of treachery. You said its people are wicked — but Tabriz in its paradise is like a mountain spring, rich and fertile. Its character is gentle and its faults are few. The impure and the base do not come there; they cannot gather and mingle among the refined.

In this place there are things one may find, and in such a state it is unpleasant. These hidden matters are in this city, and in each corresponding location the settlements are scattered, such as Sarkhab, Sarlghab, Jaranda, Yekpol, Shanab, Olyān, Kah, Sepyānān, and other districts, with tombs, minarets, and the shrine of Mirak.

The scholars and luminaries gathered here include: Abu Ibrahim, Kāmānhā, Bābā Qarra Khān, Bābal-Hasan, and Khāja Sāyn al-Dīn, and the Kālinī and Māl-banī of Tabriz, Mohsen Bolghādi, and Sheikh Nūr al-Dīn of Isfahan. Also among the tombs are those of the poets: Anwarī, Khāqān, Zahīr al-Dīn Fāryābī, Shams al-Dīn Sajāsī, Qal'akī Shirwānī, and other poets and secretaries — including Khwāja Baku Bānī, Badir Shād, and companions of the Prophet.

Among the shrines is the mausoleum of Abu al-Muja Kurd, and the tomb of Firayr, and the tomb of Qays, and the shrine of Daratāw. There is also the tomb of the brother of Hamza, and near Sarkhab is the tomb of the Amir ibn Amir ibn Amir, and various memorial shrines of eminent persons throughout the city and its districts.

This account, if recorded fully, would extend at length. The city itself is settled around seven hundred and eighty-eight [units of measure], totaling five thousand dinars in assessed value, and it has seven districts. The first district is Sahrātu, lying to the east of the main city, at a distance of a few farsakhs; among its notable places are Asfankh and Sa'dābād and other significant sites. The second district lies to the south, with gardens connected to the city — however, these gardens are now cut off and one cannot distinguish them, as they have become separated.

To the south, sloping toward the west, the land is pleasant and fertile. The third district is known as Gholdar-Āb, with cool waters and fine attributes. The fourth district is known for the river Bābil, lying to the west, a few farsakhs from the city. It is a fertile and verdant region, like a single orchard, abounding in silver and prosperity.

The region of Moshqi and Rashk has about twenty-five villages. Nawabil, Khwabarshan, Milan, and Askuna are among the great places of that fourteenth district. The city of the Afghans is in the region of Afghanistan; its orchards produce figs and Frankish fruits, and its walnuts follow the rule of the governor. Pears, walnuts, and other fruits are found there, and some thirty villages belong to it. Most of its notable features include its red pottery, its singers and musicians, and its potters. The Sufis and others make up the fifth district, two leagues to the north of the city of Bilan. The city of Farhanuk is fully described; all its villages and the people settled there number about forty villages. There are Armenians, merchants, traders, Valyaqi, and Awfar among its notables. The sixth district is the Khanrud, and the seventh district is toward Bustan — both lie in the direction of the city. The court grants thirty units of distance to Qadirgah, and its inhabitants are among the notables, with the revenue registers known. These districts together have one hundred thousand dinars of worldly wealth, and that place lies between the districts. The fixed stipend for Ghanani is one hundred and seventy tuqman, and five thousand dinars are recorded for expenditure and administration. The revenue of the province amounts to seven tuqman per annum, and up to the wealth of the great city it amounts to hundreds of units. If one proceeds from the homelands via Dabil and Mozan, through Khiji and Makhni, the sciences and learning flourish from Saral-Faram. The fourth homeland is in the fourth climate, and its climate records are kept. From that region's tributaries of the Mihran and its branches, names appropriate to it include many villages. It was built; it is known and celebrated as a city in Islam. The king built it and praised it; its estimate runs to thousands. It is mostly those whose origin is from Sihind — its origin is from fodder and vegetables — and there are elephants and camels. Its people have fair complexions and are of the Shafi'i school of law; its fruits are wholesome and its people in their entirety hold the revenue rights of the court.

The revenues of Tiflis (Tbilisi) are modest, and its estates in certain districts are under the jurisdiction of governors, yielding little income. Its foundations and endowments are maintained without interruption; its gates and roads bring together the learned from inside and beyond, and it draws from the greatest of the high places. For seekers, its water channels, rivers, and pastures make it pleasant, and its settlements are well-regarded. Its climate, below the mountain, is temperate; its orchards are plentiful and its springs good. From those mountains come streams and springs, flowing from Maku to Jabeel, fulfilling the proper rights of the treasury at certain times.

Ardabil is a recorded city and is supported by endowments from the gates of al-Bar by Abu Said's grant. Talish region and its districts belong to that same realm. Before the coordinates, from the line of the equator, the mountain of Sabalan rises prominently in the region of Baku. Sabalan has been added; its slopes and summit are such that its peak can be reached only in certain seasons of the year, and beyond the peak no other summit has been attained. From the mountain of Sabalan flows a spring whose water is not drinkable, and for this reason it is called Kol (the Blind).

Most of the inhabitants follow the Shafi'i school, and all are disciples of the Qutb, the pole of the world, the master of the seekers — Shaykh Safi al-Din — whose line and lineage is celebrated. The fortress of Sabalan was under the command [of that family], and according to what is told in the Shahnameh, at a certain time the castle was placed under blockade, and the Ghajis arrived but were repelled. Now Babak's stronghold is said to be in that mountain. The endowments of the mountain region of Ardabil amount to eighty-odd thousand dinars, and it is a middle-sized city. At present it is said to have one hundred prosperous villages. Kabishsad is a town with villages and a district, having fine estates and orchards. Its dependencies include Sabounshar (Soap City), Niyrabad, and other towns recorded by name.

The ruler resided there, and its governors used to say nothing was like it. After a rest, he descended to Khatal. The ruler settled there. Now that half-sleep, and in that region of majesty and villages, in the direction of the uplands, and on two sides are springs whose water flows continuously and strikes the ground, and on the side of Qafa near Karna and Farnasa. Another spring in whose water by force, in the region of Khatlān, stands upright like a wall to the right. It rises up with great height, and the water descends in the form of droplets, flowing between the channels, and there are watermills there. The flowing water of Khatlāl flows and splits, scattering like a millstone. Animals come to drink, and hunters find good prey there and catch game. The revenues of the divan of that region amount to several hundred thousand, and the governor's appointed revenue is twenty thousand dinars, and the total of those great amounts equals that much. The climate of its highlands is temperate, inclined toward warmth, and its produce is abundant. Its people follow the Imami school of thought. The divan revenues are two thousand, and in the districts there are seven famous places. Khataabad and its surroundings and the sub-districts — the name of its region has been sought and its governors requested. It suffers from certain ailments. The governor who settled there summoned people, and its climate is temperate and favorable, but the north wind and its cold prevent the trees from thriving, and the population has grown old. Some of its people follow a certain school, and the divan revenues there amount to so much per year. The military fief assigned to it is so many tumans, recorded in Murghab and its dependencies. The villages of Kuhistan of Bunbulān are ruined, and Qasirabād and the lower villages.

Sanasalan was built — "Hara" meaning "possessed of splendor" and also meaning "the black king" — and it is also called Nadi and Asarkhan. Before it, a place was also built called Huli, which is temperate in climate, and the waters of Anku flow through it. Silan and the orchards and gardens have been endowed there, and grapes and fruits are abundant. Dawud gave it, and it has twenty-odd locations in its vicinity. Its revenues amount to seven thousand dinars. The city itself is small, its air is warm and reddish, and its water comes from below; it is said that from the surrounding mountains of Shakniz flow springs and channels of Tamalash, grain and grapes, and from its fruits are collected [revenues], and its religious school is noted there. The population is about fifteen thousand inhabitants. It is now desired that Tamalash provide grain and good land.

The district of Hayad and the town previously — toward the south of Sabalan — is said to have been situated: Sabalan is to the north and has nearly disappeared. Its air inclines toward mildness and its water is from those [sources], and it is suited to orchards. Andlab is its judge and the people there are mostly of mixed [origin]. It has a strong fortress. Presently it yields only grain, and Janbad is a fine place.

In Talbin and its district, in the midst of the mountains of Nayrat, there is a fine fort, and the land is good, and its climate is temperate and its water comes from the river, yielding grain, grapes, and fruits. The Turks and Tajiks are settled there; they follow [a certain] doctrine, and its revenues amount to one thousand dinars.

In former times it was the principal town of the region, but now the province and its district are inhabited by a community of Mongols. Tamalash grain, grapes, and the people of Mashalnuk live there. Kilad-i-Now and Qishlan and its territory are near, about five stages away, in the direction of Talish.

In its vicinity, from among those mentioned, aside from what is present, the characteristics of grain and Panjdar Talanuk are good. Marhan Taqim and Kalayft are about five stages away, toward Karrufi, and the revenues from those places: grain, grapes, and fine fruits are found there, and some places are situated on the banks of the Aras River. Its revenues amount to eight thousand seven hundred and five [dinars]. The fort of Shrambt has been brought under [control], and each one who comes receives a deed and letter. In addition to these, about five localities are now its dependencies: Ahral, Bahlul, Hind, and others.

Among its greatest features is that its governor Dawad rules wisely, and there the blessed Prophet's teachings have taken hold. The climate of that region is pleasant and its particular natural qualities are excellent. It has many gardens and orchards, and its waters and air are wholesome. The revenue of that place amounts to fifteen thousand men. Its cattle are found plentiful in the records of kings. It consists of about thirty villages, and among them the air is inclined toward pleasantness, and its produce is grain and other crops. Its annual revenue is a thousand dinars, and it has four cities: Hizri, Salmas, and others.

It is said that this is the fourth clime, extending from the island to the equatorial line. Its central city has a population of six thousand households. Its climate is pleasant and its waters come from the Jabalans and Persia. It has many orchards, and its annual revenues are fifty to sixty thousand dinars. It has abundant timber, and its men are noble, handsome, and well-bred, and they are known in Turkestan as generous hosts. It has eighteen established settlements.

Salmas, from the fourth clime: its length extends from the islands of Baqal and its latitude from the equatorial line. It is a large city. Taj al-Din Alishah Tabrizi built its structures and its population is eight thousand. Its climate is mild, and its waters come from the Kurdish mountains, where there are orchards and fine fruits, grain, and other good produce. Its people are hospitable, and their character is known for generosity. Its revenue amounts to thirty-two thousand. The fourth clime: its length extends from the islands to the equatorial regions. Its largest city has a population of ten thousand, situated on the shore of a sea. Its climate tends toward humidity, and its waters come from the mountains, and its orchards are plentiful.

It continues: among its products are timber, pears, wild pears, elm, and other trees of good quality; for this reason it is called Sadrah. If a person of that region is seen dressed in local garments, they will recognize him. The population numbers eight hundred and some, and it has provisions and industries. Its revenues amount to four hundred and some thousand. The city of Ishtasti is prosperous in trade and commerce, situated in the middle of the region. It faces south toward the qibla, its climate is pleasant and agreeable, and its produce includes grain and other crops from the surrounding mountains. The mountains yield timber and marble, and its industries are known for their quality. The population is some thousands, and the revenues are in dinars. Nobat is a coastal city of good character. The Fourth Clime: to the east lies Sabalan, facing east, and Holuish is straight and well-situated. The city is southward, and Sabalan rises two peaks high; in it is great abundance. Grain and other produce are plentiful; its marble is white and its timber is abundant. If one dresses there, a hundred parasangs of land are cultivated and forty villages are in the district; they cultivate and harvest, and the revenues for the treasury are eighty dinars. Kahrsar is another city, and Faknubiyya is pleasantly situated; in the Daylami region there are many things and varied industries. Its governors are learned, and it has much water, warmth, and generosity. The revenues from that region are more than those of Maragha; its produce is grain, grapes, and figs, and other crops are also cultivated there. Its marble is white and of excellent quality, and its people are of good character, prosperous and industrious. Tuman and Saraghach are cities in that area; Maragha is level and has two well-known districts. Maragha is in the Fourth Clime; its longitude is measured from the Fortunate Islands and its latitude from the equator. It is a great city, and it was formerly the capital of Azerbaijan. Its climate is pleasant.

It is temperate and inclined toward mildness. One thing of note is that Mount Sahand shields it from the north wind, and it has many orchards. Its water comes pure from two villages; it draws from Mount Sahand. Its chief is the mir of Khunjisht, whose servant is Ghuldbina and Ankuyis Rabiu. Most of the time it produces grain, and its six districts are: Sarakhun, Baniakhun, Narkhara, Kad, Dal, Hasht, Dah, Dahastan, Ankiran, and Bula. Among its plagues are white pepper-blight, turnips, and Pish-Miyan; most of it is Janbali. Its assessed revenues are fixed at seven hundred thousand dinars. It is cheap and affordable; eighty and several hundred thousand dinars are the outward revenues. By the order of Khwaja Nazir al-Din Tusi it was assigned to the Kokhan district, and now it is ruined. Sanqar has taken its place. Its water comes from the Hafa mountains of that region, flows into Bakhira and Khunjisht, and its produce is mainly grain; its third portion goes to the Qum treasury. Its diwan revenues are fifty thousand dinars. Nahir and Abratan are small towns of temperate climate. Their water comes from Mount Sahand; they have many orchards of Dabisan, and their grapes are beyond measure, and their produce of wheat and fruit is of the finest quality. White pepper-blight comes from it; its religion is Shafi'i. Its territory comprises eight parts; its diwan revenues amount to three thousand and some hundred dinars. Ila is a small town with many orchards; its figs, pomegranates, and fruits are excellent. The people of Dabisan live there; its water comes from Anir and Jafnud. Among its faults is that its wheat yields poorly. Its diwan revenues and the revenues of its district are recorded. Among its dependencies is Marand, which lies in the fourth clime; its longitude is such-and-such and its latitude such-and-such. Lawat is a town of moderate size with a population of eight thousand; now it has diminished. Its climate is temperate; its water comes from such-and-such a source. Its produce is grain, cotton, grapes, and other fruits and legumes, which are of excellent quality. It has sixty parts to its territory, and its produce is fine and profitable throughout.

To the south of it there is worm (silk) and crimson dye, and within a week from its head to the garden one is able to obtain it. If one does not obtain it, every station and district is administered, and its revenues in the diwan amount to four thousand dinars. And there is no doubt that in the treasury of Tibet its abundance is increased, and it is considered very productive. And elephants and a thousand loads of fine goods are among its great things; the climate there is temperate and pleasant, and flowing from the mountains its water rises, and from its abundance the produce of that area — its quality, its excellence, and its improvement and flourishing — surpasses most places. And more than all, it is connected, and from there onward the revenues in the diwan are four parts, six hundred in number, and it is established that now its men are settled there in considerable measure. And in the districts of Arin, the noble lineage of Bakr ibn Abdallah reaches the Prophet, peace be upon him, and it is well-established. And its camels are numerous and it has a fertile garden — the region of Nu'raman — from which its produce of knowledge, livestock, and fruit is obtained; it is among its noble qualities. Its revenues in the diwan amount to three thousand dinars, and it is a notable town. Its quality is pen (writing) and trade and livestock and fruit which is found there; in it is security and the dominion of awe. It is among the fourth climes; its longitude from this point is according to the tables listed, and from it to the surrounding area, its condition is warm. Its fire is active and its inscription is written and most of its regions — the produce thereof is knowledge, water, livestock, abundant fruit, and its district is vast, with several fortresses under its authority. Its order is like the Gospel and the laws of that region. Its revenues in the diwan are one hundred and four thousand dinars, and it has a small town. And its abundant water comes — it is a great city — its water flowing from deep valleys as a great source, and its water flows throughout; its inhabitants are called Turks because it is a source of Turkish settlement. Its city is well-known; its produce is knowledge, livestock, fruit, and abundant cotton — it has a good reputation. That city is great; its water and all the valleys of Qaban are pleasant, and its water is especially famous throughout.

The four wise men of Sefid Diz came together, and the agents are greedy for the dues of the divan. Eighteen thousand and three hundred dinars is its value; the fortress stands upon a rock, and in the foothills of that fortress there are such great trees that no one can walk in their shade. The plane trees and the tall pines of that valley are wondrous beyond description. In the four directions of this region there are meadows, and its air is pleasant and agreeable. Its borders reach to the province of Shirvan and Arran and Azerbaijan, and all around it are continuous territories. The divanial revenues of its atabegs were three hundred tumans; in this era it has been thirty tumans and three thousand dinars. This is the true account of those lands. The place called Mona lies along the bank of the Aras River, and the surrounding district is likewise a dependency measured in tumans. The mountain of Sabalan is so vast that its peak is not visible; plants grow upon it in the Indian manner; in it there are creatures with four legs that carry poison and benefit, and in the season of its pastures, its grasses are plentiful, and its herbs and other fodder are abundant. Because of the Sabalan mountain, these harmful Indian creatures do not remain there, and it is a joy to travelers. It is of the Fourth Clime; its longitude is measured from the fortunate stars, and its latitude from the equatorial line. Its first city was Mufan, which now lies desolate, reduced to the size of a village. And as for the King of Kings — may God the Almighty raise him in the noble Quran — in the story of Moses and Khidr, as God Most High said in His glorious word: "Moses said to his servant: I will not stop until I reach the junction of the two seas." And they went forth until they came here, as has been told — that is the city of Memphis in Egypt — and to Pir Jilan and to the monastery of Machu, and the scholars in that monastery were killed. In the arrangement of the climes it came forth, as discussed in Takhij. And for the books of Quranic commentary, this story relates to the meeting of the two seas, as has been reported, praise be to God.

Hadi

The climate of Majarwan inclines toward warmth, and its waters come from the mountains that lie between knowledge and ignorance. Its products, other than Chinese silk, are of no other kind. Since Chawnda belongs to the Fourth Climate, Talish is located there. Ibn Khalid al-Hajj surveyed the agricultural lands from the equatorial line, and the city of Basit was built and settled in the time of al-Mu'tasim, the Abbasid Caliph, by his freedman Afshtin. Now it lies in ruin, and what remains is little. Its climate inclines somewhat toward warmth, and its water is of middling quality. It has some good qualities; its products were silk. Silsalawan lies between the Fourth and Fifth Climates. The people of Salkhuwan had built it, and now only villages remain. Its water is from two streams. Its product is silk of good quality.

In the direction of Jadyar district, on the border of the domain of the Mongol Khan, he built it. From the Fifth Climate: this is the Fifth Climate, lying in the direction of Bursana. Salj, Jarbalan, and surrounding areas were once the residence of Farhad ibn Ki. Abramjan al-Qasr, Shamavand, and Fakhr Dusi are mentioned. It is said that Hisht Karbin is where Farhad beautified the world.

Ruwan: it is known that it lies between two rivers, and its province belongs to the Sultan. This is a city of the Fifth Climate; its length is given from Khalid's survey, and its width from the equatorial line. The people of Tutayn and Nasasan built it; now it is in ruins, though previously it had many fine buildings. Its climate is warm, and its products are silk, wheat, and other fine grains. This too is of the Fifth Climate; its length is given from the survey, and its width from the equatorial line. Alexander and Qubad ibn Firuz built it. It was once a place of glory; it had many cypress trees. Among its trees are the shah-baluq and other fine fruits.

This section mentions that it is in the Fourth Clime, and it is a city of Islam. Its longitude is from [the meridian of] Abu Khalid. Its latitude is from the equatorial line, in the direction of the north. It is a pleasant and elevated city, and each district has several notable features, refined and excellent in character. Among its characteristics: the air is temperate, its pastures and hunting grounds are among the finest, and it abounds in game and wildlife. It is rich in provisions and produce. It is noted for the region of Shirvan, and Kishtas. Shirvan lies on the shore of the sea of Baku; its gateway is called the Bab al-Abwab (Gate of Gates), and it is a prosperous province. It has had revenues amounting to a hundred thousand tumans. Its situation in geography and administration has been recorded.

The province of Bakr-ha is in the Fourth Clime; its longitude is from Abu Khalid, its latitude from the equatorial line, its air is temperate and its products are plentiful.

Shamakhi is a city, the seat of governance, located in the Fourth Clime; its longitude is from Abu Khalid, its latitude from the equatorial line; the air is temperate, it is well-watered and the region is prosperous.

Another city is mentioned along with the Malik al-Muluk (King of Kings) region, including Baku, Kharj, Khunj, and Zahina, all of which have various animals and produce and are prosperous climes.

Derbent: This city is on the border; Qubad ibn Fayruz built its walls; its products are silk, grain, and other cereals of fine quality.

Firuzabad: It is among the smaller cities of the Clime; it has pleasant air, its people are of good character, its climate is warm, and it produces grain and other fine crops.

Kishtasp: It lies on the shores of the province of Kishtasp.

The book that Kishtasab son of Lahrasab built is famous; from it one breaks off and inherits the rivers that flow there, and the products are grain and provisions. It is said that among its fruits and produce, old traditions and customs are observed, and its people follow the Shafi'i school of law. Their endowments are maintained, and the accounts of the Diwan and the governors' stipends are established. Under the present government, one hundred towns exist today, and eight thousand gold coins are the value of the revenues, and the military land-grants assigned there are well known. This is the Sixth Chapter: On the Settled Dwellings of the Jinn. Its air is pleasant and its latitude is high. It is continuously joined to the second clime. The governance of its clime is in the second and higher region, and the affairs of its kings, according to the opinion of authorities, have been such that in this era the budget amounts to thousands of dinars. The capital is Gurjistan and Anjara is the chief city of the clime. At present, the clime's longitude begins from Abu Ghalib, and its breadth from the equatorial line extends over mountains and valleys. Its air is extremely hot, and it inclines to warmth; its neighbors are attached in rows. It produces good grain and its fruit is exceedingly fine. The fifth clime: its longitude begins from Anjab Abu Ghalib, and its latitude from the equatorial line, and its regions include Afna, and throughout the land of Babylon and the water of Kurdha. Its plains and hills have been built and furnished with dwellings, as mentioned by name. The ancient houses of Kufa stand above, and beyond them are the warm baths. The water is warm where it rises there, and its produce of grain is exceedingly fine; its fruit is abundant. Hanan is a strong fortress, built on great rock at the top of a separate mountain.

In the Compendium of Lands, there was a city called Sabt, and in it was Tiflis, and the surrounding regions of Khuy belong to it, and it had great grain, and the land was elevated and sloping. Chapter Four: On the Nature of the Regions of Rum.
It contains about sixty cities, and it extends in all directions, and scholars have said that this region is the Dispersed of Lands.
They have said, and the prophetic tradition confirms this, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said — as recorded in Masalik al-Mamalik — and scholars have noted that when the idols were between Bayt al-Maqdis and its surroundings, they came from India, and from there great calls came, and the wool was sheared from there, and from there they were taken captive. The Seljuk customs prevailed: the captives were taken away, and after that they were driven to Ka'ba, and they wandered displaced.
The author of this book says: at this time in Iran such things occurred, and the witness to this account is that the verse "until it reaches the Farathi, except that its people are wrongdoers" should be heard — from there the dominion covers the provinces of Mazandran, Georgia, Sivas, Misr, Sham, and Ajam.
The rights of those places, as established in the covenant of the Seymedli, were two hundred tumans, and in the Seljuk era the revenues of those regions amounted to such-and-such tumans. The city of Buk is in the first region: its longitude is Tulis, from the Khaldat line, and its latitude is from the equatorial line. Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad the Seljuk sent orders there, and the city of Sivas is among its notable cities, and from there onward:
Iltan Sani is a city of the fifth region; Ashghara is of the fourth region. Its longitude starts from the Khaldat line and its latitude from the equatorial line, and it produces grain, cotton, and other goods. Anighan is of the fourth region; its longitude starts from the Khaldat line and its latitude from the equatorial line. Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad ordered its renovation and reconstruction, and it was rebuilt on a grand scale.

It is pleasant, and especially Furat is well-ordered. From this region one obtains six kinds of grain, fruit, and abundant grapes. Its government revenue is three hundred and three tumans and two thousand five hundred dinars. Raznalik: It is from the fourth clime; its longitude is here at the Khalidats, and its latitude is at the line of the equator. There is a church of extreme grandeur, the like of which in construction does not exist in any other realm. In it there is a tall dome; some call it the Pavilion of Ta'if. After the region came under the sovereignty of the Prophet of Islam, some of the Indians who come there say that on every bank Ibn Kaldia built a mosque in the shape of the Ka'ba, with the same length and width as the Ka'ba of the Muslims, and it is called Amu and Arkamba. Its government revenue is two hundred and two thousand dinars. Arlak: It is a middle-sized city; its water and air are temperate; its grain and grapes are good. Its government revenue is seven thousand dinars. Inak: It is a small city; its government revenue is fifty thousand dinars. Antma: It is from the fourth clime; its longitude is from the Islands of the Khalidats, and its latitude is at the equatorial line. It was built by Qasliw Arslan ibn Mas'ud the Seljuk. It was built in three hundred and [something]; that great region is pleasant and fine. Its grain, grapes, and fruits are abundant and good. Its government revenue is fifty thousand dinars. From Rakhan it is seven farsakhs distant; Qawbana is on the bank of the Hilla. Its government revenue is one hundred and five thousand dinars. It is a great city. Sultan 'Ala' al-Din Kayqubad the Seljuk built it; its grain is of many varieties, its air is good. It has fine gardens. It is a middle-sized city and is from the fourth clime. Its character is very fine; its citadel sits atop a mountain. And the city of Ashtikhun: the mosque of this city and the well of Khwaja Mustafa Sawamasi was built here.

And this Bashir of good character, when he demolished the remaining ruins, every stone from Dhayn al-Rum is in Bahira. It is a city near Nirab, now small, with few gardens. Its diwan revenues amount to one thousand dinars. It is a middling city, and its diwan revenues are forty thousand, three hundred dinars.
