The city of Sarbakht is small, blessed, and belongs to the fourth climate. It has a pleasant air, and its diwan revenues are twenty-nine thousand dinars. Shurukh is a small city on the coast of the sea; its diwan revenues are fifteen thousand. It lies on the coast of the sea, and ships call at it. The Simat belongs to the fifth climate. Its longitude is measured from the line of the Dhat, and its latitude from the equator. It is a great city. The dome of Anwan ibn Muʿti was honored by the presence of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and he arrived there, and within it is a sweetness. Its fruit is like almond and mastic in taste, and one can eat its skin, sweet and pleasant in flavor. No one knows what fruit this is — it is the Mamuya. It belongs to the fifth climate. Its longitude is from the line of the Dhat by a certain measure, and its latitude from the equator by another measure. In the spelling of the Franks it is called the Sea of Mecca, or Takubid, where Qistas built structures and made preparations. The diwan revenues of this city are seven hundred and seventy dinars. Falnaqa belongs to the fifth climate. Its longitude is measured from the Islands of the Dhat by a certain degree, and its latitude from the equator by another. It is a great city; carpets and rugs are made there free of cost. It is said that someone came there, and in a suburb a house was found which had for years been infested, and certain people of Yakshibeh Shushan settled in a place which became renowned, and its dust was like theriac in driving away harm. He came, and the omen drove away harm like theriac, and there was no other remedy. He who wishes to buy and finds no response — Qalaʿna is a fortress known by this name.

It is said that this city has been one of the great fortresses, worth five thousand dinars in tribute. Hasar and Abhar Shah built it, and Pheniye was constructed. This is the clime of Konya — this clime is fine. Tallish and fig trees are among its characteristic features. From its plains come fine grapes; and various lords built it up under the Seljuk Sultan of Islam, constructing strongholds in agreement with one another.

Its ancient fortifications were built to settle the frontiers and form a great defensive structure. When the city fell into ruin, Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad the Seljuk came and ordered the army, and within a few years raised it again to great heights.

Its fields and meadows are prosperous, its lands and provinces have been built up, and the fortresses under its governance are well-appointed and provisioned. On its river banks great buildings have been constructed with five fine structures made of pearl-like stone, yielding abundant grain and timber of the finest sort. Its gardens are exceedingly beautiful, and on every side one finds fine orchards. The region around it is cultivated and its grapes and fruits are harvested abundantly, and they are given as offerings. The city is exceedingly sweet and prosperous.

As long as the frontier governors remained in post, the city was populated and people continuously kept watch. Baha al-Din and his son also contributed to its restoration. This is Qaysariyya — this clime is fine. Tallish and fig trees are among its features, and Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad the Seljuk built its fortress after some years, constructing it strongly, in the year four thousand and some hundreds.

It is reported in Majma' al-Buldan that two Bilyas governed for the benefit of the princes and what was built was great. It was ever so, and in respect to its standing it was counted among the distinguished. Among those enumerated is Kat, a middling city with a temperate climate, belonging to the [seventh] clime. Its revenue is small.
Dibal: Its built revenue is two thousand five hundred and one hundred minas. The fort is small.
Its climate is cold and without richness; its water supply is meager. It is subordinate to it; its treasury revenues amount to four hundred and something thousand minas. Kol: a small city of the Andal region, the fourth [clime], with abundant fruit. Narawl: a well-developed suburban town, whose air was once pleasant; that place was plundered, yet it still has abundant fruit. Luluh: a small city of the lower clime, its air is cold and inclined [to dryness], and it has extensive pastures.
Yishkawka is numbered and reckoned from the fourth clime; its longitude is [given]; its latitude is at the line of the equator; it has two fortresses. It was founded by Ptolemy, son of the master of al-Jubayta, ascribed to Najam.
It was once a great and large city; its air was extremely pleasant, with running waters, extensive pastures, and abundant fruit; its grain and crop yields were remarkable. Its treasury revenues amount to one hundred and eighty thousand minas. Nakram: a great and central city of the fifth clime; its treasury revenues amount to forty thousand dinars and more.
Nangbar: a middling city with abundant gardens and fruit. Its treasury revenues amount to one hundred and eighty-seven thousand three hundred and [more].
Hushba: an important fortress in the province of Qarman, in the mountains. It is detailed, and in that province there are many forts separated from the land of Almoghar, Masham, and Talm. Its people follow Islam, and they dress and live [in a particular manner].

They are always engaged in holy struggle and their leaders are descendants of the Seljuks. Baba Baili is a settlement located between Qonya and Afsha. Its boundaries and water resources have no equal in the world, and all of it has been built magnificently. Qir Shahr is a city of middling construction, with fine surroundings and excellent climate and produce. Its revenue and tribute come to sixteen thousand and one hundred and fifty dinars. Larik is a small city with a pleasant climate inclining toward excellence; its revenue is twenty-seven thousand dinars. Rumna is a medium-sized city; its revenue is two hundred and sixty dinars. Balqub is a medium-sized city; its revenue is fifteen thousand and one hundred and fifty dinars. Aqaj is a great fortress situated upon a mountain. Niyanq is a market town and an important seat of governance. Its revenue amounts to four hundred and six hundred thousand dinars. Karbiyul is a settlement; its revenue is four thousand minas of dinars. Kutch Jar is a city; its revenue is seven thousand minas of dinars. Kasiyti is a medium-sized city; its revenue is twenty-four dinars. Suyi Sa is a city near Bursa. Near Constantinople is Malqaniya, a small city near Bursa, whose people's revenues total twenty-five thousand dinars. Among all these towns, Anqawi is one of them. Qaladiq, its fortresses and its power, Aqtlumush is in its environs, and the Gate of Kashit is there. Concerning the regions of Armenia: it is divided into two parts, Lesser Armenia and Greater Armenia. Lesser Armenia is not inferior to Iran, and Greater Armenia lies to the east. The second province is bordered by Greater Syria to the north, Syria to the south, and the Sahara to the second direction. In its environs are Ghurish, the lands of Sis, Trabzon, and other great cities and places including Lazla.

Every year three tumans are paid as tribute from Iran, and Arsineh is the greatest and most distinguished of the cities of Iran. Its area is reckoned at two tumans and Nutulman; Ikhla and Damshahr are well known, and the climate is temperate. Its borders extend to Lesser Armenia and to other districts, and to Kurdistan and Azerbaijan, and it is connected to Iran. Its length runs from Izn al-Raqum to Salmas, and its breadth from Iran to Aqni. The province of Ikhla — and Diyar Ikhlat is its seat of government — had in former times revenue of about two hundred and some tumans, and now it is thirty-five tumans. This was formerly the fourth in rank. Its length is from the Canary Islands (Khalidāt), and its latitude is from the equator; the climate of its air is temperate, and very fine. It has much produce, many fine orchards and vineyards. Its diwan revenues are fifty-one thousand five hundred dinars. There is a fortress whose diwan revenues are one thousand dinars. This city was formerly inhabited by the Tayy tribe. From the latitude of Khalidāt, and its longitude from the equator, the climate is temperate, and the produce is good. Its diwan revenues are fifty-one thousand dinars. Tabriz — it has a strong fortress now, and its chief product is grain and grapes — its diwan revenues are seventy-four thousand dinars. There is a fortress on the edge of Ikhlat, in the district of Takhtnik, whose diwan revenues are thirteen thousand eight hundred dinars. It is a great and fine meadow with running streams, excellent hunting grounds, and fine pastures. The Arghun Khan had a summer residence built there, and he spent most summers there. Its diwan revenues are six thousand five hundred dinars. It is a small town; in former times it was a staging post. The Banu Laghabis were its craftsmen, and it also has gardens, and the sultans would come there, and the climate is fine.

There is a desert, and in the middle of it there are various fruits, and there is a fortified city with a strong fortress on one side; the city's treasury revenue is twenty-five thousand dinars. In the main city there was a large town, now in ruins, reduced to the level of its stones; the revenue of the treasury is half a dinar. Hushab: it is a tomb-city; its treasury revenue is seven thousand and some dinars. Taribat: it is a small city, and its revenues belong to the main city; the revenue is five thousand three hundred dinars. The treasury revenue of the tomb-city is one thousand. It is a small city, situated amid gardens, vineyards, and abundant fruit, with an exceedingly fine climate; the treasury revenue is sixteen thousand eight hundred dinars. There is a mausoleum; its treasury revenue is seven thousand and two dinars. Hayr: it is a small city; its treasury revenue is seven thousand three hundred dinars. It belongs to the Fourth Clime; its longitude is reckoned from the Islands of the Blessed, and its latitude from the Equator. It now has a great fortress, pleasant governance, and a fine climate; its treasury revenue is ten thousand dinars. Wan Ta: it belongs to the Fourth Clime. It has a fortress, and the region has a main city; it is now well settled. It lies among the Fortunate Islands, at a latitude from the Equator; its air is exceedingly fine. Its waters are such that they attract people; they have fine orchards and fruits; the treasury revenue is fifty-three thousand dinars. Hayras: it is a fortress and a town at its foot; its produce consists of grain and fruits; its treasury revenue is seven thousand dinars. The ninth: dirhams and dinars of another kind are used there; it belongs to several climes, extending from there in various directions. It has winter and summer quarters, and its boundaries extend to the province of Dadam and Hormuz.

And Kurdistan and Arab Iraq are contiguous, and the city of Mosul is the seat of governance there. Its divan revenues were half assigned to the Atabegs; at the time of Baha al-Din Lu'lu', the amount was one thousand tumans, but now it is one hundred and ninety and a half tumans. Mosul belongs to the fourth climate. Its longitude from the Fortunate Isles is [such], and its latitude from the equatorial line is [such]. It lies on the bank of the Khabar river. It has two great bazaars and a thousand shops, and a congregational mosque, and monasteries and shrines without number, carved and cut in such a way that nowhere else has their like been cut from such fine timber. The noble custom was established by Baha al-Din Lu'lu'. Now most of it is in ruin. The divan revenues are three hundred and eight thousand dinars. It belongs to the fourth climate. Tall is a large city with a great citadel, and it yields grain and cotton and is prosperous. Its divan revenues are two thousand and seventy-five thousand dinars. It is from the district of Diyar Rabi'a and belongs to the fourth climate. It lies on the bank of the Euphrates river. It is a medium-sized city, and its divan revenues are twenty-two thousand dinars. It belongs to Diyar Rabi'a and the fourth climate, situated on the bank of the Euphrates. It is a medium-sized city, and its divan revenues are thirty thousand dinars. It is a medium-sized city; its produce includes grain and cotton, and its divan revenues are twenty-four thousand three hundred dinars. It is a small city. Its divan revenues are fifteen thousand dinars. It is a fine and pleasant town with good produce and grain; its divan revenues are thirteen thousand dinars. [Another place:] its revenues are two thousand dinars. It is a small city; its divan revenues are fourteen thousand dinars. It is a medium-sized city; from the fourth climate, its divan revenues [continue on next page].

Divan revenues:

Its revenue is twenty-one thousand dinars.
In the description of the climes, it says it is a small city in Balaghstan and the mountain region; its people engage in cultivation. It is from the fourth clime.
And Shir al-Arkan built the city of Bun Rakast, and from its environs there are about a hundred villages to be seen.
It has revenues and taxes; its revenue is twenty-one thousand dinars. From the fourth clime.
Its latitude from the south falls among the northern latitudes, and its breadth from the equatorial line rises in elevation.
Sam, son of Noah, peace be upon him, built the fortress of Jam Siy'a, one of the villages of Harran; a neighborhood was founded there.
The birth of the patriarch Abraham took place in that area, and the origin is that he sheltered in that village, and it is said that the Habaniyyan people were numerous there.
It was a flourishing city, and now it is ruined; its revenue is eighty-two thousand dinars. From the fourth clime, it is known as Qaba; it lies beyond and is surrounded by pastures.
Salasil was built. Its dinar value is far; it is of the fourth clime, its longitude from the south, its latitude from the equatorial line is fifty-six degrees and its size is considerable.
Its construction is fine, its territory is vast, and now it is prosperous; and now it is desired.
From the fourth clime, its longitude from the south and its breadth from the equatorial line — it was formerly called Tala Yaqus, as mentioned in the chronicle of the kings; it was a seat of prosperity.
The Caliph Ja'far appointed a governor there; it is situated on the bank of the Euphrates River, a noted city.
Its citadel was built of stone; it is two farsakhs in size; a thousand paces in length, and after it was put in order,
Nubayras Shabuy ibn Ja'far in that fortress engaged in cutting off the road, and the regions of Diyar Bakr, Syria, and Iraq were blocked on that account.
The Seljuk sultan Shah had Ibn Jumr seize it, and Shabuy along with his sons was taken captive and humiliated.
They took it by force, killed the people there who had felt safe, and from that time it has been called Quش.

In the account of vengeance it is recorded that this fortress is situated by the water, and among its qualities it is noted that during the reign of the Commander of the Faithful and the accursed Muawiya, it lay on the bank of the Euphrates, near that place up to the martyrs' shrine, where the martyrs of both sides met their end. From afar, the figures of the distinguished ones came into view, as if their bodies were still walking, and all could see them. And this is from the Fourth Clime; its latitude is from the equatorial line, and the message reached the kings, and in the description it is detailed how its people built dwellings and settled there, and others came and destroyed what they had built, and thus it has remained.
The Book of Kingdoms records that no one in the world has ever built so magnificent a structure, yet it fell to ruin.
Sawa is a city of the Fourth Clime, with a pleasant climate and fine air, its red soil is well-known, its fine plains and vessels are famous for their craft. Its population numbers six hundred thousand. Baghdad is distant from it, and it lies in the Fourth Clime. Its longitude and latitude are recorded, and it extends for thousands of parasangs in every direction. It is noted that it is well-founded and rich in gold. Its people and inhabitants live close together, house by house. It has many gardens with sumac, pistachio, fig, and pine trees in abundance. Its revenues amount to forty-seven thousand five hundred dinars.
Samarra was once a flourishing place at a location where five rivers met, at which point when the flood came and found a place and built it, and this was the first great settlement. After the flood, it was rebuilt, and now it lies in ruin.
Aqr is from the Fourth Clime, built by a king of ancient times, and it stands on an older site. Its water is plentiful but ill-smelling. Its government revenues are twenty-seven thousand four hundred dinars. Aniya is a notable city.

[Marginal note:] Mention

By the blessing of 'Imad al-Dawla, whose land has been made just and good, attributed to excellent words — it is abundant. It has revenues of the treasury; its districts number eight thousand man of dinars. It is recorded as Mutanaqish.
It belongs to the Fourth Clime. Talish: Inju ibn Khalid al-Lat, scholar, and its latitude from the equatorial line [is given]. Qara-Qisiya ibn Tahmu-rith, treasury revenues bound, attributed [to the region], Karhaliyyin — a city of blessed good fortune. The treasury revenues of its districts are twelve thousand man of dinars. It belongs to Rabi'a and is from the Fourth Clime.
Talish: Inju ibn Khalid al-Lat, its longitude and latitude from the equatorial line going further back. And Marw-Qal'a is in Bawsarasnik-Karbush; its description: it has fourteen rivers and two villages. There are several orchards and gardens in it known as Najan, and two ancient sites, bearing the name of Baghistan, watered by Radin-Rab, Abzanj. Those orchards are in the territories of Kahran; from there nearby water flows. It is about ten farsakhs in length. It produces kabuli figs, walnuts, figs, and manna; its most frequent produce is this. From that river, the treasury revenues of its districts are twenty-six, and its six cities run with water flowing through them, called Mina. Before this it was lush pastureland; now it has good open plains and fine forage. On one side is the river, and at Jaldawlan on the other side is the Qarat River; its treasury revenues are sixty-nine thousand and some dinars. It belongs to Sina Fa'ilna of the lands of Rabi'a.
It belongs to the Fourth Clime. Talish: Inju ibn Khalid al-Lat, its longitude and latitude from the equatorial line [goes to] 30. It is a fine city, of pleasant and joyful air, and its revenues in thousands — the treasury revenues of its districts are fourteen thousand dinars. It is of the lands of Rabi'a and of the Fourth Clime. From the clime of Musaybin: from Jawir Khalid al-Lat, its latitude from the equatorial line is two thousand six hundred. Half of its water is good; its air is fetid and its elevation is poor. The water of al-Kur is plain and its wine is bad, harmful, and injurious due to the foulness of the air. Overall, the best of all places up to Madyar is that of 'Afrab, the canal and the forest.

There is much in the Jami' al-Hikayat recorded about this: In our time before, those with the profession of Mansun and its like were engaged in it. In that city there remained none, and in the era of Sultan Salah al-Din Yusuf, when he remembered it, he would order service and the domains of the kings were seized, their heads were exposed and their professions sought, and the transfers to their quarters became void and fell null. On the bank of Datlaba it fell, and from there to Mashhad Yunus is six thousand steps. It is a city, and from that city to the shrine is one thousand steps.
That district is a province, its surroundings consisting of Mosandal and one hundred and fifteen [regions]. It is connected to the Arab territories and parts of Sarestan and Iraqi Ajam, and it borders Mayan, and many great [regions] are adjacent to it. Its governors: the noble men, Sulayman Shah Abo, the nobles of this age were there and now the population is one thousand five hundred [inhabitants], it is a notable town. Its waters and the yield of grain and fodder are abundant, its hunting grounds are plentiful, its meadows numerous.
It is a medium-sized city, a place of beauty and pleasant air, well-named. Its fortress is strong, situated on a riverbank with several gates, and there are villages around it.
It is a city whose fortress in the time of Sulayman was mentioned as a seat of royal power.
It is a medium-sized city, and now it has become a great and excellent place of repose.
It is a medium-sized city with a temperate climate, flowing waters in abundance.
Its air is pleasant and its people are among the fine folk of the region. It is a notable city.
Its climate is temperate and its waters are abundant; it is in the Fourth Clime, its longitude is such — God knows best — and its latitude is recorded. Its elevation is known, and Hankur lies within it.
There are Bakhtiyans and others in its localities. It is a medium-sized city with a temperate climate.
It is temperate, with abundant flowing waters and pleasant air.

The reed-beds of this Fourth Clime are in the mountain of Bisutun, built by order of Sultan Arghun Khan in a pleasant place of agreeable air, with abundant grain and crops. This Fourth Clime extends in longitude from the Eternal Lands, and in latitude from the equatorial line. There is a town called at first "Namwah" or "Kaftar," meaning a place of doves. Along the road of Madayin to the fire-temples, between the Amir and the Farsanlan, a monastery was built. The geographers say that it was called Istahrbad, and mention that it was covered with vines and planted with fields. It was long governed and ruled; Kermanshah was given another name and called by various titles. This is the Fourth Clime, its longitude measured from the Eternal Lands. Its latitude is from the equatorial line. The city was built by Lam ibn Shapur, son of Walakannaf, and Aban ibn Firuz of Farsansan renovated and repaired it, adding many fine structures. Anushirwan the Just built upon it great and lofty edifices and erected a hundred structures upon it. He held celebrations there and received the Faghfur of China, the Khagan of the Turks, the lords of India, and the Caesar of Rome. Istabos reduced the city to a medium size; now there remains the terrace of Shirin. Nearby are the districts of Khansar, Pirwin, and their surrounds. Some of these are fruitful, bearing fruit and various crops. The rest of the land between them was cultivated and filled with monasteries, various animals, and pastures. They settled there. Kirind is pleasant and stands on a height, suitable for lords. Another district, Khurramabad, has a temperate climate, suited to men and fish. It has many fields and gardens. Kangavar — called also Qasabat al-Musawwah — is such that its people are noted for their great strength, and they are numerous. They built great stones in Bisutun, such that, as is said, Kabulis numbering ten thousand...

There was another dam there, the like of which in stone does not exist. Munis al-Ustad among the stonecutters is a comprehensive master, possessing great skill and beauty — it is fitting and praiseworthy and is situated near the sea. It is located in a maritime position, independent, of Bidil ibn Bubral and Unaf Zari, of the utmost beauty. And what is among the mountains in that region and its surroundings, the fortresses of Taghir and Husayn are strongholds of great importance. The climate is moderate and the waters are flowing; Baytam is a good place to settle. In the lowland district of Shublin, the climate is moderate, the water is cool and fresh, and in Kukulkila — which Habistun surpasses in ranks and in the stairway of Ilshamir — is the Chapter on the Form of Ships of Goodness. In the two parts of the city it is of the utmost generosity; Sada Munis is a refuge for the Arabs, the people of Kirmanshah, Brahmanabad, and Fars, whose rights the Diwayish guards. The Caliph had settled, and for generations the land was inhabited. The city of Shushtar — pronounced "Qushgi" in the dialect of Shushtar — is of great importance. Its latitude and longitude are close to the equatorial line, and its climate is so. Its mint is fine and its goods are of good quality, and the city is known for its markets. The Ikhshidids came from all directions, and from Iran they came with force and gained sovereignty for a time. They acted justly and repaired the damage done among the peoples. The water of Shushtar is like sugar, and the plain is cultivated with fine settlements; the province of Shushtar is upon it — a great dam. The kings understood this wisdom and through it the water was channeled, and the dam was thus constructed. After the compilation of Masalik al-Mamalik, 'Adud al-Dawla al-Daylami built upon that river a structure greater than this one. Shapur Dhu al-Aktaf left endowments in Shushtar, and with wisdom and grace its name became renowned throughout the world.

Its air is extremely pleasant, and for the most part in summer two refreshing breezes blow through it. The city of Binazik, without any particular reason, one can sleep comfortably in, but its water is not pure — rather it is as though the masters of physic reported that water to be thick and unwholesome, and harmful to digest. In that region the heights are extremely elevated; there is no need to plant seed more than once, for it suffices for the fields. Grain and sugarcane and other crops grew well there, and water was perpetually available from those channels without cease. The people of that place are for the most part dark-complexioned and lean. They follow the Shaykhi sect, are sound in their beliefs, calm in temperament, and occupied with their own affairs. Among them there is little strife or meddling; they rarely aspire to high positions, and are content with their station, being little given to corruption or base desires. Every year the king Malikshah would come there in secret for hunting. A certain learned man compiled a work — a collection of twenty disciplines of knowledge — of which twelve are complete and the remaining eight are unfinished; and another fifteen disciplines, of which nine are complete and one thousand are recorded by name. Because of the extreme heat there, those who came from afar could not endure it, and every crop withered. They cannot turn the soil when the sun reaches its zenith, so the land revenues belong to the local people. The city has a fortress, and the governance of this clime is entrusted to it. Its longitude and latitude are reckoned from the established meridian. They built it and made the surrounding peoples subject to it, so that even the distant mountain dwellers came to submit. This region is green; its cities include Kubik, Karmar, and those along the coast of the sea, where fish are so plentiful that they are distributed by measure. From there came men of strong and powerful build, dark-complexioned and tall. The region abounds in citron, orange, lemon, fine dates and other produce...

It is so that it is the third clime; its longitude extends from a certain point, and its latitude falls within the established range. Shapur, Ardeshir, Bakan, and Shahn are among its towns, and Sha'yubur is among its regions. Its city is temperate in climate, the air is bad, water scarce, and fever and illness are common.

Huwayzah belongs to the third clime; its longitude is from the same base point, and its latitude is fixed. It lies in the direction of Sha'yubur, and its surrounding regions are flat. The city is moderate in climate, and hot, like the other cities of Khuzestan. Its characteristic is that most of its inhabitants have swollen bellies, and its mosquitoes are numerous and troublesome. Its longitude begins from a fixed point, and its latitude is the same as the third clime. Ardeshir and Bakan are on one side, and it was established at the edge of a plain, near forty-some farsangs from the city. Its bridge has five hundred paces in length, and its width is eight spans. Below it runs the river, and the city of Andimeshk is nearby. Those cities are counted among its towns, located on the eastern side, and carved out of rock. The city is built so that a stream of water flows through it. That city has many districts, mosques, and villages. In the meadows nearby there are fish of many varieties, eaten by the Turks. When the blossoms come, the flowers are plentiful and abundant, and the season is pleasant.

Sakina belongs to the third clime; likewise Sha'yubur, Ardeshir, Bakan, and the fortress of Kalain are under its rule. Its air is extremely hot and fetid. Its longitude begins from the base point of Khuzestan, and its latitude is fixed. Sha'yubur, Ardeshir, Bakan, and the surrounding regions share its characteristics. The city is moderate in size, the air is hot, and its general characteristics include slavery.

(Margin): Bulbiyah

And the servant and steward was Sabib, a city located in the middle of the third clime, of little beauty. It was built by Ibn Qanan ibn Anush ibn Shith ibn Adam, and it is among the first cities ever built. Khuzestan was adorned by Hushang who added to its cultivation and built a fortress over it such that its fortification was upon the plateau. Shapur of the wide horizons renewed its construction, and they called it after Shapur, and its layout was modeled in an established form. The tomb of the saints and the prophet's kin is there, on the western side of the city, and there is a lake whose waters are there, and the people there hold them in reverence. The people there do not welcome strangers. Askarmakum is in the third clime; it is Talish. Its dimensions are amenable and it lies toward the equator; its environs are wrapped in verdure. Shapur came to it and settled by the waterside, and two hills were placed there. At first it was called by the army's name, and the army of Talmubarsh came there and built it. The city of Chapay ibn Burk is there; it is a region that keeps to itself. That place is better, and as for the area of Hara, it has many estates. Tarak is a middle city and there the Nikraz are found, and it is more populous than others. It is one of the regions of Khuzestan and of great importance, first settled as Marfan, from the third clime. Its dimensions spread and its latitude extends toward the equator; Abrshir built it. The Jayhun river passes through it and runs along that region, and it is a famous middle city, and its gate-city is Karmeer, with twelve gates, and also Marshan Tiw Chapi.

As for Fars: the chronicle of Fars was written that the kingdom of Fars was the seat of the kings of Iran. It is well known that they, though ruling over all of Iran, were known as the family of Fars, and their power and might were such that most of the kings of half the world fell silent before them, for they were indeed the lords of this land.

This passage discusses the lands of Persia and its revenues. It begins by citing a prophetic saying: "We have chosen you as a garment and as the first of the elect," and refers to the Prophet's statement that the best of peoples after the Arabs are the Persians, for this reason people call them the noble ones.

In the chapter on the regions, it states that the Prophet called people to Islam, and the Muslim kings connected themselves to the kings of Persia, whose rule was both just and firm. They collected taxes and revenues according to law and ordinance, following the example set by the Commander of the Faithful, Umar, and the other caliphs — some taking one half, others one third, others one quarter, one fifth, or one tenth, according to the yield of the land.

It is related that the caliph had India yield more than one hundred thousand and sixty thousand dinars in revenues. Ali ibn Isa recorded that the caliph had the total sum reach sixty-three thousand men and resources. The revenues obtained from the special estates amounted to one unit per individual, and this was the standard. Their total came to eight hundred thousand, and at most times it did not fall below this. For military expeditions and maintaining armies, the amount reached five thousand thousand (five million), and now it is close to that figure.

The recorded revenue stands at eight hundred and seven dinars per tuman, plus one thousand two hundred dinars in cash.

In most provinces the revenue is collected, and the major cities serve as administrative centers. In the region of Fars, the province known as Khushak is mentioned specifically. The text then names the major districts of Fars: Ardashir Khurra, Istakhr, Shapur Khurra, and others — all of which were provinces and famous cities, as befits this account.

Boundaries [note in margin: حدود — "Boundaries/Limits"]

The boundary of this province joins the regions of Iraq, Khuzestan, Lorestan, Shabankareh, Kerman, and the rest of Fars. Its length is approximately one hundred and fifty parasangs, and its width likewise is about one hundred parasangs, so that its total area is some ten thousand parasangs, roughly speaking.

Kuhjan and Shir-Khurrah and Marvdasht — the founder of Kuhjan was Abu al-Qasim, and it is a well-known place. The first city that was built there is called Jiran, and in Persian it is known as Khayran. Ibn Darqubah, Mardashir, and Bakkan — Ja'far held this city before, and Ulay ibn Manu held it first.

Know that this is a region whose climate is temperate; it is a famous seat of Islam, and its length stretches to the meridian. Arjan — this region is bounded by the tropic, and the length of this latitude goes to the predecessors of the Shirazi line. Talha was its chief and its western zone is known. The name of the city in Fars was such, and its genealogy goes back to Ibn Masur ibn Sam ibn Nuh.

It was well established and, when Islam came, Muhammad ibn Yusuf — known as the Crystal of Hajjaj ibn Yusuf — built it. Then Muhammad ibn Qasim ibn Abi Aqil was placed in charge. He campaigned and raided, and the date was seventy-something of the Hijra, during the expedition of Talh. The blessing of God came upon his descendants and upon his children, and his army filled the city on all sides, numbering not less than twenty thousand dinars in revenue, but that prosperity has now passed and declined.

The villages of Khuzestan and Shiraz were revived by the administration of Daulat ibn Asad Allah ibn Pari, and he strove to repel the enemies and pushed them back, and the date of this was sometime in the interval, and no path was left open. King Sharaf al-Din Mahmud Shah launched a campaign against them and subdued them, and then settled there and achieved great success.

In order to protect it, this city has seventeen quarters, including the ports of Musawwir, Ilk, Musa, Baysa, Kadh, Bub, and Salm. Its wealth and prosperity are famous, and its fine qualities are well known. Now its customs and manners are pleasing, and its people are moderate in their ways and continuously occupied with their affairs. Most of the time there are markets and gatherings, and the city lacks nothing of its pleasures and amenities. The best of its inhabitants work with devotion; the people of the city include the disciples of Saad, who are renowned, and every expression of learning flourishes there. In spring, the floods come and the city appears in its finest splendor. The costs there are low and the expenses reasonable, yet sometimes provisions may be scarce. The city's atmosphere is pleasant and agreeable, and its people are of the Hanafi and Shia sects. The learned are many, and the traces of the prophets are preserved there. The people say that they are upright and truthful, and that they are honest.

[In red:] BAYIT — They are upright and truthful, and they adhere to sound religion.

Strangers are welcomed and treated generously. The people are content and occupied with proper trades. Most of the inhabitants there are foreigners, and the majority of the people live in houses. In matters of eloquence and learning they hold a high rank. It is said that whoever comes to this city with sincere intention and settles there finds it a worthy abode. But now, due to greed and worldly desire, those who settle there are drawn to the fire of worldly temptation.

Jamr ibn Layth built it for the religion of the noble and the pulpit, and it was completed at Ghara with acceptance, and the Friday mosque — Atabeg ibn Sa'd ibn Zangi ibn Salghur built it, and the mosque of Sunqur in the pavilion of Tamal. Atabeg Sunquri constructed it, and Salghur provided for its endowment, and the House of Healing by the grace of God — the Daylamis and others built guest houses, hospices, schools, mosques, and charitable gates which that abode constructed. Also, as for the prophets, in this regard of those two it is said that the dead are revived and brought to rest. But most of it is consumed by those who exploit the weak and the common people, and its revenues go to those who merely consume. In that place there are blessed shrines such as those of Imams, Ahmad ibn Musa al-Kazim, and others; Abu Abd Allah, whom the Atabegs of the Zangi Salghuri dynasty plundered, but the people defended and the Sheikh Baha al-Lul restored, and Baba Kuhi the Sheikh, and the two Bahans, Sa'di, and Sheikh Hasan Kiya, Muhajirun, Rukn al-Din, al-Kufi, and their like, are many. Most of the schools, hospices, mosques, and tombs of Khwaja Abu are within the city, and scattered about are religious endowments. At present four hundred and fifty thousand dinars of Ottoman coin are held there, and it is most likely that all of Fars draws revenues from there. That city is the main center, and in its surrounding districts there are places where the people are fed abundantly, and the water channels and the air are like those of Shiraz, with wholesome grain and fruits of all kinds. The district of Bayda is a fine region; several villages border it and Arabs settle there; the air and water are pleasant and healthy, and some attribute to it special qualities and characteristics. Besides grain, little else grows there. Several districts are mentioned; wild donkeys are found there, and across that territory there is no major city, and its produce is nothing other than grain.

Tuj was in ancient times a famous and great city, protected and watered by flowing streams. Now it is ruined. Hanabi is a city of moderate climate situated in the middle region. Around it the air is temperate; within it there grows the finest produce, and its climate is pleasant. Its water is wholesome, its fruits are both warm-region and cool-region varieties. It has a strong fortress, is well populated and prosperous, and produces abundant fruits. Hayfan is a village below Gumast; the word refers to those places that are well-watered and fertile. The land is full of narrow passes and rugged mountains with hard rocks and dense forest. The temperature there is moderate, and the people of that place are mountain-dwellers by nature. Their water comes from mountain streams and flows down the slopes. Its produce is grain and cotton in abundance. Hayba is a district entirely of warm climate; it has several villages and its chief carries arms. Fadawlan consists of several districts all of warm climate, and some of them are mountainous. Its climate is moderate and it produces cotton and various crops. Sirab was in ancient times a flourishing city, full of resources and a crossing point for travelers, both cold and working ground. Its climate there is extremely hot and its water comes from springs. Sarhistān and Kur — the climate is good and wholesome. It is of warm character; its air and water are quite contrary to each other, and it contains many pleasant gardens. Hamakān Hila is a place that had its own city. In the middle of that region there is a city called Afshar, and around it and before it one sees spread out settlements. The upper part is cool mountainous country, and in Bakhtagan there are dated palms and similar things.

Come, from the districts and environs of this realm of Karan and Labua-shtal, there is abundant provision to be gained, exceedingly so. For in summer the plains are settled and numerous streams flow, with running water and irrigation channels maintained throughout. Grain grew abundantly, and from the valleys and ravines nothing was wanting; and in the highlands it spread out so that throughout the winter the mountains were covered with rainwater, and in summer the trees and fresh herbs were clothed in greenery. Most of the inhabitants of that province are footmen and horsemen; strangers and passersby rest in those places. But because of sin and transgression, many heads were brought there and troubles arose.

Kuwam is a city that is pleasant, and its environs and climate are exceptionally fine and its air agreeable. In that place, from the month of Isfand onward, water comes up and rises from the ground. In the surrounding villages, crops, fruit, and millet are cultivated, and most of the local merchants bring many walnuts, pistachios, and almonds from there — there are plentiful figs and other produce. The author of Farsnamah says the people there are agreeable in character and follow the Shafi'i school of law. The region of Amr and Ku-Miyan has a fine climate with good air. There is grain and millet in abundance, and foodstuffs are plentiful.

The town of Suq Farhanak is nearby, with its own villages and districts, but little is produced there besides grain. If in the month of Azar or Dey the harvest happens to be early autumn, one can sell a thousand mans there; but if those two months pass without finding buyers, one may not sell at all, and the produce goes to waste. When the warm season comes, rice is planted there, and half the people depend on it. The region also has Semnak; it is a mountainous area with a fine climate producing grain, fruit, dates, grapes, and all kinds of other fruit in abundance. Most of its people live in the countryside as herdsmen, farmers, and the like.
